(111) Chaupai: As the Divine Guru acceded to the Singhs plea, Delighted did their souls feel at the Guru's grace. Once again did Gurbakhsh Singh's soul ask the Guru, How could the (sovereign) Khalsa follow his command? (112) Thereupon, the Divine Guru expressed His divine Grace, Saying the Guru had invested Gurbakhsh Singh with His powers. The Khalsa upon whom the Guru had conferred sovereignty, Would Gurbakhsh Singh be the supreme sovereign among them. (113) The whole Khalsa Panth would abide by his command, Vanquished he be whosoever dared to fight against him. (114)*° Most-heart moving of all is the sacrifice and martyrdom of Subeg Singh Jambar and his infant son. Even though he had been in the service of the Nawab and had mediated many a time between the Nawab and the Khalsa Panth, yet he was coerced to convert to Islam or face even after accepting Islam he was destined to die one day at last: Great was the Nawab, greater still was his faith in Islam, Great must be his sense of justice, he being a legal expert. Should he (Subeg Singh) convert to Islam for fear of death, Would he never die after his conversion to Islam? (10) If death is imminent even after getting converted, Why should he give up his own religion in this life? Sham Singh had the distinction of collecting a ransom of seven lakh rupees from the powerful jat ruler of Bharatpur just for honouring the jat ruler with an embrace symbolic of jat's allegiance with the Khalsa Panth. He distributed this amount among the ten Sikh Misls in proportion to their respective strength. In fact, S. Sham Singh and Nawab Kapoor Singh formed the twin pillars of Khalsa Panth under whose joint command the ten Sikh Misls functioned and carried on the struggle for achieving complete Sikh sovereignty. Rattan Singh Bhangoo brings out the glorious achievements of these ten Sikh Misls through the epic simile of Lord Krishna and his ten Yadava contingents over the evil Jamankal from the Hindu mythology. Dohra: As there were ten Misls of the Yadav clan, So there were ten Misls in the Khalsa Panth. As Lord Krishna commanded the ten Yadav Misls, The tenth Sikh Guru directed the Khalsa Misls. As all the Muslim rulers were annihilated by the Khalsa, The Khalsa Panth shouted slogans of Guru's victory. He is portrayed as an epitome of Khalsa grit and dare devilry. S. Charat Singh's mettle as a Sikh warrior with a superhuman skill and bravery comes to the fore during the most fierce battle between Khalsa forces and those of Ahmad Shah Abdali that took place around the villages of Kup and Poheer near Malerkotla. This battle is also known as the greatest massacre or Wada Ghallughara in Sikh history. S. Charat Singh is the hero of this unequal battle between the Sikhs and the Mughals. While both these are facts of history, much of the mythological baggage with which the epic writer has loaded these two incidences does not appeal to the sensibility of a modern reader. In the second incident, Bhangoo's version differs from the centuries-old Sikh belief, and perhaps historical records as well, when he states that the two younger Sahibzadas were beheaded instantly by a butcher with a sickle inside Wazir Khan's court after they refused to covert to Islam. It was many years after their execution that a platform was raised with the Nawab's permission at state expense on the advice of his Muslim clerics to rid the Nawab of several bodily ailments, which in their opinion, were a consequence of his sinful act of killing Guru's two innocent sons. This version runs counter the age-old belief that the younger Sahibzadas were bricked alive and finally beheaded. In Babur's case, Bhangoo depicts Guru Nanak blessing Babur and his dynasty to rule for seven generations by putting seven handfuls of connabis leaves in Babur's lap indicating that his dynastic rule at the end of his seven generations will be uprooted by the followers of Guru Nanak at the cost of great sacrifices, because Babur's descendents would have turned tyrants and oppressors like his predecessors the Lodhis. Although, it is historically true that the Mughals ruled effectively for seven generations, but the myth of Guru Nanak's blessings on Babur and sending the latter to heavens riding on Guru Nanak's wooden staff and showing him the highly subordinate position of prophet Mohammad among the hierarchy of world's prophets in the Divine Court and Guru Nanak's splendid position and closest proximity with the Divine seem more to be flights of his poetic fancy rather than incidents based on hard historical facts. Nevertheless, these two myths also highlight the sanctity of Sahibzada's sacrifice and Guru Nanak's divinity which fit into the overall design and scheme of this epic, though the excessive exaggeration and their mythological dimension somewhat blunts the modern readers sensibility. On the whole, his liberal use of mythology, especially of the Hindu mythology, has been very successfully and skillfully employed as has already been pointed in the introduction to the first volume of the translated version of this epic. The Hindu myths about Nehkalank Bhassmantar, Kaljaman, have been used so dexterously to emphasize the authenticity and inevitability of Sikh Sovereignty having a divine sanction that their use places Rattan Singh Bhangoo among some of the best modern Western and Eastern poets who have used myths from the ancient Greek and Hindu fertility cults to bring about the decadent aspects of their contemporary cultures and civilizations. As we analyse this aspect of Bhangoo's epic, he seems to be a man of vast erudition and scholarship, his doggerel colloquial verse covering the bulk of his epic notwithstanding. Taking into account his repeated references to appropriate hymns from the Adi Granth, Ramayan, Mahaabharata, Tantric Lore Chandi Astotar and Zafarnamah, it appears he was quite conversant with the ancient Indian classics and common beliefs and opinions of his contemporary society, though bulk of his information came through oral and traditional resources. To conclude in the words of Dr J.S. Grewal, There is some hearsay, which the author (himself) points out and there is much graphic detail which could come ultimately from first hand observation. Not only actions, but also sentiments, beliefs, ideas and emotions come into play to make the Prachin Panth Prakash arare kind of document. It embodies an understanding of the Khalsa tradition by a respectable member of the Khalsa who was deeply religious in his feelings and acutely political in his outlook on the world. This, in itself, is a telling comment on the Khalsa of his times and of the days of his ancestors. pages.searchText: Apart from being a social chronicle of the contemporary times and an epic projecting a vision Apart from being a social chronicle of the contemporary times and an epic projecting a vision of Khalsa's sovereignty and its inevitable realization due to Sikh Guru's prophetic sanction together with the portrayal of legendary Sikh warriors and martyrs, this work contains rare insights amounting to value judgements. For instance, in the first part, its author had dwelt from both Hinduism and Islam and the need to sacrifice one's progeny, if need be, to uphold One can not preserve and promote one's own ideology. Much as an agricultural piece of land over grown with weeds, Cannot give a wholesome yield of grains. (10) In the second part of this epic Bhangoo, being a direct descendent of those Sikh warriors who belonged to the Tat Khalsa (Majhail) faction of the Khalsa force, after the latter's rift with Banda Bahadur faction, has been found to be somewhat biased by some readers in favour of the faction consisting of warriors from his own stock. His deriding and debunking of Banda Bahadur, just before his defeat and death after his extreme glorification bordering almost on deification earlier, seems to confirm this impression. However, Bhangoo's catholicity of vision and impartial outlook towards personages and events comes out here as well. In a few lines of rare insight and a philosophical observation, he looks up on the miserable plight of the Tat Khalsa Singhs as a consequence of their betrayal and desertion of Banda Bahadur and his companions who were being held under seige by the Mughals at Gurdas Nangal. This reflection makes Bhangoo, not only an impartial observer of the two warring factions but also a poet with a deep analytical mind who was capable of making an indepth study of the strengths and weaknesses of the contemporary Khalsa Panth organization and presenting a balanced opinion on the whole situation. While SGPC approved version edited by Dr. Jeet Singh Seetal has given only two lines about this observation and deleted the rest of the four lines, Dr Balwant Singh Dhillon's edited version (Singh Brothers 2004) has retained the complete text of this observation. SGPC version reads: Sortha: Banda Singh had let out a curse on the Khalsa Panth, When he had to confine himself in the fort (at Gurdas Nangal). The Khalsa Panth had to bear the conseguences of their sinful act, Of not reaching out to the support of Banda Singh. (5)5 Dr B.S. Dhillon's version, however, carries the full text of this observation in continu- ation with above-mentioned lines which reads as follows: Dohra: Thereafter the scatterd Singhs hid themselves in the wilds, As in whatever little strength had they been left behind. In the editorial written in Punjabi by Giani Gurdit Singh the Prachin Panth Prakash issue of Singh Sabha Patrika, he states, S. Rattan Singh was an educated aristocrat. He could read and analyse epics written in Persian. He also had a knack for composing poetry. Above all, whereas his family lineage belongs to family of the martyrs of village Mirankot, his educational background is linked to the poet Sainapat, a court poet of Guru Gobind Singh. Rattan Singh Bhangoo himself has referred to this link in one of his other compositions. Dhillon (Singh Brothers, Amritsar 2004), SGPP, Episode 82.2, p. 198) All these insights and observations reflect Bhangoo's vision matching that of a great epic writer, and reflect his sound knowledge of Sikh history, his erudition and scholarship and his profound thinking. He could read and analyse epics written in Persian. He also had a knack for composing poetry. Above all, whereas his family lineage belongs to family of the martyrs of village Mirankot, his educational background is linked to the poet Sainapat, a court poet of Guru Gobind Singh. Rattan Singh Bhangoo himself has referred to this link in one of his other compositions. [Translation mine) Giani Gurdit has come across the manuscript of another composition written by Rattan Singh Bhanoo which is known as Hanuman Natak. In the preamble to this dramatic verse, Bhangoo has stated his educational background. Translated into English this introductory verse reads as follows: Dohra: Praise be to Sri Guru Gobind Singh Who is worthy of great name and fame. Fifty two poets had he kept in his court, Who remained immersed in the nectar (or Knowledge). (13) In this sacred pool of nectar full of knowledge, Did they daily immerse themselves at its nine steps. Among them was included (the poet) Sainapat, Who hailed from a Jat stock from Majha. (14) Amanuensis had he been to the (tenth) Guru, And a composer of innumerable melodies. Initiated was he by administering Khandey-ki-Pahul, As he endeared himself to the Divine Guru. (15)

pages.snippet: Kulwant Singh closes the translator’s prefatory material by thanking the scholars and helpers who supported the English rendering of Sri Gur Panth Prakash. The note records that both volumes now make the complete work available to English-reading students of S
pages.searchText: Translator’s Closing Note and References Kulwant Singh closes the translator’s prefatory material by thanking the scholars and helpers who supported the English rendering of Sri Gur Panth Prakash. The note records that both volumes now make the complete work available to English-reading students of Sikh history, while inviting corrections and observations for a future edition. The page then begins a references note identifying the Kulwant Singh translation of Sri Gur Panth Prakash, Volumes I and II, as the source for the quoted Punjabi and English text. XXXVi for providing him with the sponsorship for undertaking this work. For consistent discussion, explanation and exposition of several references in the body of this work, I remain indebted to the scholarly guidance of Dr Kharak Singh. Thanks are also due to Bhai Ashok Singh Bagrian and Dr Kirpal Singh for their inspiring support. Mr. Ramesh Kumar, who typed the entire manuscript, did all the type setting and compilation of the whole book in Punjabi, English and Roman script, deserves my grateful thanks. With the completion of this second volume the complete Sri Gur Panth Prakash has been translated into English. Any suggestions, amendments and relevant observations will be welcomed for incorporation in the second edition of one of the primary sources of Sikh history. I hope this humble endeavour will meet the long-felt need of Sri Gur Panth Prakash English knowing readers interested in the subject. S.A.S. pages.searchText: The Sangat Seeks a Written Assurance for the Panth The sangat receives the Granth's answer as a victorious and consoling command. Drums of joy are imagined, and the congregation turns from relief to responsibility by asking how the Khalsa is to endure and expand in the world. The damaged lines are best read as a collective prayer for the future of the community. The Singhs ask for a written assurance for the Panth so that those who try to diminish it will fail while the Guru's design remains protected. The page closes in the tone of ardās rather than argument. It presents the Panth as something sustained not by worldly cunning but by the Guru's foreknowledge, shelter, and explicit promise. It says that the power which inflicted so much suffering on the Khalsa would not stand, and that Punjab would come into the hands of the Singhs after this season of trial. The page then turns to scriptural reinforcement, drawing on saint-centered wisdom to argue that those who attack the holy ultimately lose all refuge. In that frame, the enemies of the Panth are not merely political rivals but offenders against a divine order already moving toward judgment. Even in fragmentary OCR, the movement is clear: hardship is temporary, while the Guru's community is being prepared for visible ascendancy. pages.title: Guru Succession and Nadir's Question About the Sikhs
pages.snippet: A listener asks for an account of the line of Gurus after Guru Nanak, and the reply moves briskly through the succession from Guru Angad onward. The summary highlights the transmission of spiritual authority, the miri-piri ideal, martyrdom, and the culmination
pages.searchText: Guru Succession and Nadir's Question About the Sikhs A listener asks for an account of the line of Gurus after Guru Nanak, and the reply moves briskly through the succession from Guru Angad onward. The summary highlights the transmission of spiritual authority, the miri-piri ideal, martyrdom, and the culmination of sovereignty in the Guru's final shaping of the Khalsa. This condensed rehearsal of Sikh history is not ornamental. It explains why the Panth acts with such independence: its political courage is presented as the outcome of a sacred lineage rather than a sudden rebellion. By the end of the page the narrative pivots back to imperial bewilderment. Nadir Khan asks who these raiders are, so the historical survey becomes the setup for the coming description of Sikh character and warfare. pages.title: Why the Khalsa Cannot Be Subdued
pages.snippet: The answer to Nadir's inquiry describes the Sikhs as a people who live lightly, move constantly, and refuse the comforts by which ordinary armies are tamed. They sleep with weapons near them, endure hunger without complaint, and treat hardship as part of their
pages.searchText: Why the Khalsa Cannot Be Subdued The answer to Nadir's inquiry describes the Sikhs as a people who live lightly, move constantly, and refuse the comforts by which ordinary armies are tamed. They sleep with weapons near them, endure hunger without complaint, and treat hardship as part of their discipline rather than as a cause for surrender. The page insists that persecution has trained the Khalsa into unusual cohesion: where one Sikh appears, many more seem ready to rise. Its argument climaxes in the claim that people sheltered by such a Lord cannot be defeated, because their courage is understood as a gift of divine protection rather than mere stubbornness. That logic also turns history into proof. pages.searchText: The Khalsa Rejects Nawabi and Claims Patishahi The Singhs answer worldly offers with a sharper doctrine of sovereignty. They say the Guru had already granted them patishahi, so a subordinate nawabi is too small a thing to desire or accept. From there the page imagines royal authority as something carried by the Panth itself. Wherever the Khalsa gathers in fidelity, a throne may be raised, because the Satguru's promise is portable and does not depend on the sanction of a court. The rhetoric binds political confidence to revelation. The Guru's word does not fail, and so the Khalsa treats power not as borrowed favor but as a trust already lodged within its collective discipline. pages.searchText: Khalsa Authority Compared to Guru Nanak Establishing Angad This page makes the transfer of authority visible through insignia and dress. The damaged lines describe the plume and garments being bestowed in a scene explicitly compared to Guru Nanak establishing Angad, so the Panth's honor is shown as a continuation of the Guru lineage rather than a break from it. The page also stresses that the trust has been handed over to the Khalsa as a body. Counsel, prayer, companionship, and discipline are presented as the proper means by which that authority is exercised and preserved. Its closing movement turns toward martyr resolve. The one who has received the Guru's charge must be ready to give his head without betraying the Panth, because delegated sovereignty is inseparable from sacrificial responsibility. xlii Sri Gur Panth Prakash ag 39 ffu of soul | gg aoa TH Make fea || kalgî gur sir daî lagâi. daî pushâk apnî pahirâi. guri taur singh rakkhi bahâyô. gur nânak jim angad tikâyô.9. It gathers quoted verses where Sikh speakers reject dying in flight, remember sacrifice for the Panth, and praise those who gave their heads or families for Sikhi. The quoted examples honor Bhai Mani Singh, Bhai Dyal Singh, Subeg Singh, and Subeg Singh’s son as martyrs who kept faith under torture. pages.searchText: Bhai Mani Singh as the Model Sikh and Teacher The fragment becomes a sustained praise-portrait of Bhai Mani Singh as the model Sikh. He is remembered as disciplined, learned, devout, and steady in judgment, with saintliness and organizational authority held together in one figure. The page emphasizes that his excellence is not private holiness alone. He strengthens the Panth by teaching Sikhi widely, recounting sacred history, guiding conduct, and giving ordinary Sikhs a living image of fidelity joined to intellect. In that sense Bhai Mani Singh stands here as a standard for communal leadership. pages.title: Martyr Fidelity and the Ideal Nihang
pages.snippet: The page continues a martyrdom-inflected dialogue about the head, uncut hair, and the refusal to yield Sikh identity under coercion. It treats bodily suffering as secondary to keeping faith, so outward signs become part of an inward covenant rather than mere c
pages.searchText: Martyr Fidelity and the Ideal Nihang The page continues a martyrdom-inflected dialogue about the head, uncut hair, and the refusal to yield Sikh identity under coercion. It treats bodily suffering as secondary to keeping faith, so outward signs become part of an inward covenant rather than mere custom. From that debate the text broadens into a warrior ideal, praising the ideal nihang as fearless in battle and first to step forward wherever the Panth is endangered. Courage, austerity, and readiness for sudden combat are all folded into the same religious temperament. The effect is to join martyrdom and militancy instead of separating them. The Sikh warrior is admirable not because he loves violence, but because he has already accepted loss and therefore cannot be frightened away from duty. pages.title: Martyrdom, Satnam, and the Unity of Guru and Sikh
pages.snippet: This page develops a theology of witness by insisting that Guru and Sikh cannot be separated. Martyrs accept the Guru's word as life itself, so their steadfastness is presented as proof that Panthic courage comes from grace and not from empty bravado. The frag
pages.searchText: Martyrdom, Satnam, and the Unity of Guru and Sikh This page develops a theology of witness by insisting that Guru and Sikh cannot be separated. Martyrs accept the Guru's word as life itself, so their steadfastness is presented as proof that Panthic courage comes from grace and not from empty bravado. The fragment then shifts into confrontation with political authority. Demands for submission or conversion are answered with calm refusal, because the Khalsa understands its true command as already received from the Guru. In the final movement, even a child is imagined answering the challenge with Sikh certainty. The genuine kalma here is rendered through Satnam and Vahiguru, making verbal confession itself an act of unbroken allegiance. xlvi dôhrâ gut chaupaî: 31 32 Ibid. pages.searchText: Introduction Notes: Khalsa Authority and Kapoor Singh This damaged front-matter note preserves quoted evidence, not a direct page of narrative. Its first quotation describes a power that had devastated Delhi and names Nadir or Ahmad Shah as enemies, but says the Khalsa forced Ahmad Shah’s side to flee. The second quotation turns to Kapoor Singh. It shows him humbly serving the Singhs, then records an Akal command received by the Panth to honor him with a robe of honor because his service had reached the proper station. The fragment closes with another citation from Episode 90 about arranging five camps or standards and bringing Nishan flags from Sri Akal Bunga, so the page should read as a source-note cluster about Khalsa authority and recognition. pages.title: Early Martyrs and Ahmad Shah's Search for the Sikh Raiders
pages.snippet: The page first honors a lineage of five early martyrs and nihangs whose memory frames the Khalsa as a community already tested by sacrifice. That commemorative tone matters because it turns the narrative from names of the dead toward the living reputation thei
pages.searchText: Early Martyrs and Ahmad Shah's Search for the Sikh Raiders The page first honors a lineage of five early martyrs and nihangs whose memory frames the Khalsa as a community already tested by sacrifice. That commemorative tone matters because it turns the narrative from names of the dead toward the living reputation their courage created. From there the focus shifts to the enemy court, where Ahmad Shah asks who plundered him and why his forces cannot catch the raiders. The answer presents the Singhs as austere fighters who have no fixed territory, move lightly, and refuse the settled habits that imperial power knows how to punish. In effect, the page lets even the adversary testify to Sikh resilience. pages.title: Epic Praise of the Panth and the Rise of Charhat Singh
pages.snippet: The Panth is praised in epic language that compares the Sikhs to the Yadavas and treats Guru-guided struggle as the power that breaks the Giljis and humbles arrogant Turks. The page uses that elevated frame to argue that Sikh victories belong to a sacred histo
pages.searchText: Epic Praise of the Panth and the Rise of Charhat Singh The Panth is praised in epic language that compares the Sikhs to the Yadavas and treats Guru-guided struggle as the power that breaks the Giljis and humbles arrogant Turks. The page uses that elevated frame to argue that Sikh victories belong to a sacred historical pattern rather than to chance alone. It then narrows from the collective to a single rising leader, celebrating Charhat Singh for the wounds and hardships he has already endured in battle. His renown grows precisely because his body shows the cost of struggle instead of the comfort of easy command. By the end, admirers speak blessings that he would become sovereign over a wide dominion. The page therefore works as both praise-poetry for the Panth and a political anointing of Charhat Singh's future stature. pages.searchText: Episode About Chandialias, Jandialas, and Those Who Harmed the Guru and the Panth Chandialias, Jandialas And those who harmed This page opens a denunciatory episode about Chandialias, Jandialas, and others remembered as enemies of the Guru and the Panth. The tone is moral from the start, presenting these figures as examples of how treachery can arise even around sacred institutions. The first concrete case is a poor man who comes to the Guru's langar, eats there, and serves there, yet fails to absorb the discipline and gratitude that should have followed such grace. The poor man comes to the Guru's langar in need, but the page insists that receiving food and favor is not the same thing as inward transformation. As a result, the episode begins by contrasting outward proximity with inward failure. What should have become loyalty instead becomes the groundwork for later corruption and hostility. to. Those who tried to eclipse the Gurus and harm the Sikh Panth, And who had been slandering and vilifying the devout Sikhs. (1) Of those whom the (great) Guru gave his blessings gratis, And those who failed to assimilate and imbibe Guru's message. Of those who wished to destroy the very same source, From which they had sprung up (and got sustenance). (2) Let me, first of all, narrate how he originated, Thereafter, I would reveal his (evil) thoughts and deeds. A Ghanag? Jat (by caste), a Sultani (by faith), a resident of Jandiala was he, Who lived a life of extreme deprivation and raggedness. (3) He came to know that the Guru ran a free community kitchen, Where people flocked and ate food to their hearts content. Irrespective of the fact whether one rendered any service or not, There was no dearth of any provisions and eatables there. (4) Hearing this, proceeded he to the Guru's abode there, And joined the (dedicated) band of Guru's cooks and kitchen crew. There, he kneaded flour and kept the kitchen fires burning. And had had his fill as many times as he wished to eat. (5) But he could not exorcise the ghosts of his Sultani past from his mind, Nor could he thoroughly imbibe the Sikh spirit in his character. Mind is cleansed of dross only after the Sikh spirit is embedded in it, As rigorously as rust deposited on a sword is rubbed with a chisel file. (6) But having departed from his homestead at an auspicious moment, Having been blessed with all the boons with Guru's (single) glance, This rustic Hindal Jat could not contain the Guru's benediction. pages.searchText: Hindal’s Reverent Bow in the Langar Chandialias, Jandialas And those who harmed One day Guru Amar Das went from his seat to the langar. As Sikhs bowed at the Guru’s feet, Hindal also hurried forward, but his hands were covered with wheat flour from kitchen service. Afraid of soiling the Guru’s feet, Hindal folded his hands behind his back and bowed with his head instead. The Guru recognized the care in his heart, looked on him with kindness, and blessed him for that small act of thoughtfulness. The page then turns into the next shocking episode by warning that a freely given blessing can be kept only by a deep and worthy vessel. (11) Episode 83 An Episode that is shocking Dohra: Guru's blessings received gratuitously (are difficult to contain), As people with a serious and profound disposition alone can preserve. It is as if the milk of a lioness can not be preserved, In a bowl of any base metal except that of (pure) gold. (1) Chaupai: The Guru, having awarded the custody of a congregation (to the Hindal Jat), Fixed its jurisdiction over a radius of twenty to thirty villages. Directing him to ask the devout to bow down before him as they did before the Guru, The Guru asked him to continue to visit the Guru as before. (2) Warning him against the temptation of declaring himself a Guru, Lest he should be ostracized from the Sikh Panth. The Guru, impressed by his (rare) gesture of thoughtfulness, Caste a benevolent glance on him considering his devotion. (10) Responding benevolently to such a thoughtful gesture, The Divine Guru showered his blessings on this Hindal Jat. (Thus), such a small (sensible) gesture brought so many rewards, That he became worthy of Guru's grace gratuitously. (11) Such gratuitous rewards may, fall to anyone's lot, But noble human vessels alone can preserve such rewards. A pitcher made of unbaked clay can never hold water, Whatever strategies one may adopt for its preservation. (12) Episode 83 An Episode that is shocking (Becoming a Niranjania, he eclipsed Sikhism) Dohra: Guru's blessings received gratuitously (are difficult to contain), As people with a serious and profound disposition alone can preserve. It is as if the milk of a lioness can not be preserved, In a bowl of any base metal except that of (pure) gold. (1) Chaupai: The Guru, having awarded the custody of a congregation (to the Hindal Jat), Fixed its jurisdiction over a radius of twenty to thirty villages. Directing him to ask the devout to bow down before him as they did before the Guru, The Guru asked him to continue to visit the Guru as before. (2) Warning him against the temptation of declaring himself a Guru, Lest he should be ostracized from the Sikh Panth.

pages.searchText: Episode 83 — Hindal Squanders the Guru's Grace The Guru's Cause and the Sikh Panth And those Given to Debauchery and Irascibility The episode turns from remembered grace to remembered failure. He could not maintain and preserve the Guru's rare gift, so the blessing that should have deepened humility instead feeds imitation, vanity, and spiritual ambition. The page condemns Hindal for copying the Guru's institutions while draining them of obedience. He builds rival structures, cultivates followers around himself, and begins to treat borrowed sanctity as if it were his own inheritance. What began as proximity to the Guru is therefore rewritten as a cautionary tale. False assertions about living sainthood and fabricated lineage are presented as signs that ambition has overtaken reverence. The corruption does not stop with one man. Empathising and sympathesing with the Muslims, They shared their meals with the Sultanis as well. (21) Who was instrumental in getting many Sikhs eliminated. Being wicked, he conspired and spoke ill of (the Sikhs), As he had developed cordial relations with the Mughals. But if a Sikh approached them (considering them as Guru's Sikhs), He would catch hold of him and eliminate him. (23) (Or else) he would handover the Sikhs to the Mughals at Lahore, And received the rewards in return for their arrest. Providing information, he would get the Sikhs arrested from their villages, As he kept a large battery of Mughal troops with him. (24) Which made my father and grandfather desert their home. They were responsible for the genocide of the Sikhs near Malerkotla, In which twenty to thirty thousand Sikhs lost their lives. After the Khalsa forces routed and packed Ahmed Shah Abdali, These two (wicked) Hindals patched up with the Sikhs. pages.searchText: Episode 83 Ends; Episode 84 Begins — From Sharan Dass to Tara Singh The Guru's Cause and the Sikh Panth And those Given to Debauchery and Irascibility The page closes the corrupt line by describing Sharan Dass and related figures as morally rotten, exploitative, and unworthy of continuation. The denunciation is final in tone, as if the text means to sever the reader completely from that lineage of fabrication and abuse. Then the narrative deliberately turns toward a better exemplar. Listen to the episode of Tara Singh marks the hinge, introducing a Singh whose courage and discipline will answer the decay just condemned. (6) Refusing to budge from his earlier violent behaviour, He kept indulging in acts of violence and rioting. Picking up a fight even for the stranger's cause, He kept on commanding a small battery of violent fighters. (7) Whosoever approached him with any kind of complaint, He kept on indulging in violent acts compulsively. (8) He would get himself involved unnecessarily into it. Having become such a compulsive addict to violence, He refused to abide by the Mughal's sovereign writ. (9) He boasted that he would never desist from fight, Since fighting was systemically built in the Khalsa's body. pages.searchText: Tara Singh retorted that the two Singhs were not thieves at all, An Episode that is Shocking Tara Singh retorted that the two Singhs were not thieves at all, They had rather done justice by stealing his horses, And he cared a fig for the Nawab at Lahore. (21) Tara Singh declared that he had made a resolution, That he would sacrifice his life while fighting the Mughals. That he would never seek any refuge to save his life, And shed his mortal frame after killing so many others. (22) Thus, a little incident flared up into a conflagration, As it proved to be an inauspicious moment for the Singhs, The Jat chief went and complained to the authorities at Patti, That they were living safely in the safety of their houses. (23) He informed that since the Singhs were making collections forcibly, The people could pay their revenue to only one authority. The ruler of Patti felt so outraged at the insinuation, As if a sleeping lion was provoked out of its sleep. (24) When the Patti ruler asked Sahib Rai about the Singhs location, He informed that they were picketing at a village Wan! of Buttar Jats. There the (Tat Khalsa) Tara Singh had constructed his Mansion, And had spread his terror all around the place. (25) Then, the Patti ruler asked him for further information, As to how much force he had managed together there. The Chaudhary Jat informed him that Tara had no fort of his own, But a couple of two storeyed rooms for his shelter had he. (26) He kept a force of ten to twenty Singhs regularly, While Singhs, in small batches, kept visiting his place. Some of these Singhs were armed with swords and spears, With Sahib Rai leading this force from the front. This whole force, consisting of five horse riders and eighty foot soldiers, Launched on an expedition enthused with high spirits. (28) This force rushed post haste (from their headquarters), Lest the Singh should escape (before their arrival). They intended to surround the place before day break, And dispatch the Singhs to Lahore (after capturing them). (29) Dohra Chaupai: Dohra Sri Gur Panth Prakash Tara Singh retorted that the two Singhs were not thieves at all, Instead he (Sahib Rai) was a criminal who destroyed others crops. They had rather done justice by stealing his horses, And he cared a fig for the Nawab at Lahore. (21) Tara Singh declared that he had made a resolution, That he would sacrifice his life while fighting the Mughals. That he would never seek any refuge to save his life, And shed his mortal frame after killing so many others. (22) Thus, a little incident flared up into a conflagration, As it proved to be an inauspicious moment for the Singhs, The Jat chief went and complained to the authorities at Patti, That they were living safely in the safety of their houses. (23) He informed that since the Singhs were making collections forcibly, The people could pay their revenue to only one authority. The ruler of Patti felt so outraged at the insinuation, As if a sleeping lion was provoked out of its sleep. (24) When the Patti ruler asked Sahib Rai about the Singhs location, He informed that they were picketing at a village Wan! of Buttar Jats. There the (Tat Khalsa) Tara Singh had constructed his Mansion, And had spread his terror all around the place. (25) Then, the Patti ruler asked him for further information, As to how much force he had managed together there. The Chaudhary Jat informed him that Tara had no fort of his own, But a couple of two storeyed rooms for his shelter had he. (26) He kept a force of ten to twenty Singhs regularly, While Singhs, in small batches, kept visiting his place. Some of these Singhs were armed with swords and spears, While some others stayed there without any weapons. (27) Hearing this, the Patti ruler advanced (towards Tara Singh's seat), With Sahib Rai leading this force from the front. This whole force, consisting of five horse riders and eighty foot soldiers, Launched on an expedition enthused with high spirits. (28) This force rushed post haste (from their headquarters), Lest the Singh should escape (before their arrival). They intended to surround the place before day break, And dispatch the Singhs to Lahore (after capturing them). (29) 19

As this Mughal contingent was compelled to get back, Put up his camp at a village known as Kamboki, From this camp, he intended to proceed to Lahore, To make an appeal for reinforcements from the Nawab. (40) To Khan Bahadur!?, the then Nawab of Lahore. Hearing this development, the Singhs felt concerned, And approached Tara Singh to share their concern. He would rather prefer to follow the Guru's injunction, As the great Guru had ordained (in the time of an ordeal). pages.searchText: Tara Singh’s Companions Gather for Martyrdom An Episode that is Shocking After some companions failed to keep their promise of sacrifice, Tara Singh decided to inform the remaining Singhs and leave the choice to them. He remembered that they had all pledged themselves while eating from the same bowl. The page names the first group who answered: two Buttar brothers, Tara Singh’s own relatives and devoted warriors; Wasawa Singh and Koer Singh, Brahmins from a village read as Jhalli; and Samund Singh and Jhabar Singh, his Multani companions. pages.searchText: Episode About Tara Singh — The Mn Tara Singh — The Mn All these Singhs (who volunteered to fight) were twenty two in strength, Neither any fort nor a boundary wall they had for protection, Except that they were too keen to make sacrifice in battle. As the custodian of Patti approached the authorities at Lahore, He narrated the account of his ignominous defeat. (2) Hearing this, the Nawab of Lahore felt as much infuriated, As a sleeping lion gets infuriated at someone's disturbance. After he had hounded and eliminated every Singh, The more the Mughals had exhausted themselves in eliminating the Singhs, The more had the Singhs multiplied in their strength. (4) At this the Qazi taking the Nawab aside, remarked That the latter knew nothing about the mystery of Singhs resurrection. pages.searchText: He said that as many Singhs rose from the ground once again, Tara Singh — The Mn He said that as many Singhs rose from the ground once again, As the number of drops of Singhs blood fell on the ground. (5) He advised the Nawab that the Singhs be captured alive, And their bodies be beaten and crushed with wooden clubs. Not a drop of blood be allowed to spill from their bodies, Then alone can the increase in their strength be checked. (6) Then at such a suggestion of the Qazi, a soldier interjected, That the revered Qazi was really speaking the truth. For this (holy) cause should the Qazi be made to lead the troops, So that he could help the troops in catching the Singhs alive. (7) He had never had an encounter with the mighty Singhs, He would never unite with his wife after an encounter with them. At this remark, the Qazi felt so much exasperated, That he could not speak a single word in his defence. (8) Then, the Nawab of Lahore made a pronouncement, That they must now proceed to crush the Singhs. He asked if there was any brave warrior among his troops, Who could crush the Singhs by laying a seige. (9) Was there anyone who could take revenge from the enemies of Islam, Who would not allow the Singhs to escape and take refuge? The Hindus must be eliminated even if one broke a thousand vows, Such had been the injunctions from the Prophet. (10) Thus, was Momin Khan despatched on this crusade, At the head of the command of twenty two hundred horse riders. Equipped with forty camel-loaded guns and five elephants, As well as four light artillery guns (of medium range). (14) He advised Tara Singh and his companions, That they had no other option except to hibernate themselves. They had only one night for these maneavours, As the Mughal troops would be upon them with the day break. (15) The messenger returned after giving this information, But (dear readers), listen how did Tara Singh react. Tara Singh feeling extremely charged with emotion, remarked, That he himself was too keen to sacrifice to stigmatise the Mughals. (16) He would fight to the finish at his own camp, Instead of seeking a refuge in the dense wilds, He would prefer to confront death in a straight fight. (17) Where could one seek shelter by taking a flight, Death kept a trail of us (like our shadow), As had been revealed by revered Satguru's words. (18) If one could escape death by taking a flight, How can one run back from the looming death? Episode 86 Invasion of Moman Khan Er Moman Khan launched on an expedition to crush the Singhs, Accompanied by a host of Muslim warriors. His horse having covered a distance of fifteen miles, Must he return to Lahore (before day break)for his survival. (14) He advised Tara Singh and his companions, That they had no other option except to hibernate themselves. They had only one night for these maneavours, As the Mughal troops would be upon them with the day break. (15) The messenger returned after giving this information, But (dear readers), listen how did Tara Singh react. Tara Singh feeling extremely charged with emotion, remarked, That he himself was too keen to sacrifice to stigmatise the Mughals. (16) He would fight to the finish at his own camp, Nor would he desert his place to find escape elsewhere. Instead of seeking a refuge in the dense wilds, He would prefer to confront death in a straight fight. (17) Where could one seek shelter by taking a flight, Where could one remain untraced by death. Death kept a trail of us (like our shadow), As had been revealed by revered Satguru's words. (18) If one could escape death by taking a flight, Then which direction should one choose for fleeing? When death is looming large wherever one goes, How can one run back from the looming death? No one has ever devised any such technique, Which one could exploit to escape death's fatal blow, When nothing avails Oh! foolish human being, Why don't you smilingly submit before death? (Bachittar Natak-96) Episode 86 Episode About how S. Tara Singh Attained Martyrdom Moman Khan launched on an expedition to crush the Singhs, Accompanied by a host of Muslim warriors. (6) No doubt, what he had conveyed was for the former's benefit, And it was also factually correct (to adopt this strategy). But since he (Tara Singh) had resolved to make a sacrifice, He would not run away anywhere from there. (7) He could very well run away to save his life, And could easily return to his place as well. But since his fraternity would accuse him of being a coward, So he would never run away to save his life. (8) On the other hand, hearing about the arrival of troops, The residents of Dalla village came out to meet them. Assuring that they being the loyal subjects of the Mughal sovereign, Their entire village had no rebel Singh among them. (9) The Singhs then challenged the Mughals with the beat of a drum, Which the Mughal troops heard from a distance. With this, the Mughal troops became aware of the Singhs, And the location of the Singhs houses and hamlets. (10)

pages.searchText: A (friendly) Pathan, too, came running on a horseback, Invasion of Moman Khan Er A (friendly) Pathan, too, came running on a horseback, Warning the Singhs not to lose their lives in vain. As he had intimated them about the approaching troops, They should escape and take refuge in the wilds. (11) Tara Singh (acknowledging his service), told him, That he (Tara Singh) was indeed grateful to the brotherly Pathan. But since he had taken a vow to make a sacrifice, He would certainly sacrifice his life at his own place. (12) At that time S. Tara Singh was serving the other Singhs, By filling a big tub with water for bathing the Singhs. Then these Singhs beseeched Tara Singh while serving them, That he had already done a plenty of service to them. (13) Now it was their turn to do some service to him, So that they could also sanctify their bodies with his service. At this, S. Tara Singh addressed his companions, That one's body was sanctified only after being wounded in a war. (14) As the devout get their bodies sanctified, By getting themselves branded at Dwarka. Similarly, when a warrior gets wounded in war. His body gets sanctified with the touch of a weapon. (15) As S. Tara Singh went out to fetch water, Returning, he announced to the Singhs once again, That anyone willing to escape should escape now. (16) Otherwise, they should come out with their weapons, And stand in the battlefield leaving their shelters. Hearing this, the Singhs came out in the open, Leaving their shelter, they stood on the battlefield. (17) The Mughal troops launched an attack from the other side, With the beat of war drums and other trumpets. Launching their attack from all the four sides, They scattered like players in the rustic game of Sonchi?. (18) S. Bulakha Singh was the first to attack the invaders, Who wounded many Mughal soldiers with his sword. pages.searchText: Then the Singhs stood in a circle with their backs towards each other, Invasion of Moman Khan Er Then the Singhs stood in a circle with their backs towards each other, As if they were going to participate in the game of Sonchi. As the Mughal troops attacked these circled Singhs, They kept on repulsing their attack from their side. (20) So much dust and din was raised from both the sides, As if a dust storm had broke in at night. The Mughal soldiers while riding on their horses, Intended to crush the Singhs with horse's hooves. (21) But as the Singh chopped off the horses heads, Their riders fell down feeling exhausted and defeated. And fell down, blocking the passage of their own troops. (22) As the soldiers from both the sides collided against each other, The passage got blocked with the falling bodies. As more and more soldiers came attacking, They too kept on falling on the heaped bodies. (23) While a few Mughal soldiers got wounded with their own weapons, Some others were hit by the weapons of advancing Singhs. There occurred such a blood bath from both sides, That soldiers from both sides got completely exhausted. (24) Thus, the attacks from both the sides slowed down, As it became difficult to wield small weapons in a close encounter. So the Mughal troops fired and shot arrows from a distance, And started killing Singhs while standing at a distance. (25) Although the Singh had not any muskets or small fire arms, Yet the Mughals bullets hit their own soldiers on the other side. Once again got an attack launched on the Singhs. (26) At that Takki Khan, while advancing on his horse's back, Hearing this, S. Tara Singh asked him to proceed a little further, And gave him option of attacking him (Tara Singh) first. (27) As Takki Khan shot an arrow while riding on a horse, Leaping up, Tara Singh caught hold of Takki Khan's horse's reigns, Even as Takki Khan's entire body was protected with a steely armour. Tara Singh Attained Mantra ie A few among these Randhawas joined the Khalsa Panth, After initiating themselves and ordaining the Khalsa armour. (3) As was ordained by Satguru (Guru Gobind Singh), They resolved to follow the Guru's ordained path. Joining the Khalsa Panth, they resorted to the path of fighting, And started waylaying (the Mughals) on the Lahore-Delhi highway. (4) Adopting the same tactics as followed by the Khalsa Singhs, They also raised the pitch of their fighting (against the Mughals). Hearing the news of their daily skirmishes and fights, The Mughals launched an attack to eliminate them. (5) These Singhs did not have any fortified fortress, So they would escape and hide themselves in the wilds, And in the swamps and ravines in their surroundings. (6) Whenever they heard about the impending invasion of the Mughals, They would desert their homes and hide in the wilds. Their families which were left behind in their village, Would somehow survive by mixing with the other people. (7) The Singhs would not stay at their homes during day time, But they would return home with the fall of night. So during the first Mughal raid the Singhs survived, And the Mughal force had to return empty-handed. (8) As they had to return empty handed from their expedition. Feeling crestfallen like a hunting tiger missing his prey, They stepped up their efforts to eliminate the Singhs. (9) As the Mughal troops were on the prowl to kill the Singhs, The Singhs, somehow, tried to mark their time. The Singhs fantasized that a time would come, When the Mughals too would have to run for their lives. (10) They (Singhs) too would have sovereignty over their land, And would collect revenue from their own territory. They were facing hardships in anticipation of that hour. So they would escape and hide themselves in the wilds, And in the swamps and ravines in their surroundings. Tara Singh Attained Mantra ie Dohra: The Singhs, having relatives and friends throughout the country, They stayed with them (away from their own homes). Thus, they passed their time somehow and kept surviving, By taking refuge yet keeping their dress code and identity intact. (12) Chaupai: Now, dear readers, listen to the episode of those Singhs, Whom the enemies of (Sikh Panth) got massacred. There was a village Shahzada? of Sultani* residents, Who, though claiming to be Hindus, behaved like Muslims. (13) These Sultanis contrived with the Muslims Kalals, Who happened to be in service of the Mughals. Both of them conspired to agree on a resolution, That they should get the Randhawa Singhs massacred. (14) Since these Randhawa Singhs have fallen into their trap, They should first get the Singhs land transferred to their names. (After getting this landed property entitlement, transferred), They should get the Singhs progeny eliminated even to the extent of foeticide. (15) In this way, they would earn the pleasure of the Mughals, And they would receive robes of honour from the Mughals. Thus, contemplating the commission of both these crimes secretly, They unfolded their (evil) plan before the Mughals. (16) Dohra: So whatever proposals they made to the Mughals, The latter accepted their proposal ad verbatim. It not only included great honours and foeticide of Singh females, But transfer of ownership of (Singh) lands to their names as well. (17) Chaupai: The Mughals were already looking for such an opportunity, Whereby they could carryout a massacre of the Singhs. So as this Sultani-Kalal duo kept on spotting the Singhs, They wished to seek more concessions from the Mughals. (18) Dohra: The Singhs did not receive any information, That their own neighbours were informing against them. So they kept on hiding in the wilds during the day, And returning to their homes at night. (19) Chaupai: Whichever night or day was fixed for the Singhs assembly, The Singhs would assemble at a place on the fixed night. Both of them conspired to agree on a resolution, That they should get the Randhawa Singhs massacred. pages.searchText: As he had been planted as an informer by the Mughals, how S. Tara Singh Attained Mantra ie As he had been planted as an informer by the Mughals, He reported about the Singhs assembly to the neighbouring Jats. These (non-Sikhs) peasants further informed the Mughals, With the motive of getting the Singhs eliminated. (21) Although these Jat peasants claimed themselves to be Hindus, But their deed were worse than those of the Muslims. Being Hindus, they became instrumental in the capture of Hindus, And getting their own brethren/Hindus/Sikhs slaughtered. (22) With death looming large over their heads, Where could the Singhs seek shelter on such a night? The wicked informer having reported the Singhs's assembly, The Mughal troops laid a siege to the village. (23) As the Mughal troops took positions all around the village, The wicked Hindu Jat peasants too reached there. That not even a dog could escape through the siege. (24) As the wicked Sultani Jats directed the Mughals, Their troops kept on following their directions. So both the Sultanis and the Mughals massacred the Singhs, Laying their hands on the fourteen Sikh elders, They massacred all of them (on the spot). Whosoever else they came across from their families, They slaughtered those taking them to be Singh's progeny. (26) Whichever Singh or their progeny came into sight, They slaughtered him there and then with their swords. He might have survived out of their progeny. (27) In this way, the Majhail Singhs had endured all these ordeals, In the hope that their defiance would establish Khalsa Panth's sovereignty. They had hoped for a sovereignty at the cost of their lives, That is why they achieved sovereignty in due course of time. (28) Somebody might raise this question (about those Singhs), Did anybody survive this ordeal out of their progeny? I would try to give a hint about their survival. (29) Dohra Chaupai: Dohra Chaupai: Dohra Sri Gur Panth Prakash As he had been planted as an informer by the Mughals, He reported about the Singhs assembly to the neighbouring Jats. Being Hindus, they became instrumental in the capture of Hindus, And getting their own brethren/Hindus/Sikhs slaughtered. (22) With death looming large over their heads, Where could the Singhs seek shelter on such a night? The wicked informer having reported the Singhs's assembly, The Mughal troops laid a siege to the village. (23) As the Mughal troops took positions all around the village, The wicked Hindu Jat peasants too reached there. They laid such a formidable siege all around, That not even a dog could escape through the siege. (24) As the wicked Sultani Jats directed the Mughals, Their troops kept on following their directions. So both the Sultanis and the Mughals massacred the Singhs, Sparing none whosoever they spotted there. (25) Laying their hands on the fourteen Sikh elders, They massacred all of them (on the spot). Whosoever else they came across from their families, They slaughtered those taking them to be Singh's progeny. (26) Whichever Singh or their progeny came into sight, They slaughtered him there and then with their swords. Had some odd person among Singhs gone away from village, He might have survived out of their progeny. (27) In this way, the Majhail Singhs had endured all these ordeals, In the hope that their defiance would establish Khalsa Panth's sovereignty. They had hoped for a sovereignty at the cost of their lives, That is why they achieved sovereignty in due course of time. (28) Somebody might raise this question (about those Singhs), Did anybody survive this ordeal out of their progeny? Did they get back their landed property and political power? I would try to give a hint about their survival. (29) 49

pages.searchText: Had they given a chase to the fleeing Mughal troops, Nawab Kapoor Singh, The Nihang Chief Had they given a chase to the fleeing Mughal troops, They would have massacred them there and then. They had always been claiming themselves as great warriors, Who never behaved cowardly in a moment of crisis. (54) As they were still confabulating over what had happened, A contingent of a few Singhs arrived there instantly. This had always been the tradition in the Khalsa Panth, That when ten Singhs died, twenty more arrived there. (55) As these Singhs had heard the sound of gunfire at that fort, They had rushed there to assist their brethren. As their strength increased to one thousand there, The Singhs were filled with new vigour for a new attempt. (56) Then a Singh arrived there with a fresh information, That the Mughals were still not keen to enter Lahore. They, too, were thinking of launching an attack on the Singhs, Although they might attack (with gunfire) from a distance. (57) Hearing this news, the Khalsa Singhs went into a rage, As if a flint-stone was hit with the force of gun's trigger. The Singhs then resolved to make preparations for an attack, Either to eliminate the Mughals or sacrifice their own lives. (58) Girding up their loins they rushed to launch an attack, As they had no horses to harness and mount. Since they had no baggage or equipment to be carried, They just rushed after invoking blessings of Guru Gobind Singh. pages.snippet: Aslam Khan reacts to the Khalsa victory with mixed feelings: he mourns the Mughal losses, yet he is relieved that the Delhi revenue force has been destroyed before it could arrest him for failing to meet imperial demands. The blow that ruined others gives him
pages.searchText: Aslam Khan Reframes the Defeat and Sends Subeg Singh Mulkhayan and Biwastay and Dinikhudian Aslam Khan reacts to the Khalsa victory with mixed feelings: he mourns the Mughal losses, yet he is relieved that the Delhi revenue force has been destroyed before it could arrest him for failing to meet imperial demands. The blow that ruined others gives him breathing room, and he immediately begins calculating how to turn the crisis to his own advantage. In the letter he sends onward, Aslam Khan suppresses the humiliating parts of the story and instead describes the Khalsa as a grave and growing threat. He argues that the power once associated with Banda Singh has not ended but has increased, and he presents the danger in terms designed to move Delhi without exposing his own weakness. From that calculation he turns toward conciliation as strategy rather than surrender. He drafts terms meant to flatter the Singhs, proposes to use soft promises before force, and calls for Subeg Singh to carry the proposal so talks can begin with the Khalsa. 74 tug dôhrâ gut chaupaî: tug dôhrâ suet chaupaî: Sri Gur Panth Prakash: WASH Hlo fona ôl Hó oe oft ae | He set A YA SU He de A ues Igi asalam khan nibab ke manai bhag dui bhai. mug talbi só khush bhayô mug din só pachhutâi.4.: JS mM H6AA SH | 8S AHS 355 MUS A | ca uqg ü JH 3 Sifa | usa es Š fest ARI Jul hut nabâb mansûbç baja. un samjhayó bhal apnô kâja. take pujat thc ham tc nânhi. mujh kô phard lai dillî jânhi.5. oot set I GÍF Hg Te | 38 oa A [Hu yr ue | JHII ads a HoU eS | TSH HÌ Udu GH ud mE E| bhalî bhai jô ui mar gaç. bhal¢ bhâg sô singh â pac. hamhi kahan kô banyô valâu. ghanîm balî paryô ham par âi.6. pages.searchText: (After this defeat), Nawab of Lahore, Aslam Khan's mind, Mulkhayan and Biwastay and Dinikhudian (After this defeat), Nawab of Lahore, Aslam Khan's mind, Went through two (contradictory) thoughts of joy and sorrow. He felt happy at the death of the revenue collecting force of Delhi, But grieved at the loss of those who died for Islam. (4) The Nawab who had been a great manipulator felt, That this defeat was a blessing in disguise for him. Had he failed to deposit the stipulated revenue to Delhi, The Delhi contingent would have arrested him to take to Delhi. (5) It was a God sent dispensation that the Delhi contingent died, And good that it died at the hands of the Singhs. This defeat had provided him an opportunity to claim, How formidable was the enemy who fell upon them? (6) That the death of Banda Singh was not the extinction of a powerful enemy, Which had rather multiplied fourfold after his death. He sent a dispatch to Delhi containing such an import, Citing the death of the Delhi contingent as evidence of his assessment. (7) He did not mention the loss of Islamic ideological crusaders, Writing only those facts which served his own designs. He started a move to seek reconciliation with the Singhs. He is to congratulate the Khalsa for removing a burden from Lahore, speak of mutual advantage, and persuade them that negotiated recognition would serve both sides better than another round of open warfare. The offer becomes concrete through land, cash, and promises of settled authority. Subeg Singh is instructed to speak of jagir arrangements, local peace, and continuing goodwill, all designed to draw the Panth into a relationship the Lahore administration can manage rather than fear. pages.searchText: Subeg Singh Reaches the Khalsa Camp Mulkhayan and Biwastay and Dinikhudian Subeg Singh arrives at the Khalsa encampment and finds not a quiet court but a martial congregation alive with standards, drums, horses, and armed vigilance. The camp is busy, public, and disciplined, making clear that the Khalsa is a gathered people as well as a fighting force. He sees Singhs reading scripture, singing shabad, preparing food, cleaning weapons, tending horses, fetching water, and serving one another in ordinary tasks. The scene emphasizes that the Panth sustains itself through prayer, labor, and mutual service rather than through the pomp of imperial administration. Recognizing where he stands, Subeg Singh dismounts in humility, folds his hands, and approaches with cries of Vahiguru ji ki fateh and Akal. (21) As this shrewd emissary Subeg Singh arrived there, The Khalsa Singhs were holding a religious congregation. Gurbani hymns were being recited to the accompaniment of music, As well as cannabis leaves were being grounded and meat roasted. (22) While a few Singh were grooming and sprucing up their horses, A few others were cleaning and sharpening their weapons, While a few others were practicing shooting of arrows and firing of guns, Some one else was rotating a circular ring over his finger. Another Singh was seen fetching a bucket of water, For giving a bath to his fellow (elderly) Singhs. (24) While a few were cleaning their teeth and bathing themselves, Others were changing their undergarments (after a bath). Instead of having feelings of rivalry against each other, Everyone was too keen to serving each other. pages.searchText: The Khalsa Hears the Offer and Rejects a Lesser Sovereignty Mulkhayan and Biwastay and Dinikhudian Once Subeg Singh has explained himself, the Khalsa lets him speak and hear out the proposal from Lahore. Money, honors, and political assurances are placed before the gathering, and the Singhs debate whether to reject the offer entirely, take what can help the Panth, or bend the negotiation toward the protection of the weak. The discussion does not descend into confusion. The Khalsa weighs the proposal collectively, keeps the focus on justice, and receives the material gifts as something to be redistributed rather than privately hoarded by a single claimant. The decisive issue is rule itself. When the question of title arises, the assembly insists that the Guru has promised true sovereignty to the Khalsa, and that no Mughal rank can replace the destiny already bestowed upon the Panth. 80 Sri Gur Panth Prakash ofS URS dd WEA ott | ote serfs sun ag HG | ur5H TAH ala Um sae! pages.searchText: Khalsa Sovereignty Is Declared and Kapoor Singh Is Noticed Mulkhayan and Biwastay and Dinikhudian Darbara Singh’s refusal becomes a wider Panthic argument on this page. The Singhs say that Satguru had conferred sovereignty on the Khalsa Panth, so it would be shameful to trade that divine grant for a title dependent on imperial favor and revocable at a ruler’s whim. The argument widens from one office to the whole political relationship with the Mughals. The Khalsa will not exchange its future for a lesser arrangement, because Guru-given authority reaches wherever the Panth stands firm and cannot be reduced to a borrowed dignity. As the debate turns from refusal to selection, attention settles on Kapoor Singh. pages.searchText: Kapoor Singh Receives the Robe of Honor Mulkhayan and Biwastay and Dinikhudian The Khalsa resolves the matter by choosing Kapoor Singh, not because he has sought office, but because the Panth recognizes service, endurance, and courage in him. The congregation presents the robe of honor to Kapoor Singh as a collective decision rather than as an imperial appointment imposed from above. The elevation raises the public standing of the Khalsa. Mughal officials now speak more carefully, payments and concessions begin to flow, and the arrangement gives Lahore a temporary way to reduce pressure while acknowledging a power it cannot simply crush. Even so, the political balance remains sharp. pages.searchText: Kapoor Singh Governs Through Collective Discipline Mulkhayan and Biwastay and Dinikhudian Life at Akal Takht continues under Kapoor Singh with an emphasis on humility and shared deliberation. He does not behave like an isolated courtly ruler, but keeps authority tied to the congregation and to Panthic consultation. Administrative order now becomes visible in practical terms. Whatever money entered the Sikh coffers was treated as common wealth, gathered into approved channels, and entrusted to named servants responsible for stores, kitchens, weapons, and other necessities of the community. The page closes by linking institution to discipline. pages.searchText: Kapoor Singh Reorganizes the Growing Khalsa Mulkhayan and Biwastay and Dinikhudian The Panth continues enforcing discipline even in a quieter interval. Men returning from home acknowledge their absence, seek forgiveness, and hand over what they have brought back so that personal gain does not outweigh collective responsibility. At the same time the Khalsa is spreading outward. Some Singhs build homes, resume cultivation, open centers of congregation, or return with new companions, so the community grows broader and harder to manage as a single body gathered in one place. Seeing that change clearly, Kapoor Singh brings the question before the assembly and argues that the Khalsa must reorganize into a few contingents. pages.searchText: Such an offender after returning from his home, Mulkhayan and Biwastay and Dinikhudian Such an offender after returning from his home, Would voluntarily stand up and seek forgiveness for absence. Whenever a Singh brought some money from any adventure, He would deposit the same in the central treasury. (17) After the Singhs relaxed and passed sometime in peace, Many Singhs proceeded to their homes to see their families. While some of them got their residential houses constructed, A few others established centres for holding congregations. (18) While many Singhs returned to the traditional occupation of agriculture, A few others got entangled in the snares of their wedlock. While many Singhs were kept confined to homes by their mothers, A few others returned along with many new recruits. (19) As the strength of the Singh ranks increased manifold, It became difficult to keep them stationed at one place. Then Nawab Kapoor Singh contemplated over this organizational issue, And thought of devising a strategy to manage his organization. (20) He called a congregation of the Khalsa panth on the same day, At the (historic Sikh shrine) of Sri Akal Takht Sahib. News quickly reaches the officials of Lahore, who send Khizar Khan to capture him. The future leader first appears in an atmosphere of prayer rather than war, where mother and son are bound together through sacred routine and public devotion. Their piety draws them toward the assembled Khalsa, and the sangat receives them with warmth when they come to pay homage. The narrative stresses that the mother-son pair do not arrive seeking status, but as sincere devotees whose reverence naturally brings them into the orbit of the Panth. Kapoor Singh then draws the child close, initiates him into the Khalsa, and begins training him through humble duty. pages.searchText: Jassa Singh Blessed by Nawab Kapoor Singh the Title of nawabship on S. Kapoor Singh The young Jassa Singh came crying to Nawab Kapoor Singh because he could no longer distribute feed and was being beaten by others. Kapoor Singh called him close, placed his hand on the boy’s head, and blessed him affectionately. Kapoor Singh told him that he would one day issue feed to thousands of horses. The same Khalsa Panth that had made Kapoor Singh a Nawab would, in time, make Jassa Singh a sovereign, and from that moment the boy was known as Jassa Singh Kalal with royal promise. The page emphasizes insecurity, shortage, and mobility, showing how survival depends upon constant movement rather than settled control. Even in that uncertainty, local bonds matter. Men such as Gohar Singh and Gurbakhsh Singh sustain the Singhs with food, shelter, and political goodwill, demonstrating that service to the Panth could reshape regional power just as surely as battlefield prowess. Ala Singh rises within this world of alliance and provision. pages.searchText: Ala Singh’s Expansion and the Decision to Strike Sirhind Jassa Singh (Ahluwalia) The narrative first follows Ala Singh and allied chiefs as their local influence expands, helped by Khalsa protection and the weakening of older authorities. Territory, kin connections, and prestige all widen together, so the page reads as a record of growing power rather than mere survival. Need soon pushes the Khalsa back toward direct action. The Singhs want resources to travel for the congregation at Amritsar, and they ask Kapoor Singh for permission to strike a wealthy center that can finance both devotion and movement. Sirhind becomes the chosen target because memory and justice weigh alongside opportunity. pages.title: Raid on Sirhind and the Khalsa’s March to Amritsar
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Jassa Singh (Ahluwalia)
pages.snippet: With Kapoor Singh’s approval, the Singhs move swiftly against Sirhind and strike before the city can organize an effective defense. The attack is presented as both vengeance and necessity, joining old grievance to the immediate need for supplies and mobility.
pages.searchText: Raid on Sirhind and the Khalsa’s March to Amritsar Jassa Singh (Ahluwalia) With Kapoor Singh’s approval, the Singhs move swiftly against Sirhind and strike before the city can organize an effective defense. The attack is presented as both vengeance and necessity, joining old grievance to the immediate need for supplies and mobility. The raid is methodical rather than chaotic. The Khalsa occupied the five main entrances to the city, carries out a concentrated sack, gathers animals and valuables, and avoids becoming trapped in a prolonged engagement that would invite a stronger Mughal response. After only a short stay, the Singhs regroup and begin moving again, now better provisioned for the road to Amritsar. Their success also deepens Khalsa influence in Malwa, where communities see both the Panth’s striking power and its willingness to answer local appeals. 102 dôhrâ gut chaupaî: tug dôhrâ gut chaupaî: Sri Gur Panth Prakash sari satigur kç bachan kar singh thórdhç hî phatc pânhin. dhan chalaingg hal gadhai din thôrdan kç mânhi.7. ad saa as feu 3 ufeS va ad ge | urs Js À m es ust Afos Hfg Sc Iç! kahi nabâbai bat im tau paiô panth kar chhit. parât hôt sô ja vard¢ pai shahir mahin lût.8.: ffw ome aft Un a UA | 8ô cg=r UA I zga BSG uu us Hrg | we Tama Q fed 9= ICI singh hajar tahin pafij ku pujj¢. unai darvâjc ja pafij mufijc. turak labhyô dayô singhan mara. laç hindûan kç jcvar utâra.9. gif HES M 35 Chr | wet CH da vas att | afea usd f35 Be HTT | SE gu va wet Moral 190 | chandi suinôn au bhal chîza. lai dekh chang chakkan kija. duik pahar tin lit machâî. bhag bhûkhç chak khái mithâî.10. vad Haft ese Gore | US Bau AG wa west | H3 eS fHu fas jt grfg | 3 Stadt eo ude we 1991 chaknc jégi darab uthâî. ghôrdç labhyô sôâ layó ladai. murd daurdg singh tit hi rahi. tau thîkrî várç pahufichg jai.11. z3 Hee fad us we | fas Ha ÍSJ Sad MÈ | HJdg WEA Q su US | Ad WHAT fas faH 981921 vard málvç phir ghôrdç lac. kite mulak tih nazrai ag. kharach khâlsg kç bhayô pall¢. sare ammrtasar bin kim chall6. 12.: NS REG fea AC su va au fsm | Has Zaz â Sot faes fga TS 1931: mglô âiô dhig jôû tab panth bhayô tiar. marnôn tart¢ thc nahin ginan jittnô hâr.13.: HHJ HBS HM Ho UT | nie Ue ol vet TU | S oy Ae Fe cŠ AIS US | Jgs UE JH MÀ AS 1981 khabar malvayyan jab sun pai. án panth kó dai vadhâî. judg judg daç sabhhan ghôrdg. chardaht panth hath agai jôrdc.14. nà sod Ue ÍH& afo | ad AS MU gH Uf | H JH ud SIA Uefa +g | HAI SE JH Ma HJd au age badhyô panth siun rahi. kar mglô âyô ham pâhi. jô ham par turak pavahi jêra. khabar ló ham ân bahôra.15.

On arrival the Singhs find desecration and damage at the sacred center, a reminder that Mughal hostility has targeted not only Sikh bodies but Sikh space and memory as well. The response is immediate and collective. pages.searchText: Bhai Mani Singh at Amritsar and the Prophecy of Dismemberment Nawab Kapor Singh Bhujangi Bhai Mani Singh appears here as a learned, disciplined, and deeply trusted servant of the Panth. His authority is rooted in devotion, scriptural knowledge, and closeness to the Guru’s mission, making him a figure of moral as well as institutional weight. The page then turns to his formal responsibilities under Mata Sundari’s direction. He is sent to Amritsar to guide the sangat, supervise sacred administration, and take control of the offerings at Amritsar so that gifts placed before the Guru may be directed toward the needs of the community. The closing movement becomes darker and more prophetic. pages.searchText: Bhai Mani Singh Accepts the Sangat’s Verdict Nawab Kapor Singh Bhujangi The force of the congregation’s earlier words now settles fully upon Bhai Mani Singh. He does not protest the verdict or try to separate himself from the sangat, but instead recognizes that the Panth’s spiritual authority stands inseparable from the Guru’s own command. In humility he asks forgiveness and reframes the issue away from bodily fear. He tells the congregation that preservation of faith for a Sikh is a rare phenomenon, while mere preservation of the body is of little worth if it comes at the cost of fidelity to Sikh discipline. The page resolves through prayer and acceptance. pages.searchText: Diwali Assembly Approved, Then Undermined Nawab Kapor Singh Bhujangi Permission is initially granted for the Diwali congregation at Amritsar, and officials set terms meant to turn the gathering into a manageable arrangement rather than an outright prohibition. The page records this fragile accommodation as a moment when Mughal power appears willing to tolerate Panthic assembly under supervision. Money quickly becomes part of the political calculation. A ten thousand rupees tax is fixed in connection with the gathering, and while invitations spread through the Khalsa, hostile advisers work to persuade Lahore that armed Sikhs will never remain quiet once assembled in strength. What begins as permission therefore turns into a trap. Troops move into position, confidence drains away, and a once-hopeful fair becomes a site of looming confrontation in which peace is increasingly difficult to preserve. 110 Sri Gur Panth Prakash cust: worst aA E AS wT | SJao ô H ca TA | =H da gur SATIA | cfonte ws f35 eda FTG 1201 chaupaî: duâlî kô thé mela laya. turkan nc thé taka chukâyâ. das hazâr rupyyâ thahirâyâ. takian khatar tin darôgâ bahâyâ.20. pages.searchText: Mani Singh Refuses Surety and Offers His Life Nawab Kapor Singh Bhujangi The expected confrontation arrives as the scattered gathering fails to produce the money that Mughal officials demand. Bhai Mani Singh and other Singhs are seized, and the question of unpaid obligation is turned into an opportunity to pressure the Panth and its leaders. Supporters in Lahore try to intervene, hoping to satisfy the authorities with guarantees or negotiated payment. Mani Singh prohibited all surety, however, refusing to let others rescue the situation through money when he sees that the real issue is no longer taxation but the testing of faith. By rejecting both immediate rescue and deferred payment, Mani Singh effectively offers his own life in settlement. pages.searchText: Clerical Verdict and the Order to Dismember Mani Singh Nawab Kapor Singh Bhujangi Once Mani Singh refuses conversion and rejects compromise, the Nawab turns to qazis and mullas to frame the punishment in legal and religious terms. The Sikh prisoners remain firm, insisting that they will not abandon their path even under the threat of exemplary violence. The verdict that emerges is designed to terrify. Mani Singh is sentenced to be dismembered limb by limb, a ruling that echoes the congregation’s earlier prophecy and transforms a court punishment into the literal fulfillment of words already spoken over him. At the place of execution, Mani Singh shows unshaken composure and even corrects the executioners when they begin too crudely. pages.searchText: Realising the inevitability of the moment of making a sacrifice, Nawab Kapor Singh Bhujangi Realising the inevitability of the moment of making a sacrifice, Mani Singh abandoned every possibility of a negotiation. He believed that Singh congregation's prophecy could never go in vain, Even if a million attempts were made to put it off. (38) Since the moment for the fulfillment of prophetic cause had approached. Summoning the members of the Muslim clergy and theologians, He sought their advice (for the execution of Mani Singh). (39) The Nawab asked the Singhs to get himself converted into Islam, If they wished their life to be spared by the Mughals. The Singhs remarked that they would never betray their faith, As they could forego many lives for the sake of their faith. (40) The Nawab asked the clergy to suggest ways of executing the Singhs, Exactly as it was prescribed in the Book of Koran. Then, as interpreted and directed by the theologians, The Islamic judge pronounced the manner of execution. (41) Mani Singh's whole body be dismembered limb by limb, So that it became a deterrent for the whole world. What was predestined was expressed through the cleric's words, Even as the Islamic judge became an instrument to unfold that curse. (42) That is why this manner of Mani Singh's execution, Came to be quoted from the books of the Islamic text. Since whosoever tried to subvert these would perish. (43) Then the Nawab of Lahore made a declaration, That Mani Singh's body be dismembered bit by bit. The official executioners, getting hold of Mani Singh instantly. Made him sit in the central place known as Nikhas* square. (44) At this Mani Singh reprimanded his executioners, Did they not know the meaning of cutting limb by limb? (45) As he would go on demarcating each organ of his body, They should go on chopping off his organs with their knives. Directing them to first chopp off the nodal parts of his fingers, Thereafter they should sever his fingers from their joints. pages.searchText: Mani Singh Endures Dismemberment Joint by Joint Nawab Kapor Singh Bhujangi The execution continues exactly as Bhai Mani Singh had demanded: joint by joint rather than in a single crude stroke. After the first cuts at the fingers and wrists, the butchers move on to elbows and shoulders while he remains absorbed in prayer and refuses to let the sentence be softened. The page dwells on the terrible precision of the punishment. Each limb is reduced piece by piece, yet Mani Singh keeps reciting Gurbani and accepts the ordeal as a conscious martyrdom rather than a defeat inflicted by the state. Witnesses who had come merely to watch are shaken by what they see.
