After that, whereas the butcher intended to dismember his shoulders, Bhai Mani Singh insisted on getting his arms cut from the elbows. (47) After the elbows, he got his shoulders chopped off, Getting the left shoulder-severed after his right shoulder. He got his second hand fingers cut in the same manner, Thus, getting his fingers and thumb severed inch by inch. (48) Just as both right and left arms were got severed, Similarly he got his feet severed inch by inch. Then, as the nodes of his two feet were got severed, Similarly he got his heel joints and knees dismembered. (49) The executioners witnessing this such a gory spectacle, They started gasping for breath with tension. They had heard about a mystic (Siddha) known as Dhandli, One of whose disciples was harassed by some people. This harassed disciple had let out a curse at one of the cities, Which sank a cluster of eighteen towns in an instant. (51) So, the executioner, taking out his sword from its sheath, Slashed out Mani Singh's head from his neck. Bhai Mani Singh, being engrossed in the recitation of Gurbani, His (mortal) human body did not register any pain. (52) Since his soul had got alienated from his body, His soul kept on reciting Gurbani even after (physical) death. pages.searchText: The Poem Exalts Mani Singh Above Earlier Martyrs Nawab Kapor Singh Bhujangi After describing the final cuts, the narrative turns from the scene of execution to praise. It compares Bhai Mani Singh with famous sufferers such as Mansur, yet insists that Mani Singh bore a still harsher trial because his body was severed joint by joint before death. The page argues that he remained greater than Mansur because he kept Sikhi intact under torture and refused every inducement to break faith. His martyrdom is treated not as a private death but as the fulfillment of the congregation’s prophecy and the triumph of disciplined devotion. The poet closes by ranking him among the foremost Sikh martyrs and by fixing the event in remembered history. pages.searchText: From Mani Singh’s Death to the Wider Persecution of the Khalsa Nawab Kapor Singh Bhujangi This page is a hinge between two narrative movements. It first recalls that Mani Singh accepted death after recognizing the weight of the Sikhs’ curse and that his body was carried to Nikhas Chowk Lahore, where the sentence was fulfilled as a public warning. The text then notes that companions with Mani Singh were also seized and executed, widening the tragedy beyond one celebrated martyr. Their deaths show that the authorities intended to punish an entire community rather than a single defiant leader. From there the poem opens the next episode by broadening into a survey of state persecution under Khan Bahadur and Zakariya Khan. Different methods of execution, mutilation, and terror are introduced so that Mani Singh’s shahidi becomes the prelude to a longer campaign against the Khalsa. 120 Sri Gur Panth Prakash cas: Hat Mu Has HIfS6 flue HU UES | Ja fsan add H veut arte fers 12 | dôhrâ: manî singh maran mândiô sikkhan sarap pachhân. chauk nikâs lahaur main chalyô bajâi nishân.2. cos: Hot fu à Aa A eS fu 8 id | He TIH TIRTA Ta fa &dd 13 | dôhrâ: mani singh kç sath Jó phardg singh the aur. mârg charakh chardhâikai chaunk nikâs lahaur.3. tg. mẹ sreg Hrg at (as 3 fea ast Ag...) 94. sakhi nadar shah ki (kâbal tc ik kuttâ mangain...) tug: AST À umes We Hgreg OF | &o sg =u ffws Ju unt ws ugr 141 dôhrâ: sattr¢ sai pachânvg khan bahâdar nabâb. un bahu dukh singhan dayô papi badaô kharâb.1. Shedding his mortal frame at Nikhas square at Lahore, Bhai Mani Singh's soul went to heavens with a thunderous applause. (A hound from Kabul would be ordained to be brought) Dohra: It was the year seventeen hundred and ninety-five, When Khan Bahadur (Zakariya Khan) was the Nawab of (Lahore). He had persecuted Singhs on a large-scale, As he had been a sinner and a highly diabolical person. (1) When Bhai Mani Singh* was executed (by him), His body was ordered to be hacked into pieces. Many other Singhs who perished along with Mani Singh, It is difficult to keep a count of all those. (2) Many others were blown up by cannon fire or sliced with knives. While many were crushed to death with conical clubs, Many others were drowned and dragged to death. (3) All those who were buried alive, hanged or blown up, It is difficult to keep a count of thousands of them. Including all those who were made to sit in lines, In order to chopp off their heads with the swords. (4) While the hands and legs of a few of them were chopped off, Eyes of a few others were gouged and others skin peeled off. Whosoever was spotted out with the hair unshorn, Was eliminated irrespective of being an infant or an adult. (5) Dohra: It was on the mistaken identity of being a Singh, That (an innocent Hindu) Hakikat Rai? too was executed. It was as if a vegetarian trader, in his lust for a meatdish, Relished a spicy roasted preparation of rock pieces. pages.searchText: Divine Judgment and Nadir Shah’s Advance on Lahore Bhai Mani Singh's Martyrdom The poem argues that the mass persecution of the Khalsa created such an outcry that it reached the divine court itself. Heavenly judgment now turns against the Mughal order that had tormented the Sikhs and prepares the way for a devastating invader from the northwest. In that frame, Nadir Shah reaches Lahore while Zakariya Khan is forced into humiliating submission and heavy payment. The invasion is presented as punishment for tyranny, not merely as another military episode in imperial politics. At the same time the turmoil opens roads and supply lines to Sikh action. The Singhs begin striking traffic along the Kabul-Delhi road, using the confusion of empire to challenge the very state that had tried to exterminate them. 122 Sri Gur Panth Prakash cust: FE MSA sg gu cui | grg aS N Hg H sü | AG Hd Hou Bf HE | gst teres Ale gafa 121 chaupaî: jabai khals¢ bahu dukh dayô. char kunt main shór su bhayô. sôû shôr sunyô ui thai. hut? adalat jahin dargâhi.7. Since Mughal power was already devouring itself, the Singhs say that one thorn removes a thorn: one violent force can uproot another and expose the weakness of Delhi’s persecuting regime. Prophetic language then frames the crisis as long foreseen. A hound from Kabul is said to have descended upon Hindustan, and the page links that prophecy to the chance for the Khalsa to regroup, shout Akal, and step forward without waiting for favor from any court. Kapoor Singh emerges as the leader who recognizes the moment clearly. pages.searchText: Laying their hands on the invader's cash, horses and valuables, Bhai Mani Singh's Martyrdom Laying their hands on the invader's cash, horses and valuables, The Guru's beloved Singhs would rob the invaders. The Singhs would say that it was God sent moment for them, Since the Mughals themselves were killing each other. (16) Since it was a moment of Mughal's decimation on both the sides, It was also a moment for the expansion of Khalsa Panth as well. As a thorn is used to pull out a thorn from the flesh, The second thorn is abandoned after pulling out the first. (17) The Singhs remarked that the destined moment had arrived, Which the Guru had predicted through his prophetic words. The Guru had ordained the summoning of a hound from Kabul, Who would be instrumental in decimating the Delhi rulers. (18) Thereafter an army would be marching from the South*, Thereafter, would come the Khalsa troops in rugged clothes, Who would get united with the other Khalsa!9 troops. (19) Not only would the Delhi empire get dismantled, But the seven hill principalities too would be demolished. Not only would the twenty-two Mughal states be destroyed, But the Mughal rulers and their ministers too would be eliminated. (20) Not only would the Mughal war drums cease to beat, But the Khalsa Panth's war slogans of Akal! Akal! Would fill the air. Since the prophesied historic moment seemed to have arrived, The Singhs were free to loot and plunder as much as they wished. (21) The one who was Nawab among the Khalsa Singhs, He was known by the name of S. Kapoor Singh. He made it known to all the Khalsa Singhs, That that was the most opportune moment for realization of their goal. (22) When S. Kapoor Singh uttered these words to the Singhs, All of them lent their ears to his prophetic words. Hailing his prophetic words to be absolutely true, They bowed their heads in reverence to his visionary acumen. (23) How much wealth did (Nadir Shah) plunder from Delhi? pages.searchText: Nadir Shah Carries Off Delhi’s Treasures Bhai Mani Singh's Martyrdom The poem now catalogs the plunder taken by Nadir Shah in language of astonishment and excess. At the center stands the Takht-e-Taus worth nine crores, alongside jewels, pearls, and courtly marvels that symbolize the prestige of the Mughal throne. Other prized objects are listed to deepen the sense of imperial humiliation: rare gems, storied heirlooms, and even celebrated curiosities associated with musicians and kings. The conqueror strips away both treasure and aura, turning Delhi’s claims to greatness into portable spoil. By ending on written transfers of territory and payment, the page shows that the loss was political as well as material. pages.searchText: The Scale of Plunder and Slaughter in Delhi Bhai Mani Singh's Martyrdom This page sums up the devastation left by the invasion in stark, collective terms. The poet says that wealth beyond counting was carried off from the Mughal dominions and that the destruction of Delhi exposed the fragility of a court that had imagined itself unassailable. Human loss is counted alongside treasure. The narrative highlights that seventy thousand killed in Delhi were largely defenseless people, making the catastrophe a moral indictment of imperial failure rather than a mere change of rulers. The conclusion is that the Mughals had effectively ruined themselves through their own corruption and violence. pages.searchText: Nadir Shah Hears Why the Khalsa Cannot Be Broken Nadar Shah Nadir Shah asks Khan Bahadur who these Sikhs are after hearing repeated reports of their resistance. The answer begins with admiration: the Khalsa endure hunger and hardship, go without comfort in heat and cold, and still keep fighting with the energy of people sustained by conviction rather than provisions. The page then sharpens that praise into martial proportion. The poem insists that each Singh fights a hundred, not because of numbers or equipment, but because death has lost its power to frighten those who see struggle for the faith as honorable. Khan Bahadur traces their origin back to Guru Nanak and admits that Mughal injustice against the Gurus has brought its own punishment. pages.searchText: After Nadir Leaves, Zakariya Khan Turns Again on the Singhs Nadar Shah The page first closes the Nadir Shah episode with a reflective note: some persecutors died in the turmoil, while others survived only long enough to continue unfinished violence. The poet presents this as received tradition, heard from elders who remembered both judgment and survival. It then pivots decisively after Nadir left for Kabul. Humiliated rather than corrected, Khan Bahadur and Zakariya Khan return their rage toward the Sikhs and prepare a renewed campaign to scour the land of keshdhari Singhs. That transition matters because it marks a change from imperial collapse to local repression. Some are hiding in ravines and forests, others in distant villages or among sympathetic households, while still others try to pass as ordinary cultivators living close to the soil. A written proclamation across Lahore orders that even Sikhs quietly farming or trading are not to be spared if they keep unshorn hair, turning visible Sikh identity into a mark for state violence. Bounties and permissions follow from that decree. Informers are rewarded, looters are indulged, and people are encouraged to hand over Singhs for questioning, imprisonment, or death, which lets private greed work together with official persecution. The poem then personalizes the suffering through stories of betrayal, family loss, and the seizure of elders linked with Bhai Taru Singh. pages.searchText: Zakaria Khan’s Proclamation Deepens the Anti-Sikh Terror Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan Zakaria Khan’s proclamation turns the persecution of the Sikhs into a wider social campaign. Villagers are pressured to inform, those who shelter Singhs risk destruction, and whole districts become unsafe as fear and greed begin serving the Nawab’s policy. The result is another scattering of the Khalsa. Some flee into forests, hills, and distant courts, while others survive by concealment and mobility because normal village life has been poisoned by surveillance and bounty seeking. Reports spread of the desecration of Harmandir Sahib after Massa Ranghar takes possession of the sacred precincts and treats the shrine as a place for worldly revelry. Mehtab Singh’s anger becomes the center of the page. He cannot bear that Amritsar should suffer such humiliation while the Khalsa remains scattered, and he challenges the Singhs around him to answer dishonor with courage. Being caught between the devil and the deep sea, They could neither retaliate, nor bear with those indignities. (14) The Mughals had committed the greatest sacrilege, In the sacred precincts of Darbar Sahib at Amritsar. The chief among the Mughals had kept a Courtesan, (For lewd dancing) in the sanctum sanctorum of Harmandir. (15) And Massa Ranghar was the name of this chief. Being a great sinner and a notorious evil doer, He had been desecrating the sanctity of Harmandir. (16) Hearing of this desecration, Mehtab Singh felt greatly incensed, As if he had been stung by a poisonous scorpion. He asked if there were no Singhs present there, Who could crush the head of such a defiler? (17) Had the Singhs abandoned their mission to defend the truth, Or Had they abandoned their mission of performing noble deeds? Counter-questioning him for his flamboyant bravado, Singhs asked, Why did he himself shirk from that daring challenge? (18) As he himself had fled away for saving his own life, How could he blame others for not facing the challenge? As he had saved his life by fleeing from the scene, So had others fled away following his footsteps. pages.searchText: Mehtab Singh and Sukha Singh Accept the Mission Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan The taunts and lament now harden into decision. Sukha Singh joins Mehtab Singh and the two accept that the duty of striking Massa Ranghar cannot be postponed to some safer season. They therefore take leave of the Khalsa with full awareness that they may not return. The page treats their resolve as readiness for martyrdom, because success will require entering hostile ground where capture is almost certain if the plan fails. Preparation follows resolve. pages.snippet: Mehtab Singh and Sukha Singh reach Amritsar at a carefully chosen moment. During the peak hour of the noon, when heat, rain, and routine have dulled the vigilance of the guards, they enter disguised as revenue officials carrying business for the local authorit
pages.searchText: Mehtab Singh Beheads Massa Ranghar at Amritsar Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan Mehtab Singh and Sukha Singh reach Amritsar at a carefully chosen moment. During the peak hour of the noon, when heat, rain, and routine have dulled the vigilance of the guards, they enter disguised as revenue officials carrying business for the local authorities. Inside the desecrated complex they find Massa Ranghar absorbed in entertainment and unprepared for danger. Mehtab Singh strikes decisively and chops off his head before the garrison can understand what has happened. The deed is both revenge and restoration. pages.searchText: It being the peak hour of the noon in the month of September, Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan It being the peak hour of the noon in the month of September, The Sun was at its hottest in this (humid) month. As it rained and stopped at intermittent intervals, It proved very convenient for accomplishing their mission. (31) As the scorching heat made the guards recede into shade, The rest of the troops receded to their barracks to escape rain. Along with the melodies from the Rag Malhar. (32) With some of the guards dozing off or half-asleep, None of them could notice the entry of the Singhs. The two Singhs were able to reach the main entrance, Without any let or hindrance on their way. (33) Positioning their horses on each side of the main entrance, They concealed their spears behind the wall. They hid their swords beneath their loose robes, So that no security guard could object to their arms. (34) Who had come to deposit revenue proceeds. While some guards were distracted by the live music, Others were hypnotized by the courtesan's lewd dance. (35) As the Singhs thought this moment to be most opportune, As Divine Will wished to set everything right, It made their presence unnoticed by the watching eyes. (36) Both the Singhs finally reached the central spot, Where the musicians were playing on the music. Pulling out his sword from its sheath beneath his dress, Mehtab Singh lunged it courageously at Mass Ranghar's head. (37) As one plucks a pumpkin from a creeper. Whatever jewels Massa Ranghar was wearing around his neck, The other Singh took these off his neck guickly. (38) As there was raised a lot of hue and cry all around, The two Singhs mounted their horses and fled away. As the two Singhs, spurring their horses, disappeared into the wilds, Their brave act ended the (notorious) tale of Massa Ranghar. (39) Dohra Chaupai: Dohra Chaupai: Dohra Chaupai: Sri Gur Panth Prakash 147 It being the peak hour of the noon in the month of September, The Sun was at its hottest in this (humid) month. As it rained and stopped at intermittent intervals, It proved very convenient for accomplishing their mission. (31) As the scorching heat made the guards recede into shade, The rest of the troops receded to their barracks to escape rain. Massa Ranghar ordered the Court dancer to play Rag Sarang, Along with the melodies from the Rag Malhar. (32) With some of the guards dozing off or half-asleep, None of them could notice the entry of the Singhs. The two Singhs were able to reach the main entrance, Without any let or hindrance on their way. (33) Positioning their horses on each side of the main entrance, They concealed their spears behind the wall. They hid their swords beneath their loose robes, So that no security guard could object to their arms. (34) Some security guards took them for Mughal soldiers, Who had come to deposit revenue proceeds. While some guards were distracted by the live music, Others were hypnotized by the courtesan's lewd dance. (35) As the Singhs thought this moment to be most opportune, They proceeded hastily towards their cherished target. As Divine Will wished to set everything right, It made their presence unnoticed by the watching eyes. (36) Both the Singhs finally reached the central spot, Where the musicians were playing on the music. Pulling out his sword from its sheath beneath his dress, Mehtab Singh lunged it courageously at Mass Ranghar's head. (37) He chopped off Massa Ranghar's head as easily, As one plucks a pumpkin from a creeper. Whatever jewels Massa Ranghar was wearing around his neck, The other Singh took these off his neck guickly. (38) As there was raised a lot of hue and cry all around, The two Singhs mounted their horses and fled away. As the two Singhs, spurring their horses, disappeared into the wilds, Their brave act ended the (notorious) tale of Massa Ranghar. (39)

Noordin addressed Natha Khehra and demanded either the hidden Mehtab Singh or the child who represented his line, refusing any plea for mercy. Natha Khehra understands that surrender would only invite more humiliation and death. He resolves instead to protect Mehtab Singh’s son even if the choice means abandoning safety and accepting battle on unequal terms. The page therefore turns from siege to rescue. pages.searchText: Natha Khehra Escapes with Rai Singh Under Pursuit Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan Once the escape is discovered, the Mughal hunt begins in earnest. Natha Khehra escapes with Rai Singh and orders his companions to think first of the child’s survival rather than their own comfort or honor. He instructs his own kin to carry the boy onward while he and a few others stay near the rear to delay pursuit. The decision is strategic and sacrificial at the same time, because every moment gained may save the child but increase the danger to the rescuers. Since death was hovering over their heads all around, It would no longer avail them to seek a shelter. pages.searchText: The Last Stand Narrows to the Child Rai Singh Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan The fighting grows still more desperate as losses mount around Natha Khehra. At the turning point Natha’s bow breaks, forcing him into close combat with the sword while mounted troops and muskets tighten the noose. One by one the defenders fall until the scene contracts around the endangered child. Rai Singh survives the clash only by fleeing, stumbling, and hiding where the attackers assume no one could endure for long. The page keeps the reader close to that vulnerability. What had been a battle narrative now becomes a survival narrative in which the future of a lineage hangs on one wounded child slipping through chaos. 158 suet chaupaî: dug dôhrâ gut chaupaî: tug dôhrâ gut chaupaî: Sri Gur Panth Prakash: ôH SÌd HifI 35 Sor | H dl UHdJ Sg [HUU | 34 fad Jeg Ü set | B39 oo BA KR gi (cul natthç tîr jânhi tan laya. sê lag dôsar ôr sidhâyâ. tab phir hônhâr yaun bhaî. utar kamân us chilliôn gaî.85. pages.searchText: A Market Woman Rescues the Wounded Child and Episode 98 Opens Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan The attackers leave the child behind, convinced their blows have finished him. Yet he remains alive, and the story takes an unexpected turn when a passing woman carries him in a basket rather than abandoning him to the field. She brings him toward Rudiala, where his wounds are sewn and his survival is credited to divine protection. The rescue gives the narrative a moment of mercy after prolonged pursuit, slaughter, and attempted extinction. At the same time the page serves as a hinge into a new chapter of Sikh defiance. Bota Singh! — the Martyr (He was charging an anna for a bullock cart and a penny for an ass) Let the author narrate the episode of (Bota) Singh, As he had heard it with his own ears. He was the one, who being unable to hear ill of the Singhs, Sacrificed his own life to keep their dignity. pages.searchText: Bota Singh Decides to Prove that the Khalsa Still Lives Mehtab Singh, Sukha Singh The new episode begins in an atmosphere of false triumph for the persecutors. So many Sikhs have been hunted that many people now say the Khalsa is finished, and Bota Singh mocked as an impostor becomes the sharp expression of that public disbelief. Those insults do not drive him into hiding. Instead they persuade him that only a bold open gesture can prove the Khalsa still lives and still has the courage to act before the eyes of the state. Bota Singh therefore establishes a post near Nurddin’s Sarai with a low-caste companion and starts collecting a token toll from passersby. pages.searchText: Bota Singh Writes a Defiant Toll Letter Mehtab Singh, Sukha Singh Bota Singh wrote a letter that turns hiding into open defiance. He announces that he and his companion are openly stopping traffic, demanding an anna for a bullock cart and a penny for an ass in order to show that the Khalsa still refuses erasure. The letter is meant as a public insult to Mughal authority, so the Nawab dispatches troops at once. Yet the page frames the challenge less as robbery than as deliberate political theater staged by men who want the state to face them directly. When the soldiers arrive, the Singhs refuse compromise. pages.searchText: The Two Singhs Rush Into Unequal Combat Mehtab Singh, Sukha Singh Negotiation is dismissed with contempt, because the Singhs say they have no business in court when the issue is already settled by tyranny and resistance. Instead they rush the Mughal force with staffs, stones, and spears, turning improvised weapons into marks of fearless resolve. The page delights in the disproportion of the contest. Against cavalry and trained troops, the Singhs move with the suddenness of a lion and refuse to give the enemy the psychological victory of seeing them hesitate. Every fresh attack only hardens their stance. pages.searchText: Bullet Fire Fails to Break the Singhs Mehtab Singh, Sukha Singh Close fighting does not subdue the two Singhs. They wrench out arrows, strike at horses with their sticks, and force their opponents to abandon the easy confidence of mounted combat. Only after those efforts fail do the Mughals resort to muskets and opened a heavy shower of bullets. Even then the page emphasizes not the success of the volleys but the astonishing persistence of the wounded Singhs, who continue pressing forward after terrible injury. pages.searchText: Bota Singh's Martyrdom and the Opening of Sukha Singh's Story Mehtab Singh, Sukha Singh The page closes the encounter by honoring the two Singhs for fighting eye to eye until martyrdom. Their deaths are treated as the sealing proof of a public challenge that neither the Nawab nor his troops could morally answer except by overwhelming force. The narrator then deliberately pivots away from mourning and into exemplarity. Now hear the story of Sukha Singh, whose life is introduced as the next demonstration of the same Khalsa daring in a new setting. This transition matters editorially because it turns one martyr episode into the threshold of another. pages.searchText: Sukha Singh Is Betrayed at Home and Jumps Into a Well S. Bota Singh — Th Martyr Sukha Singh avoids his home because Mughal surveillance makes family space dangerous. His parents, however, try to reclaim him from the Panth by arguing that their household has no place in Sikh sovereignty and by treating his Khalsa commitment as a dishonor to caste expectations. Their deception culminates in intoxicating him and cutting his hair. When he awakens to that violation, his grief is so fierce that he refuses ordinary consolation and jumped into a deep well rather than continue under disgrace. The page therefore frames the crisis as spiritual betrayal rather than domestic conflict alone. What has been attacked is not merely Sukha Singh's appearance, but the covenantal identity by which he belongs to the Khalsa. 172 Sri Gur Panth Prakash phauj murd: jab ut tc gai. vahi khabar us pit mata bhai. is khauph tç singh ghar na âvç. mat pita us bada lac have.5. tog: Hrg fs GA PH AY GH Mulo fA aur AH | gH 9 WS arasi? u[SHTdÌ A Aur ami IÉ I dôhrâ =: mát pitâ us im kahain ham singhan siun kaya kam. ham hai jat Kamînnî0 patishâhî són kaya kâm.6. zut: fu df Se ad ufa | gH =nles ud A aa mrt | ufsardt we Fe THAT | rü MY wre arf 121 chaupaî: singh hôi lain chahain patishâhî. ham kaminan ghar sô kab ahi. patishahi dâvô jatt kamahin. âpai bijain ape khahin.7. pages.searchText: Sukha Singh Is Redirected Toward Purposeful Martyrdom S. Bota Singh — Th Martyr An elder Singh intervenes to stop Sukha Singh from wasting his life in despair. He tells him to die fighting the Mughals if death is what he seeks, because martyrdom in service of the Panth is meaningful while self-destruction is not. Sukha Singh accepts the rebuke and rejoins disciplined action. He enters the Khalsa ranks with renewed intention, resolving to strike the enemy cleverly and effectively rather than merely to advertise wounded pride. The page closes with movement toward Lahore. After hitting the Mughals at random through stealth, He would disappear before they could retaliate. (18) There was a headmen of his own village, Who had in his possession a mare of very fine breed. Sukha Singh, on the pretext of taking the mare for water, Took away the mare in order to join the Khalsa ranks. (19) Sukha Singh, after joining the ranks of the Khalsa, Finally reached the camp office of (general) Sham Singh. Getting himself initiated from the (sacred) hands of Sham Singh, The latter developed a filial bond with his disciple. (20) Then, with a thought crossing Sukha Singh's mind, He decided to compensate his village headman for the mare. With this thought, he proceeded in the direction of Lahore, Disguising himself as a rustic peasant of the area. (21) With very little hair on his head (after the forced shave), He entered the centre of the sprawling city of Lahore. As he entered the market dealing in Gold and silver, He found traders carrying pouches filled with gold coins. (22)

pages.searchText: Sukha Singh Funds the Khalsa Through Daring Lahore Raids S. Bota Singh — Th Martyr Inside Lahore, Sukha Singh proves both audacity and speed by seizing wealth in the city and escaping before the alarm can trap him. The exploit is narrated as tactical intelligence rather than random theft, because his true loyalty lies with the Khalsa rather than with personal gain. Back among the Singhs he settles what he owes for his horse and contributed the entire booty to the community kitchen. The gesture is central to the page, showing that courage without service would be incomplete and that the raid feeds the Panth before it elevates the raider. The closing lines sharpen his martial profile. Sukha Singh is remembered as a fighter skilled across many weapons, but that prowess is nested inside humility, discipline, and communal giving. 176 tug dôhrâ gut chaupaî: gdr dôhrâ suet chaupaî Sri Gur Panth Prakash fea Bet Mu fame mal | cg sum Mu we Huet | as ust TITA Su | =l ô Í3ô ag HIS Aa 1231 ik thailî singh darishtg ai. phard kandhyôn singh lar main pai. chhcrd ghôrdî darvâjyôn langha. kari na tin kachhu marnô sanga.23.: wat afea fes sus a ffu su ue Q ôH | qa aiul xJ3 dd Mur Ha até fon èF 1281 ghardî duik din rahat thé singh bhayô paun kç bhg¢s. gayô gayô kahtç rahe singh mukkh ki6 nij d¢s.24.: oe de ag sft ug | sa Š DM HU STSÌ ae | saa GW fas Had edt | A Su aG sae fas nist 121 raulâ gaulâ jab tahin para. tab lau singh madh jhardin ralâ. turak phauj kit magrôn dauri. só langh gayó taraph kit auiî.25. af gad Mus veut | 5 ust o 9 SIS | ste A guu uu 9N ate | wet GUdÌ A srg sete 1261 jai raly6 singhan dal mahin. mull ghêrdi kê dai turtahi. tin sai rupyô dayó us jai. lat chaudharî són bat banâi.26. wid fue Q sare uret | ust 5 we fo Š fus yet | fel sis fu fos sfo tS | Sc H BTS HTS ged 1221 aur singhan kç langar pai. ghalî na ghar jahin thc pit mai. isi bhant singh nit tahin daurdain. lutt su layâvain mal chuph¢r¢.27.] yds Wu fas sa Bafo | CA H9 veS A NGUK | AS HAS ot fea We | JrH ute 8A HJS ASS OC | bahut singh chit bhayô uchhâhi. us mar hatâvain Jó gail¢ pâhi. sabh shastarn ki viddyâ janai. hath pai us bahut satânai.28. pages.searchText: Sukha Singh's Reputation, Domestic Return, and Excommunication S. Bota Singh — Th Martyr The narrative balances Sukha Singh's reputation for bravery with quieter camp virtues. He performs ordinary service, recites bani, remains prepared for combat, and thereby shows that Sikh heroism includes devotion and labor as well as battlefield prowess. Family pressure nevertheless draws him back home long enough for marriage and domestic entanglement. After the death of an infant daughter, accusation and suspicion gather around him until he is ex-communicated by the Khalsa Panth and left in painful separation from the fellowship that defined him. The page makes exclusion itself a form of torment. pages.searchText: Abdali Marches to Delhi and a New Sikh Challenge Opens S. Bota Singh — Th Martyr The page closes the previous emotional thread quickly and opens a wider military horizon. Ahmed Shah after occupation of Lahore proceeded on an expedition towards Delhi, leaving part of his force behind and creating a fresh field of conflict around the remaining Afghan presence. Those troops move against a Sikh village and force a local band across the river, but the gesture only invites a sharper confrontation. Rather than ending Sikh resistance, imperial occupation multiplies occasions for challenge and reply. By the close of the page a taunting epistle has been sent to the Singhs. pages.searchText: The Durranis and the Singhs Exchange Formal Challenges Bhai Sukha Singh’s bravery This page is built around taunt and answer. The Pathans try to define the Singhs as cowards who flee at mere arrival, while the Khalsa responds by stating its own terms for honorable combat rather than accepting the enemy's theatrical advantage. The Sikh reply narrows the issue with striking confidence: they will fight only when they are armed with their small firearms, because the form of combat must match the discipline and practice that the Guru has sanctioned for them. Public negotiation thus becomes another way of asserting Panthic self-definition. The atmosphere tightens toward a single-combat trial. Accusing the Singhs of being liars and fake Singh warriors, They branded the Singhs as cowards, slaves and serfs. (8) Challenging the Singhs either to stand face to face before them, Or to return and have a straight fight with them. Inviting the Singhs boastfully to advance in batches of two, And let each pair test their muscles against a single Durrani soldier. (9) The Singhs, organizing a (special) religious congregation, Went through the despatch and deliberated upon its contents. pages.searchText: Sukha Singh Kills the Pathan and the Khalsa Charges Bhai Sukha Singh’s bravery The duel turns savage as shield, sword, and horse all begin to fail under repeated blows. What began as formal combat collapses into a close struggle on the ground, showing how evenly matched and determined both fighters are. At the decisive moment, Sukha Singh seizes a fallen knife and kills the Pathan. The victory preserves Khalsa honor precisely because it is won after endurance, improvisation, and refusal to yield when the contest becomes desperate. The single combat immediately widens into collective battle. pages.searchText: Dohra: With such mighty strokes from both the sides, Bhai Sukha Singh’s bravery Dohra: With such mighty strokes from both the sides, Shields of both of them fell down after splintering. With each blow of their unmistakable strokes. (44) Chaupai: As the supporting belts of both were cut with sword strokes, All the dangling daggers and knives from the belts fell down. As the tips and sharp edges of their swords broke down, Both of them started grappling with each other. (45) As all the blood had drained out of the wounds, Their horses also lost their energy to support them. As each one's horse struck against the other's horse, Their riders too came too close to each other. (46) Dohra: Thus hitting and grappling with each other, Both of them tumbled down staggering on the ground. Getting seriously wounded due to the gaping head injuries, Both of them fell down and fainted on the ground. (47) Chaupai: As Sukha Singh regained little consciousness after some time, He raised his neck to survey the scene. Picking up a small knife he thrust it into Pathan's belly, Which scraped through the lungs and heart of the Pathan. (48) As he pulled it out of the Pathan's belly with full force, It took out all the intestines and arteries with it. As the great Guru had stood by His Khalsa Singh, Who had been extremely arrogant and defiant. Thus has Rattan Singh narrated this episode, As he had heard it from his elderly Singhs. As Karma Chhina made a dash with his spear, Sukha Singh repulsed his attack with a shield. (13) Soon after, Sukha Singh wielding his own sword, This was how Sukha Singh slaughtered Karma Chhina, And listen further to other exploits of Sukha Singh. (14) As the Mughal troops came to dominate the region, They prohibited the Sikhs from having a dip in sacred pool at Amritsar. As large Mughal army put up a camp at Amritsar, The Sikhs were desperate to hold a religious congregation there. (15) Episode 102 Another Episode About Sukha Singh's Brave Act (I will take a dip in the Sacred Pool in Daylight with Satguru's Grace) Since the day Bhai Mani Singh was taken into custody (by the Mughals), No Singh could enter the precincts of the holy Harimandir. So the Singhs would either take a dip in the sacred pool at night, Or they would go for ablutions at odd hours of the day. (1) At this the Muslim cleric made a surmise that, The Amritsar's holy influence was responsible for Khalsa's growth. That was why despite the untiring repression on the Singhs, They could not be eliminated by any means. (2) Then the Mughals set up a police post at the shrine, Which kept on killing the Akali Singhs day and night. Thereafter, the Mughals raised towers and minarets, Positioning their sharp shooters on these all around. (3) The moment they observed a little movement in the sacred pool, They fired a volley of shots from their muskets. After this, the Singhs would take a dip without any noise, Without being spotted by the Mughals in the darkness. (4) The Muslim cleric, being more infuriated by these furtive visits, Ordered for an army picket to be set up at the shrine. The Mughals were dumbfounded to witness such a scene once his Sikh identity became clear in the very place they had tried to seal off. Although it came in a flash as a lightening from the skies, Even then the Singhs gave a good account of themselves. pages.searchText: Episode About Mehtab Kot Sukha Singh's Brave Acis Those Singhs who had gone out on errands hear the firing and return without hesitation, ready to die if needed beside their companions. The Singhs greeted the night as one greets a sunrise, because darkness weakens Mughal confidence while restoring freedom of movement to the Khalsa. In that changed atmosphere, the fighting turns sharply. An exposed Mughal officer is struck down and the enemy line begins to lose its order, allowing the Singhs to convert a near-disaster into a night battle fought on more equal terms. The page closes by stressing renewal rather than mere survival. pages.searchText: Khalsa Conduct and the Lion Cave Episode Begins Mehtab Kot The page continues its portrait of persecuted Khalsa life by showing that the Singhs hide by day and move by night, refusing to surrender initiative even when heavily outnumbered. Their survival is presented not as passive concealment but as a disciplined rhythm of stealth, endurance, and sudden action against Mughal camps. From that wider description the narrative narrows into a specific ordeal, introducing the tale of Singhs who must take shelter in a lion's cave near Mirankot. Laddha Singh emerges as the central name in this setting, and the new sub-episode begins to translate collective Khalsa conduct into one intense local test. The transition matters because it shows how general persecution produced improvised refuges and legends of defiance. pages.title: The Lion Cave Is Betrayed to the Mughals
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Mehtab Kot

pages.searchText: The Lion Cave Is Betrayed to the Mughals Mehtab Kot Inside the cave, the hidden Singhs preserve a strict communal ethic, sharing whatever food can be gathered and making room for any brother who reaches the refuge. Small night journeys for grain and vegetables keep them alive, but the arrangement remains precarious because concealment is their only shield. That shield fails when the cave is betrayed to the Mughals, who learn who is inside and close in around the refuge. Laddha Singh Bhangoo, Ram Singh, and Sulakhan Singh Gill are identified, and the attackers begin to treat the cave like a trap that can be reduced by patience and force. The besiegers choose musket smoke as their first main method, hoping to suffocate or drive the Singhs out without facing their resistance in open combat. The page thus turns the cave from sanctuary into a battlefield shaped by confinement, ingenuity, and endurance. 210 chaupaî: aug dôhrâ gut chaupaî: tug dôhrâ Sri Gur Panth Prakash rati pardat singh ghar kê jana. ghar te milai su ral mil khâna. un singh pas kóü aur singh avai. usai khulâikai tau áp khâvai.7. fan Hu ú oH oe vo | SR uae mu sfg 8 | ng ag fiw Gah de | cA Úq së Q es A It jisç sikkh pai kam hôi china. usai khulâvai ap rahi fina. jôû jôû singh udmî hôi. das pañj ral kai daurdain sôi.8. pages.title: The Singhs Endure the Siege of the Lion Cave
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Mehtab Kot
pages.snippet: The Mughal assault on the cave becomes methodical as the attackers pour smoke into the opening, force villagers to dig, and then look for new ways to make the hiding place unlivable. Pressure from outside is relentless, but the trapped Singhs answer with the s
pages.searchText: The Singhs Endure the Siege of the Lion Cave Mehtab Kot The Mughal assault on the cave becomes methodical as the attackers pour smoke into the opening, force villagers to dig, and then look for new ways to make the hiding place unlivable. Pressure from outside is relentless, but the trapped Singhs answer with the same stubborn improvisation that has marked the entire episode. Within that struggle, the Singhs block the opening against smoke and fire by sealing gaps, using cloth and damp material, and refusing to panic while the siege intensifies. Their defense is as much moral as physical, because each improvised barrier declares that they will not simply be flushed out like animals. Local villagers also slow the attackers by dragging out the labor demanded of them, and nightfall finally breaks the immediate momentum of the operation. The moral of the episode is therefore not escape alone, but proof that persecution could not break the Khalsa's inner resolve. From that conclusion the book makes an explicit hinge into a new sakhi: Episode 105 opens with Subeg Singh Jambar, introduced as a firm Sikh whose standing is recognized widely enough to draw both confidence and scrutiny. The page marks the change clearly, using the end of one ordeal to prepare a different kind of martyrdom narrative. Once Subeg Singh enters the frame, the nawab's court begins pressing him with the familiar mixture of summons, offer, and coercive expectation. pages.snippet: Brought before the nawab and threatened with death, Subeg Singh refuses to convert and treats apostasy as worse than bodily destruction. His answer frames martyrdom as fidelity to dharam, not as a tragic accident, and it denies the court the moral satisfaction
pages.searchText: Subeg Singh Rejects Conversion and Mounts the Torture Wheel Khalsa's Conduct Brought before the nawab and threatened with death, Subeg Singh refuses to convert and treats apostasy as worse than bodily destruction. His answer frames martyrdom as fidelity to dharam, not as a tragic accident, and it denies the court the moral satisfaction of thinking fear can purchase assent. The authorities then bind him to the torture wheel, but even there he continues to invoke Akal and remember Guru Nanak rather than bargain for release. The page presents physical torment and spiritual steadiness side by side so that the violence of the regime only clarifies the firmness of the Sikh prisoner. By the end of the scene, the nawab has failed to shake Subeg Singh through threat alone and begins looking for new methods of pressure. At this, lowing his head in acceptance, Subeg Singh remarked, Blessed be that instrument and the moment (when he dies for his faith). (8) He begged the Nawab to put him on the torture rack, And have done with him without any further loss of time. As he had been a devout Sikh of the great Gurus, He would feel blessed to shed his mortal frame for his faith. (9) Great was the Nawab, greater still was his faith in Islam, Great must be his sense of justice, he being a legal expert. Should he (Subeg Singh) convert to Islam for fear of death, Would he never die after his conversion to Islam? (10) If death is imminent even after getting converted, Why should he give up his own religion in this life? He would gladly convert to Islam to escape death, As Islam was very dear to the worthy Nawab, So was his (Subeg Singh's) own religion very dear to him. He pleaded to be immediately executed on the torture rack, And be done away with without any further loss of time. Thereafter, issuing the orders for his execution, Subeg Singh's body was fixed between the wheels with spokes. pages.searchText: The Nawab Torments Subeg Singh’s Son before His Father Khalsa's Conduct Unable to move Subeg Singh directly, the nawab has Subeg Singh's young son tortured and hung up before his father's eyes. The violence is calculated to turn paternal grief into religious surrender, making the child a lever in the attempt to break the elder Singh's resolve. Instead, Subeg Singh blesses the child's firmness and reads the boy's suffering as honorable rather than shameful. The page turns what should have been emotional blackmail into another witness to Sikh steadfastness, with father and son reinforcing one another under terror. The nawab then shifts from spectacle to temptation, offering life, estate, protection, and future status if either of them will accept Islam. Torture and reward become two faces of the same coercive project, but neither is yet enough to compel consent. 218 suet chaupaî: aug dôhrâ gut chaupaî: Sri Gur Panth Prakash: Sy Tes SH ote | gia eid ag Cue ler | ws uJudÌ TIS waar | Aaa flu a do feu 1321 tab chandâlan vais¢ kina. bandh tang kar ultô dina. chârdah charkhardi bahut ghumâyâ. subçg singh kô nain dikhâyâ.17. pages.snippet: The executioners, carrying on the orders of the Nawab, Hung the infants body upside down with his legs tied. As they moved the spoked wheels with full force, Subeg Singh was made to see the torture with his own eyes. (17) Overwhelmed with emotion, Subeg Singh
pages.searchText: The executioners, carrying on the orders of the Nawab, Khalsa's Conduct The executioners, carrying on the orders of the Nawab, Hung the infants body upside down with his legs tied. As they moved the spoked wheels with full force, Subeg Singh was made to see the torture with his own eyes. (17) Overwhelmed with emotion, Subeg Singh kept remarking, Blessed be his son and blessed be the day of sacrifice. Blessed be the person who died for his faith, Blessed be he who yearned for the lotus feet of the Guru. (18) Thereafter bringing the child down after so much torture, The Nawab tried to bring him round through these mortifications. Telling the child that he, being immature, lacked wisdom, Why should he lose his life by being obdurate? (19) Informing the child that while his father had enjoyed every joy of life, What good purpose would it serve to keep his faith, If he ended his life without enjoying the comforts of life? (20) Impressing upon the child to get converted to Islam, The Nawab offered to grant him a vast landed property. So long as the country remained under a sovereign rule, Nobody could deprive him of his possession of that property. (21) Addressing Subeg Singh once again, remarked the Nawab, That he should save his son's life from the executioner's sword. He should keep his family line alive by saving his son, By swearing on the Islam's Koranic religious verses. The Gurus themselves surrendered their sons for the Panth, so he cannot preserve his own line by abandoning the very faith that gave his household meaning. That appeal to precedent transforms private suffering into continuity with Sikh history. What the court sees as stubbornness, the narrative presents as disciplined remembrance of how the Gurus placed truth above lineage, comfort, and worldly security. Frustrated by argument, the nawab abandons persuasion and orders the child's torture to be intensified again. pages.searchText: Inevitability of death was an accepted universal norm. Khalsa's Conduct Inevitability of death was an accepted universal norm. How could man escape death as it is inevitable. The Sikh Gurus had served the cause of Khalsa Panth, Even as they sacrificed their lives together with their progeny. (27) All the four sons of the Guru had given up their life, Sacrificing their lives at the altar of goddess of war. As they had sacrificed their whole family for the sake of the Sikhs, What distinction would the Sikhs earn preserving their progeny? (28) As this dialogue continued for some time, The Nawab had different thoughts in his mind. As the kind of advice Subeg Singh was tendering his son, The child was getting more and more adamant in his conviction. As the child's body would writhe in excruciating pain, He would forget everything about his Guru and guide. (30) The Nawab ordered to subject the child to extreme tortures, As well as grant land gifts if the child so desired. Thereafter, the executioners began to torture the child severely, With dragging him from his feet and giving blows on his face. (31) Revolving his whole body by dangling it from a single leg, Pricking his body with the their sharp teeth and nails, Inflicting pain by pulling at his nose and ears, They would threaten him with knocking down his teeth. The executioners and court, however, are not prepared to let the drama end there. Instead, the child is revived and pressed toward conversion, surrounded by those who try to rename his ordeal as rebirth into another faith. This maneuver aims to rewrite the meaning of suffering itself, turning near-death into an instrument of ideological capture. Subeg Singh is left astonished and heartsore as he watches the regime attempt to manufacture consent out of exhaustion and confusion. pages.searchText: As the executioners got exhausted with their job, Khalsa's Conduct As the executioners got exhausted with their job, Exhausting all means of torturing a human body, The child also went into a spell of deep silence, As a fit of spasmodic convulsion hit his system. (35) At this, the executioner gave an indication, That the child was on the verge of death. Subeg Singh felt elated at this remark, As the revered Guru had upheld his self-respect. (36) Blessed be his son and blessed be the womb who begot him, As their faith had been vindicated through their noble deeds. Subeg Singh recalled another similar incident (of religious conviction), Where a father had voluntarily got his son sawn into two pieces. (37) Thereafter ordering a servant to fetch some water, The Nawab, after sprinkling a bit on the child's face, put it in his mouth. As the child regained a bit of consciousness, The Nawab patted him to bolster his self-confidence. (38) Telling the child that since he had been born again after regaining consciousness, He would not be accused of converting to Islam after a new life. Summoning all the Hindus who had converted to Islam, He made them stand by the side of the child. (39) Persuading the child through their glib talk, These converts prompted him to say he would convert to Islam. Drifting between spells of unconsciousness and awakening, He spoke a few words with a staggering tongue. (40) The Nawab heaved a sigh of great relief, As he made the child say, I would convert to Islam. The child has been misled to convert through threats of torture, Subeg Singh heard his own words reverberating into his ears. (41) Being bewildered (at this sudden turn of events), Subeg Singh felt extremely pained at heart. Summoning the child to where Subeg Singh stood, The Nawab remarked that the child was converting to Islam. To Subeg Singh's query: What made him think of converting to Islam? The child replied that he could no longer bear the torture. Hearing this, Subeg Singh was stunned into dumb-foundedness, As he felt extremely desperate at such a catastrophe. pages.searchText: Subeg Singh Reads the Boy’s Forehead and Challenges the Nawab Khalsa's Conduct Refusing to accept appearances, Subeg Singh asks to see the boy closely so he can understand what has happened under torture and pressure. The request gives the scene a sudden intimacy, shifting attention from the court's spectacle to the father's searching discernment. When he studies the child, Subeg Singh asks to see the boy closely in a spiritual as well as physical sense, interpreting the moment through destiny, inscription, and the Guru's Name. He symbolically wipes away the fate he reads on the boy's forehead while uttering Akal and Satnam, turning the body itself into a site of contest between imposed identity and recovered truth. The nawab, unsettled by that act, immediately tests whether the child will still repeat the kalma or return to Sikh speech. pages.searchText: Episode 105 Closes and Bhai Taru Singh Enters the Narrative Khalsa's Conduct Rattan Singh closes the previous sakhi by saying he has written it as he heard it from his father, then turns the reader toward a new narrative movement. The page is a hinge rather than a single scene, because it deliberately finishes the earlier account before announcing a fresh episode. Episode 106 opens with Bhai Taru Singh, presented as a fearless martyr from the Majha village of Poolha whose scalp could be taken from his head but whose faith could not be taken from his heart. He is introduced as a disciplined, truthful, and devout Singh whose steadfastness will condemn the oppressor rather than save his own life. The page also frames the political problem that drives the episode: the Lahore nawab cannot understand how the scattered Singhs continue to live when they hold no offices, pursue no ordinary trade, and are hunted on every road. That question leads directly into the search for the hidden networks that keep the Khalsa alive. 228 Sri Gur Panth Prakash cust: Fat Ant dum H sts | BH ot fet wo fu ss | Ast Hat Sst gH adt | mA AS Hô afs set 1€21 chaupai: sunî sâkhî thi pas su tâti. tim hî likhi ratan singh bâti. j¢ti suni tçtî ham kahi. âgai aur sunó gati nai.62. ao€. mi set srg flu graft fadd HdÌu at (mrt 5 HIS 350 =...) 106. sakhi bhai tard singh bhujngi bidchî shahid ki (asin na marnôn natthan vârc...) cog: Hm 3y fu ot Hô THU Ho oe | Awe ged Š sau dust fad gz 191 dôhrâ —: sâkhî târâ singh ki sunôn singh man lâi. pages.searchText: How the Hidden Singhs Were Sustained Subeg Singh Jambar The nawab boasts that the villages linked to the Singhs have been ravaged, their kin dragged out of hiding, and Mughal parties sent everywhere to strike them down. On the surface, the regime appears to have cut every ordinary path of livelihood and reduced the fugitives to hunger and disguise. Yet the hidden Singhs were still being fed, and that stubborn fact unsettles the court. The page turns on the contradiction between relentless persecution and the continued survival of men who should, by the nawab's reasoning, have already perished from want. A malicious informer then reveals the answer: local Sikhs and sympathizers feed themselves only after feeding the Khalsa, willingly accepting privation so that the hunted Singhs can keep moving. The regime's military pressure has therefore failed to break the moral economy that sustains the Panth. 230 Sri Gur Panth Prakash jin pinndan main singh kó bhayô. sôî pind ujârd main dayó. chhôda gaç vai apnc d¢sh. bhûkhç hôi vatâvain bh¢s.7. pages.searchText: Harbhagat Names Taru Singh of Poolha Subeg Singh Jambar The nawab now demands names, ordering his men to identify those who send provisions to the Singhs so they can be destroyed as examples. Harbhagat Niranjania answers by turning suspicion into accusation and directing state violence toward specific Sikh householders. He points to Taru Singh of village Poolha, describing a cultivator who pays what is due, keeps only a little for himself, and sends the remainder onward to the Khalsa. Taru Singh is thus portrayed not as a rebel sustained by wealth, but as a village Sikh who converts ordinary labor into support for a persecuted community. The page widens that portrait by bringing in Taru Singh's mother and sister, who live austerely, reject rival devotional claims, and move supplies discreetly toward the Singhs; it then introduces Mehtab Singh as another dangerous supporter living more openly in militant fashion. His mother and sister who lived with him in his home, Keeping themselves alive on the barest minimum victuals, They covered their frail bodies with course clothes. Offering whatever they could save from their earnings, They reposed their faith in none else than the Singhs. (19) They made no offerings of any kind to the Muslim or Sultani Pir. Worshipping the Sikh Gurus and praying to the Gurus alone, They were least scared of dying for their faith. (20) Shunning to have immersion in the sacred Ganges and Yamuna rivers, They were content to take a dip in the Sikhs sacred pool. Branding Jagannath as a Hindu deity with arms maimed, They did not recite hymns in praise of Lord Rama and Krishna. (21) Dohra: Remaining still during the day, while moving at night, They kept themselves unnoticed by the Mughal patrols. Carrying a bundle on their heads, containing provisions, They made those provisions available to the Singhs. (23) Carrying out his raids in local and distant helmets, He supplied provisions to the Singhs through loot and plunder. Always having a band of fifty odd Singhs under his command, He waylaid the people and robbed them of their possessions. There was a Singh named Taru Singh, engaged in agriculture, Who paid state revenue along with all his fellow villagers. (17) After paying his dues and keeping a little bit for himself, He had been sending the rest to the Khalsa Panth Singhs. His mother and sister who lived with him in his home, They also earned some money doing some odd jobs. (18) Keeping themselves alive on the barest minimum victuals, They covered their frail bodies with course clothes. Offering whatever they could save from their earnings, They reposed their faith in none else than the Singhs. (19) While plugging their ears against the loudly audible Muslim Azan, They made no offerings of any kind to the Muslim or Sultani Pir. Worshipping the Sikh Gurus and praying to the Gurus alone, They were least scared of dying for their faith. (20) Shunning to have immersion in the sacred Ganges and Yamuna rivers, They were content to take a dip in the Sikhs sacred pool. Branding Jagannath as a Hindu deity with arms maimed, They did not recite hymns in praise of Lord Rama and Krishna. (21) Dohra: Remaining still during the day, while moving at night, They kept themselves unnoticed by the Mughal patrols. Carrying a bundle on their heads, containing provisions, They made those provisions available to the Singhs. (22) Chaupai: Mehtab Singh, being another member of the same fraternity, He hailed from a village known by the name Mirankot. Since the day he had beheaded Muslim feudal Massa Ranghar*, He had escaped into the wilds after deserting his own village. (23) Carrying out his raids in local and distant helmets, He supplied provisions to the Singhs through loot and plunder. Always having a band of fifty odd Singhs under his command, He waylaid the people and robbed them of their possessions. (24)

pages.searchText: Arrest of Bhai Taru Singh and the Bhardana Sikhs’ Rescue Plan Subeg Singh Jambar The narrative first recalls Mehtab Singh's rough methods of extracting resources, after which the nawab orders Harbhagat to seize him with a substantial force while sending a smaller detachment for Taru Singh. The contrast shows that the court reads Mehtab as a field threat but Taru Singh as a household supporter who can be captured more easily. The detachment succeeds in taking Taru Singh and carries him toward Bhardana, where crowds gather for a glimpse despite official blows and intimidation. In that tense pause between arrest and transfer, the Bhardana Sikhs wanted to free him and began to discuss rescue as a sacred duty rather than a mere act of local loyalty. When the proposal reaches Taru Singh, however, he refuses to let the sangat risk themselves for his release. pages.searchText: Bhai Taru Singh on the Gurus’ Sacrifice for the Panth Subeg Singh Jambar Taru Singh answers the rescue proposal by declaring that he will not run from death when death has come through service to the Panth. For him, martyrdom is not an accident to avoid but a conscious offering that aligns his own fate with the path already shown by the Gurus. He argues that the Gurus had given their own heads for the Panth, and not only their own heads but also the lives of sons and descendants. The point is not rhetorical excess: it grounds his refusal in a remembered chain of sacrifice through which Sikh dignity and collective purpose were preserved. From that memory he draws a political lesson as well, namely that any hope of sovereignty or communal honor under Mughal oppression demands willingness to suffer rather than compromise. His answer turns personal arrest into a meditation on how the Panth grows through costly fidelity. 236 Sri Gur Panth Prakash WHY 6 HIS Soo SS | MATA HATI yaw vers | JH fas ordo did fHg SS | us UST Uo MU ATS 1381 asin na marnôn natthan varg. asin ju mari hain mugal duvârc. ham sikkhan karan gur sir lâc. put pótrç pun ap kuhâc.34. ue aeS usd SET | EH rust did aw TST | GA a YA JN Her: | TH HIS 3 fan 66 WE |SU | panth badhâvan khâtar tain. im apni gur kul gavâî. us kç panthi hamain sadâcn. ham marng tç kim nath jagn.35. tog: Yama a args SS ale Cure | gu Ad fon H3 ve THI sda cë OTe 136! dôhrâ: panth râkhan kç kárnç çtç kîc upâi. dûkh sahe nij sut daç sir turkan dag lâi.36. oust: T HÍSdld HÌ Hu Sad | A fHg Š did we foad | gu wag we ast | 95 que se MU [Hog 1321 chaupaî: jô satigur thi mukh tc kahi. só sir dai gur lâj nibhî. chauthg babar laç kahâi. un bachnan bhag âp bikâi.37. nì fdg ufsrdt ufo 9 aet | HA ce fas fed o He | mH gga fie ug ue arg. | &U Bo fhe AIA S= SC | jô hindi patishahi chahi hai kôî. sis dîc bin phirai na sôî. jab turak hindi par pâvain bhar. lâyô un sir sis utâr.38. pages.searchText: Declaring that he would never flee from his impending death, Subeg Singh Jambar Declaring that he would never flee from his impending death, Definitely would he offer himself for sacrifice to the Mughals. The Guru had not only sacrificed his own life for the Sikhs, He had sacrificed his sons and garandsons* as well. (34) It was for the glory and expansion of the Khalsa Panth, That Guru had put an end to his own family line. The Sikhs being the devout followers of the Sikh Gurus, How could he flee from making a sacrifice? (35) It was for the preservation of the glory and dignity of the Khalsa Panth, That so many sacrifices were made by the Sikh Gurus. The Guru not only suffered himself and sacrificed his sons, He blamed the Mughals squarely for these sacrifices. (36) Whatever had the Guru professed from his sacred lips, He fulfilled his sacred vow with a supreme sacrifice. The Guru getting himself slaughtered by the fourth Babur, Sacrificed his life for the sake of keeping his vow. (37) The Guru had ordained whenever the Hindus (Sikhs) wished to regain sovereignty, It would never be regained without making a sacrifice. Whenever the Mughals committed oppression on the Hindus, The Sikhs should hold the Mughals responsible for their sacrifice. (38) This message which Guru Nanak had given to Guru Angad Dev, Had been passed over to Guru Amardas by Guru Angad Dev, While Guru Amardas had communicated it to Guru Ram Das, Guru Arjun had fulfilled this mandate with his own sacrifice. (39) Thereafter Guru Hargobind and Guru Har Rai carried on, But they did not get an opportunity to make sacrifices. Guru Harkrishan, reaching Delhi after being arrested, Sacrificed after putting the entire blame on the Mughals. (40) Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur accepted the Guru's mandate gracefully, After contemplating over Guru Nanak's ordained message. The Guru accepted Mughal's persecution voluntarily at Delhi, Getting himself beheaded by the Mughal's oppressives sword. (41) The great Guru Gobind Singh, following the glorious tradition, Fulfilled the mendate as ordained by Guru Nanak, the same way. Sacrificing his own life along with those of his whole family. pages.searchText: Bhai Taru Singh Explains Why the Guru’s Vow Cannot Be Undone Subeg Singh Jambar Continuing his reply, Taru Singh says one sheath cannot hold two swords and that two sovereign claims cannot share one throne. The image compresses the page's argument: the Khalsa's path and imperial domination cannot both be preserved intact, so sacrifice becomes the price of truth. When the gathered Sikhs ask why the Gurus accepted such suffering, Taru Singh says the Guru's utterance cannot be erased because it was written in the divine court. What has been spoken and sealed in that higher register must be fulfilled even when fulfillment demands bodily loss. He therefore insists that a Sikh cannot seek to save his own life after the Gurus have spent theirs for the community, while also pointing the sangat back toward the older history of Guru Nanak and Babur. pages.searchText: Episode 107: Sakhi of Babur Subeg Singh Jambar Episode 107 opens with the Sakhi of Babur and explicitly announces a retrospective turn away from Taru Singh's immediate scene toward the older cause of Guru-suffering. The page frames this as the beginning of an explanatory history rather than a break in devotional seriousness. Using the comparison of an incautious boon, the poet says Guru Nanak's utterance toward Babur later required endurance and suffering for the sake of the Sikhs. Readers are asked to listen closely because the new episode explains how a spoken blessing can reverberate through later generations. From there the narration starts laying out the political stage around Talvandi Rai Bhoi, Daulat Khan Lodhi, and the conditions that will draw Babur into the story. pages.searchText: Daulat Khan’s Sons Rise, Then Fall under Bairam Khan Bhai Taru Singh — A Fearless Manyi The page continues the account of Daulat Khan's household by saying that Daulat Khan's wives received Guru Nanak's blessing and then bore the sons they had long desired. Those sons are named and positioned as the fruit of grace before the narrative shifts to their political advancement. As the four boys mature, they enter service and become nawabs or high officials at the Delhi court under the Lodhi order. Their rise links Guru Nanak's blessing with worldly prominence, but only briefly, because court politics remain unstable and dangerous. After Sikandar Lodhi's line passes on, Bairam Khan's arrogance ruins experienced governance, and Daulat Khan's sons are among those destroyed in the ensuing violence. pages.searchText: Daulat Khan Flees to Guru Nanak after the Slaying of His Sons Bhai Taru Singh — A Fearless Manyi After the murder of Rai Bhoi and the spreading fear at court, confidence in Bairam Khan collapses and officials begin to scatter, hide, or think only of escape. The courtly world that had once rewarded Daulat Khan's house now feels exposed to arbitrary destruction. News reaches Daulat Khan that his sons have been killed, and Daulat Khan fled toward Eminabad in search of the one refuge still imagined as trustworthy. The movement is both geographic and spiritual, carrying him away from compromised political power and toward Guru Nanak's presence. By the end of the page he is no longer a grand court figure but a bereaved father hurrying to fall at the Guru's feet. Dohra Chaupai: Sri Gur Panth Prakash 245 After Rai Bhoi's murder most foul, All the courtiers felt threatened. Visualising the emperor as a tyrant, They lost all hope of a dignified existence. While some deserted, others went underground, Some others hurled defiance at the ruler, While some died others withdrew from royal service, Thus the emperor lost whole of his army. (17) Sending a message through a messenger, Daulat Khan's sons informed their dear father: That his innocent sons had been killed, By the arrogant and haughty Bairam Khan. They advised their father to flee to Kabul, Otherwise, he, too, would be eliminated. He, too, should never miss an opportunity to retaliate, If he ever had any love for his sons. (18) He must pay his obeisance to Guru Nanak, If he wished his cherished goal to be realized. He would not fail in his endeavour, If he got himself blessed by Guru Nanak. The Guru being Omniscient about everything, He must seek Guru's intercession in his venture. He must inform the Guru about the murder of his sons, Who were born on this earth with his blessings. (19) Getting news of the murder of his sons, Daulat Khan bolted out leaving Ludhiana. Asking for a route leading to Emnabad*, He rushed with the speed of a fast running messenger. Doning black robes on his body, He ran for his life day and night. Remaining unmindful of feeding himself, He was obsessed with escaping from there. (20) The spot where Guru Nanak was meditating, While sitting on a mound of rocks and pebbles, Desperate Daulat Khan fell prostrate, At the lotus feet of Guru Nanak. (21) Although the great Guru was omniscient, But he kept silent for the sake of his devotee.

pages.searchText: Daulat Khan Urges Guru Nanak to End Pathan Rule and Take the Throne Bhai Taru Singh — A Fearless Manyi Having laid out the facts of his ruin, Daulat Khan places himself in Guru Nanak's refuge and asks for protection against the Pathan order that has devoured its own supporters. The page presents him as a petitioner who now sees truth more clearly than he did while secure in office. In the boldest part of his plea, Daulat Khan urged Guru Nanak to take the throne of Hindustan so that tyrannical rule might be broken at its root. His request is not merely personal revenge; it is a proposal that spiritual authority should replace failed and violent kingship. Guru Nanak does not seize that invitation, instead remaining detached from worldly ambition and indicating that he has come to bestow sovereignty, not to hoard it for himself. The page thus closes the appeal by distinguishing divine mission from temporal possession while leaving the political problem fully exposed. 246 Sri Gur Panth Prakash chaupai: thc satigur sabh jani jan. uskâ rakhng khâtar mân. satigur bât sabhô sun laî. sabh hakîkat daulat kahî.22. (22) After listening to Daulat Khan's woes, the guru kept silent, Nor did he answer his pleas in haste. At this, Daulat Khan pleaded for the Guru's blessings, Placing his headgear at the Guru's feet. (23) May the Guru protect him or cause him to perish. Since Bairam Khan had slaughtered the Guru's devotees, Daulat Khan was pleading before the Guru for justice. (24) The Guru, for upholding the dignity of his devout followers, Since the Pathan ruler had turned cannibalistic, Pathans sovereignty over India must be done away with. (25) Either the great Guru himself should become a sovereign ruler, Or he should anoint his son as the new sovereign. The sovereignty over India being of great significance, The Guru must preserve it in his own household. (26) Hearing this, the great Guru told Daulat Khan, That he was in no need of any sovereignty. Of what consequence was the sovereignty of India, When he had renounced millions of such sovereignties. (27) It was for the task of bestowing sovereignty on others, That the Divine Lord had sent him (the Guru) in the age of Kaliyuga. Since the life of a sovereign was always a bed of thorns, The Guru experienced great happiness in meditation on the Divine. (28) Why should he (the Guru) take over such a sovereignty, That Daulat Khan was talking about time and again? Would the people not heap ridicule upon him, For having grabbed it after forsaking it earlier? Hearing this, all hopes of Daulat Khan about, Guru's acceptance of sovereignty were dashed to the ground. After this, Daulat Khan abandoned all efforts, To press the Guru again and again to become a sovereign. (29) In case the Guru refused to accept sovereignty himself. Since the life of a sovereign was always a bed of thorns, The Guru experienced great happiness in meditation on the Divine. (28) Why should he (the Guru) take over such a sovereignty, That Daulat Khan was talking about time and again? Would the people not heap ridicule upon him, For having grabbed it after forsaking it earlier? Hearing this, all hopes of Daulat Khan about, Guru's acceptance of sovereignty were dashed to the ground. After this, Daulat Khan abandoned all efforts, To press the Guru again and again to become a sovereign. (29) Thereafter, Daulat Khan made another proposal, In case the Guru refused to accept sovereignty himself. 247

The prophecy does not merely promise a change of rulers; it tells Daulat that he is asking for a transfer he will never be able to undo. Guru Nanak then turns prediction into instruction. He tells Daulat Khan to go swiftly to Kabul and place the matter before Babur, making clear that the coming upheaval has already entered the field of destiny. Encouraged by that command, Daulat Khan leaves joyfully in disguise rather than as a grand courtier. pages.searchText: Daulat Khan Reports Hindustan's Disorder to Babur Bhai Taru Singh — A Fearless Manyi After initial difficulty reaching the conqueror, Daulat Khan was given audience with Babur and finally able to speak about conditions in Hindustan. He lays before Babur the secrets of Delhi and the weakness of the Lodhi-Pathan establishment, turning private grievance into a full political briefing. His complaint is that misrule has become structural rather than accidental. Experienced officers and wazirs were slain or discarded, while immature and incapable men were elevated into posts that required judgment, discipline, and strategic sense. He got into touch with Babur in a moment's time. (39) Babur, according a state honour to Daulat Khan, Heard the whole account about India from the latter. Disclosing all the state secrets of Delhi court to Babur, Daulat Khan revealed the complete strength of the Lodhi Pathans Army. (40) Disclosing Bairam Khan's slaughter of all the seasoned custodians, The new custodians, failing to govern their states efficiently, Had started accusing their predecessors for misgovernance. (41) He had slaughtered all the higher officials of the state, Together with the Provincial custodians and ministers. In their place, he had appointed immature rustic adolescents, Giving them higher positions of state and court officials. (42) The miniscule number that survived this ruler's tyranny, They, too, had lost every hope of their survival. All the feudal chiefs, too, became frustrated with the situation, Even as the Maratha custodians in the south were also replaced. (43) Rai Bhoi who, being the seniormost among the ministers, Was also the wisest and the most sensible among them. As he witnessed the elimination of all the senior functionaries, He realized that the state administration was going to the dogs. (44) Being the emperor's well-wisher he advised the king in good faith, That the dwarfs could never accomplish tasks worthy of giants. Neither should the great warriors deserved to be killed, Nor could the petty people accomplish the higher tasks of the state. pages.searchText: Rai Bhoi's Death and the Minister's Counsel to Babur Bhai Taru Singh — A Fearless Manyi The page closes the Rai Bhoi thread by showing how badly wisdom is repaid under corrupt rule. Rai Bhoi was slain without offense, and there was great outcry because the ruler had destroyed his own well-wisher instead of listening to him. From that lament the narrative pivots into Babur's next decision. Though Babur was made ready to advance on Hindustan, his advisers insist that conquest cannot be undertaken blindly in a land guarded by saints and holy men. The minister's counsel focuses above all on Guru Nanak. pages.searchText: Babur Challenges Nanak's Authority and Marches to Meet Him Babur Babur reacts skeptically when Daulat Khan says Guru Nanak can bestow or withhold sovereignty. He asks who Nanak is to grant kingship and then resolves that let us go and see him, treating the encounter as a test of spiritual claim rather than an act of devotion. His tone remains threatening as well as curious. Babur says that if the saint proves false he should be punished or converted, while if he is genuine Babur will judge the matter from direct experience rather than rumor. The army therefore advances toward the Guru with a mixture of challenge and expectation. Babur kept on entrusting the enroute territory after getting a ransom. Thereafter, he ransacked a village occupied by Pathan residents, Which was known by the name Saidpur at that time. (15) For having shown disrespect to Guru Nanak once, The residents of this village had to bear this devastation. Thereafter, summoning Daulat Khan to his own camp, Babur issued orders to him to the following effect: (16) Nanak's seat had been reported to be near Emnabad. Assuring Daulat Khan of not ill-treating Nanak in anyway, That no scare of any kind could unnerve the great Guru. The Guru, being the creator and destroyer of the whole world, The whole universe prospered under the command of his Divine Will. (19) Dohra: The spot where Guru Nanak sat in deep meditation, Was situated upon a mound of hard rocks and pebbles. So immovable remained Guru's seat that it never shook, Even if the whole earth and mountains shook and guaked. (20) Spotting out the Guru's seat after arriving in its vicinity, He started walking on foot after dismounting from his steed. pages.searchText: Daulat Khan Brings Babur Toward Guru Nanak Babur Daulat Khan reports the situation to Guru Nanak and explains that Babur wants an audience with him. The Guru does not rush toward imperial summons; instead he calmly directs the movement of the meeting on his own terms. To prepare that encounter, Mardana is told to play the rabab so that music rather than force becomes the medium through which Babur and his people are drawn near. The page uses that moment to show that the Guru's court gathers itself through sound, serenity, and command rather than through royal ceremony. Babur also asks what sort of offering should be brought before such a pir, and Daulat reminds him that spiritual and temporal authority alike rest with the Guru. He wants to know whether he is raw or ripe, true or false, as though spiritual authority were something that could be tested like a courtly riddle. Guru Nanak refuses that frame. pages.searchText: Babur Submits and Seeks Guru Nanak's Favor Babur Babur now realizes that Guru Nanak already knows the intention he has not fully spoken aloud. That recognition breaks his earlier arrogance and convinces him that the Guru stands near the divine in a way no imperial calculation can master. He therefore approaches with visible respect and admits what he has heard from others. Calling Nanak the great Hindu pir, he asks whether the hopes that brought him here can truly be fulfilled.
