pages.title: Cursed miracles are the fancy of temporal monarchs,
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Babur ...
pages.snippet: Cursed miracles are the fancy of temporal monarchs, Who seize others belonging with coercion and duress. If ever a saint indulges in working out miracles, He is sure to find himself alienated from the Divine. (41) Upon this, Babur realized Guru Nanak's omnisci
pages.searchText: Cursed miracles are the fancy of temporal monarchs, Babur Cursed miracles are the fancy of temporal monarchs, Who seize others belonging with coercion and duress. If ever a saint indulges in working out miracles, He is sure to find himself alienated from the Divine. (41) Upon this, Babur realized Guru Nanak's omniscience, Since the Guru had laid bare all Babur's secret thoughts. He decided to share all his fears and aspirations, After he felt assured about Guru Nanak's omniscience. (42) Babur felt convinced after his interaction with Guru Nanak, That the latter had really an intimate relationship with God. Since there existed no distinction between God and Guru Nanak, He must seek his blessings for getting a sovereignty over India. (43) If, God willing, the Guru Nanak answered his prayers, All his dreams and aspirations will get materialized. If, God forbid, Guru Nanak declined his prayers, He would not lose anything substantial of his own. (44) Why should he poison his future through his insolence, After this, folding his hands in supplication, Babur put forth, His dire necessity in words couched in politeness. (45) Prostrating at the lotus feet of Divine Guru Nanak, Babur begged for his aspirations to be fulfilled, Acknowledging Guru Nanak as the great Hindu prophet, He had sought the Guru's blessings in his dire need. (46) Acknowledging Guru Nanak to be as great as he had heard, Babur declared the Guru as the greatest among spiritual prophets. Admitting that after having a glimpse of the Divine Guru, He felt assured of Guru Nanak's Divine attributes. (47) Finding the Guru as venerated as in narrations he had heard, Babur found the Guru spiritually Supreme after a through probe. Whatever divine attributes of the Guru had Daulat Khan narrated, Babur had observed and confirmed with his own eyes. (48) The way the (Lodhi) Pathans had got the Guru's followers assassinated, Daulat Khan had narrated the whole account to Babur. Babur also knew about Guru's displeasure with the Lodhi Pathans, As well as the Guru's will to dispense with their rule over India. He says he came because he was called and asks Guru Nanak to grant him the throne of Hindustan rather than leaving the matter hanging in hints and half-confessions. Guru Nanak refuses to flatter that ambition in worldly language. If Babur claims kingship under God and appeals to pirs and prophets, then he must carry the question beyond politics and seek its answer through the higher court he himself invokes. Babur accepts the rebuke and asks for a way to approach that reality. pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Babur ...

pages.searchText: It was Guru's will to call the Mughals from Kabul, Babur It was Guru's will to call the Mughals from Kabul, As the Guru, being omniscient and privy to the Divinee Will. Babur told the Guru that the former had arrived at Guru's bidding, Since Daulat Khan had invited him (Babur) in the Guru's name, The Guru must protect and stand by his humble servant. Babur begged the Guru to make him occupy India's throne, Dohra: Babur said he had approached Guru Nanak with a fond wish, That the great Guru be Babur's spiritual mentor. Babur begged for a sovereignty over the Indian throne, So that his writ might run over the twenty-two states. (52) Chaupai: Upon this Baba Nanak reminded the supplicating Babur, That the latter wished to be made a sovereign by Prophet Mohammad. Babur expressed his inability to seek Prophet's (Mohammad's) blessings. (53) Since his prophet was inhabitant of the Divine Court, It was located across the seven skies (in heavens). How could Babur (a human being) reach that Divine abode, About which he had heard but never seen it with his eyes? (54) The Guru reminded Babur that he had boasted of being an emperor, Whose writ ran over half of humanity on the earth. How could he not reach his Islamic Prophet Mohammad, As he boasted of having the powers of five spiritual prophets? (55) Promising Babur to enable him to reach his prophet, The Guru directed Babur to seek sovereignty from his own prophet. Babur should reach the Divine Court in his prophet's company, Where his prophet would get a written sanction for his sovereignty. (56) Dohra: Hearing this, Babur bent on his knees in thankfulness, Begging Guru Nanak to enable him to have a glimpse of his own prophet. Being extremely confident of his prophet's divine powers, Babur was sure of getting India's sovereignty sanctioned. pages.searchText: Babur Enters the Heavenly Court by Satnam Babur Guru Nanak now equips Babur for a visionary ascent rather than a political bargain. He teaches him the repetition of satnam and marks him for the journey, turning the emperor's request into an initiation that depends on remembrance instead of force. Led upward toward the heavenly threshold, Babur discovers that rank alone gains him nothing. The gate opens when he invokes satnam, proving that even an emperor enters the higher court only by the Name rather than by sword, lineage, or command. Inside, Babur beholds Guru Nanak's banner, devotional music, scripture, and radiant assembly in divine presence. pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Babur ...
pages.snippet: With burning jos-sticks and a lamp, he should prostrate before the staff, After which it would take Babur wherever he wished to go. With the continuous recitation of God's holy Name Satnam, The Guru's staff would take Babur and his prophet to heaven, Where nob
pages.searchText: With burning jos-sticks and a lamp, he should prostrate before the staff, Babur With burning jos-sticks and a lamp, he should prostrate before the staff, After which it would take Babur wherever he wished to go. With the continuous recitation of God's holy Name Satnam, The Guru's staff would take Babur and his prophet to heaven, Where nobody would stop their entry into the Divine Court. The same Divine Court was it where prophet once had gone, But was made to return the same moment to his abode. (60) With Guru's staff with them, they could stay there for many hours, While his prophet could converse with God for long. Staying there in the Divine Court for a longer spell, He and his prophet could seek whatever they wished. (61) With a respectful bow did Babur depart from Guru Nanak, Wondering at heart at the promised great miracle. Babur departed after holding the Guru's staff. (62) The moment Babur performed the proffered incantations, The Guru's staff took him on a flight the same moment. Flying across the seven skies with the Guru's staff, Babur reached the exclusive territory of the Divine Court. (63) He found the Divine Court bolted and barred from inside, Which did not open even at the approach of prophet Mohammad. But the moment Babur recited the Guru's word Satnam, In an instant opened all the doors that were barred and locked. (64) Babur witnessed Guru Nanak's standard fluttering in heavens, And heard spiritual hymns being recited from the holy books. Spiritual melodies were being recited to the accompaniment of music, Filling the whole environment with a spiritual ambience. (65) Thus, Babur saw with his own eyes after reaching there, Guru Nanak's standard fluttering inside the Divine Court. Observing Nanak's standard fluttering at the entrance, Babur had a glimpse of God seated on the Divine seat. (66) Sparkling as the crystal waters of the scared Ganges, Its saffron cloth fluttered as majestically as, If a spark of lightening had flitted across its surface. pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Babur ...
pages.snippet: Babur is shown Guru Nanak's heavenly dharamsal, a radiant spiritual court filled with saints, holy attendants, and every sign of divine abundance. The page lingers over its trees, fragrance, pillars, and jeweled architecture to show that Guru Nanak's authority
pages.searchText: Babur is shown Guru Nanak's heavenly court Babur Babur is shown Guru Nanak's heavenly dharamsal, a radiant spiritual court filled with saints, holy attendants, and every sign of divine abundance. The page lingers over its trees, fragrance, pillars, and jeweled architecture to show that Guru Nanak's authority exceeds any earthly throne. After this heavenly tour, Babur is taken onward to the enclosure associated with the Prophet, where he sees the mosque, the standard, and the gathered assembly at prayer. He is brought forward before the prophet so that he can present the desire weighing on his mind. Babur asks for the throne of India, hoping that his petition will be granted from that court. pages.title: The Divine Court had, on its premises, five mythological trees,
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Babur ...
pages.snippet: The Divine Court had, on its premises, five mythological trees, Bearing the names of Parjat, Kalap Birchh, Santaan, Harichandan and Mandhar. Besides, there were other trees laden with flowers and fruit, As well as the mythical cows of the Kamdhen breed. (69) W
pages.searchText: The Divine Court had, on its premises, five mythological trees, Babur The Divine Court had, on its premises, five mythological trees, Bearing the names of Parjat, Kalap Birchh, Santaan, Harichandan and Mandhar. Besides, there were other trees laden with flowers and fruit, As well as the mythical cows of the Kamdhen breed. (69) With rare Chinta Mani? stones were the walls of Divine Court built, With fragrant golden paint were these rare walls painted. With Vaduraya? stones were pillars of Divine Court erected, With the fragrant Sandalwood was its majestic roof inlaid. pages.searchText: Guru Nanak grants Babur conditional sovereignty Babur Babur pleads that he entrusted himself to Daulat Khan only because he had staked everything on Guru Nanak's name, and he now asks the Guru to preserve his honor. Guru Nanak responds with compassion, accepts the petition, and prepares a symbolic act to show how the boon will be measured out. He asks for Babur's bag of intoxicant and pours out seven handfuls of bhang, granting a line of rule that will run through seven generations. The gift is real, but it is given as a marked favor rather than as an unconditional right. Guru Nanak then warns that India has been bestowed for a trifling exchange and can also be taken back. pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Babur ...
pages.snippet: Guru Nanak answers Babur by explaining that a boon can be withdrawn when the recipient proves unworthy of preserving it. Gifts received freely carry obligations, and divine favor does not remain with rulers who violate the moral terms under which it was grante
pages.searchText: Guru Nanak warns Babur that a boon can be withdrawn Babur Guru Nanak answers Babur by explaining that a boon can be withdrawn when the recipient proves unworthy of preserving it. Gifts received freely carry obligations, and divine favor does not remain with rulers who violate the moral terms under which it was granted. He then turns prophetic and tells Babur that Mughal sovereignty will be revoked if his descendants persecute the later Gurus. Babur folds his hands in protest, insisting that his house reveres the Guru and that such betrayal should not come from his line. The narrative immediately begins to test that claim by turning toward the later emperors. pages.searchText: The Mughal line breaks Babur's covenant with Guru Nanak Babur The prophecy unfolds across the Mughal generations as court clerics and emperors turn against the Sikh Gurus. The page recalls the harm done under Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb, connecting imperial power to the suffering inflicted on Guru Arjan, Guru Harkrishan, Guru Tegh Bahadur, and the Guru's household. These persecutions prove that the Mughal rulers broke their covenant and failed to preserve the sovereignty that had been granted conditionally. What Babur received through supplication, his successors squandered through arrogance, violence, and religious hostility. By the close of the page, Guru Nanak's warning stands vindicated: the dynasty's seven-generation lease on power is exhausted by breach of trust. Harbhagat and Mughal forces move to seize Mehtab Singh, but his fame as a fearless Singh already terrifies his enemies. (6) Laying the blame for his sacrifice squarely on Lahore's Nawab, Bhai Taru Singh would make the Nawab face Divine retribution. Keeping his faith with hair intact till the last breath, Bhai Taru Singh would lay the blame squarely on the Mughals. (7) Acquiescing and abiding with the will Divine, Would Taru Singh succeed in proving the Mughals guilty. Praise be to the Singh who wages a religious war, Praise be to him who sacrifices accusing the Mughals. (8)

pages.searchText: Mehtab Singh Resolves to Join Bhai Taru Singh (Taru Singh) The page opens with a reflection on martyrdom: death is fruitful when one keeps faith and Sikhi even while facing the Turks or Mughals. It praises Bhai Mani Singh, Bhai Dyal Singh, Subeg Singh, and Subeg Singh’s son as examples who held their faith under torture. Mehtab Singh then measures himself against that line of martyrs. He asks what merit there is in preserving his body while hidden, how he could sit near those martyrs in the Divine court, and why he should waste a human birth without seeking the status of martyrdom. Thinking of Bhai Taru Singh as his intimate companion, Mehtab Singh decides to go toward Lahore and join him through sacrifice. The account dwells on Mehtab Singh's execution on the spoked wheel as an act of fearless witness rather than defeat. pages.searchText: Bhai Taru Singh rejects the Nawab's demand Mehtab Singh Bhai Taru Singh enters the Nawab's court with Sikh greetings and immediately provokes anger by refusing to show fear. He questions why he is being harassed when he pays revenue, lives honestly, and shares his earnings in charity. The dispute sharpens when the Nawab presses him to abandon Sikhi and accept Islam. Would never convert to Islam, Taru Singh insists, because fidelity to the Guru matters more to him than life itself. The page therefore frames his ordeal not as a political interrogation but as a public test of religious steadfastness. pages.searchText: Bhai Taru Singh entered the court with traditional Singh greetings, Mehtab Singh Bhai Taru Singh entered the court with traditional Singh greetings, So incensed felt the Nawab hearing these Sikh greetings, As if somebody had rubbed salt after slicing his fingers. He had been paying the prescribed tax on it as well. (4) He had been sustaining his family on that income. He had been sharing those provisions with others in need. (5) What did the Nawab lose by the latter's austerity, That he (Nawab) was bent on persecuting the latter? Being incensed and outraged by Bhai Taru Singh's argument, The Nawab used unparliamentary words against the latter. (6) The Nawab asked Bhai Taru Singh to get converted to Islam, Otherwise the former would not spare the latter's life. Bhai Taru Singh retorted that he, being a stranger to fear, Could conversion to Islam save him from death, And must uphold his faith till his last breath. (8) Thereafter, the Nawab repeated his proposal once again, The latter must convert to Islam if he wished to live. In terms of financial package or landed property. (9) He could also ask for a Mughal Pathan bride, As well as live in comfort in a palatial mansion. Upon this, Bhai Taru Singh made these remarks: The Nawab must grant what was dearest to the latter's heart. (4) Whatever legitimate income he earned after paying taxes, He had been sustaining his family on that income. Whatever little he saved out of his own meager nutritional needs, He had been sharing those provisions with others in need. (5) What did the Nawab lose by the latter's austerity, That he (Nawab) was bent on persecuting the latter? Being incensed and outraged by Bhai Taru Singh's argument, The Nawab used unparliamentary words against the latter. (6) The Nawab asked Bhai Taru Singh to get converted to Islam, Otherwise the former would not spare the latter's life. Bhai Taru Singh retorted that he, being a stranger to fear, Would never convert to Islam under any circumstances. He must keep his faith rather than pandering to Nawab's offer, And must uphold his faith till his last breath. The latter could also ask for any favours he wished, In terms of financial package or landed property. (9) He could also ask for a Mughal Pathan bride, As well as live in comfort in a palatial mansion. Upon this, Bhai Taru Singh made these remarks: The Nawab must grant what was dearest to the latter's heart. (10) 289

pages.searchText: If it pleased the Nawab to be compassionate towards him, Mehtab Singh If it pleased the Nawab to be compassionate towards him, He must not ask Taru Singh to convert to Islam. The Nawab must suggest such a way out to Taru Singh, As would enable the latter to keep his faith till his last breath. (11) Feeling highly enraged at these words of Bhai Taru Singh, The Nawab started using abusive language against the latter. Ordering his minions to give severe shoe beatings to the latter, He ordered the barbers to shave off his sacred hair. (12) Thereupon, Bhai Taru Singh said (in a prophetic vein) to the Nawab, That this ordered shoe-beatings would recoil upon his own head. The Sikhs who were perfect in their faith in their Gurus, They would sacrifice their lives with their sacred hair intact. As the barbers tried again and again to do their job, Their hands became numb and bereft of energy. He then turns from defense to prophecy and declares that the Nawab will not escape the consequences of persecuting a saint. The page explicitly opens the next episode by warning that The Nawab developed a blockage in his urinary tract as the divine answer to this cruelty. Neither posture, clerical recitation, nor established Muslim holy men can ease the torment that has seized him. His suffering grows more terrifying because he begins to imagine The spirits of martyred Singhs closing in around him with weapons drawn. What had looked like a worldly illness is now understood as a visitation tied directly to Bhai Taru Singh's words. (1) A minute on the floor, a minute on the bed would the Nawab stretch, Resting for a while, soon would he get up with a start. Claiming that they would heal the Nawab of his ailment, Were the Muslim clerics summoned to the royal court. The more they cast their spells after chanting the Koranic verses, The more shrieks did the tortured Nawab let out. (3) Appearing in the guise of blue robes with heavy clubs in hands, Did the spirits of martyred Singhs thrash the Nawab with heavy clubs. The more the clerics invoked the Muslim spiritual prophets, The more did the spirits torture and punish the Nawab. (4) Directing the wicked Nawab to crawl ahead of them, Did the Singhs spirits chastise the Nawab in this way. Noticing the Singh spirits standing in front of him, Did the Nawab see them bradishing their daggers and quoits. The more he invoked the prophets through various incantations, The more the prophets spirits felt scared of the Singh spirits. (6) His spirit came rushing in aid of the Nawab. But with the touch of their sharp daggers and quoits, Did the Singh spirits chase and pursue those spirits. (7) Did the Nawab abandon his dependence on the Muslim clerics. Thus abandoning all hope of being relieved of pain, Did the Nawab seek protection of the Khalsa Panth. (8) Whenever a person gets afflicted with any affliction, He takes no delight in any activity of this world. pages.searchText: The Nawab seeks pardon through the Singhs Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom After failing to obtain relief from one set of holy men after another, the Nawab finally admits that ordinary remedies cannot undo what a saint has spoken. He comes to believe that Singhs alone could uplift the curse meted out by a Singh, because only the Panth can answer the wrong done to Taru Singh. That realization drives him to summon Sikh intermediaries and plead for help. He is no longer bargaining from power, but begging for access to the mercy of the very community he persecuted. The page marks a sharp reversal in authority. pages.searchText: As people fail to get relief from some of these prophets, Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom As people fail to get relief from some of these prophets, They proceed to worship the prophets of other religions. Wavering in their own faith, they worship others prophets, Thus these fools lose faith in their own religious ideology. (10) Very few there are perfect in their faith and piety, Who repose their faith in their own spiritual saints in adversity. There are a few devout Sikhs in this world of ours, Who do not renege from their faith in the time of adversity. (11) Ordering the release of all the prisoners from the state prison, Did the Nawab prostrate in front of them in vain. Neither did the blockage in his urinary tract get cleared, Thereafter, did it occur in the (harassed) Nawab's mind, That Singhs alone could uplift the curse meted out by a Singh. They alone could save him from the impending doom, As the Nawab of Lahore summoned the Singhs of the city of Lahore, They arrived at the court feeling scared of Nawab's wrath. Prostrating before these urban Sikhs with folded hands, The Nawab begged them to seek a pardon for his sins. (14) Beseeching them to persuade Bhai Taru Singh to pardon him, He requested them to replace Bhai Taru Singh's scalp on his skull. As these Sikhs conveyed Nawab's petition in subdued tones, Bhai Taru Singh responded to Nawab's appeal as follows: (15) Of what avail was the Nawab's desperate appeal now, How could his (Taru Singh's) scalp be restored to its original place? Warning the Nawab to use all his powers to save himself, Bhai Taru Singh would not let him stay alive in this world. (16) Then did the Nawab realize in his heart of hearts, That no person on earth could save him from death. Whosoever dared to intercede on his behalf, He too would get damned along with the Nawab. (17) The more the Singh spirits thrashed him with their clubs, The more convulsions did the Nawab's body undergo. The more the Singh spirits threatened and scared him, The more short of breath did the Nawab's lungs feel. pages.searchText: Subeg Singh fears a saint's curse Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom The Nawab's plea reaches Subeg Singh, who listens but does not rush to intercede. He warns that The Khalsa Panth alone could be the sole arbiter of his fate, because no courtier can casually overturn a saint's judgment. Subeg Singh also fears that merely carrying the Nawab's case might expose his own household to ruin if Bhai Taru Singh refuses. The Nawab therefore has to abase himself further, touching feet and pleading for someone willing to take the risk. This page slows the story into moral deliberation rather than instant rescue. pages.searchText: Upon this, did it occur to the Nawab once again, Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom Upon this, did it occur to the Nawab once again, The Khalsa Panth alone could be the saviour of his soul. Getting S. Subeg Singh released from the state prison, The Nawab narrated the tale of his weal and woe to him. (19) Telling him that Singh spirits were out to wreak vengeance on him, The Nawab had exhausted all endeavours to invoke his prophets. The Singh spirits chased and decimated the prophets spirits. (20) His last hope of survival being vested with the Singhs, The Khalsa Panth alone could be the sole arbiter of his fate. Shaking his head as a gesture of disgust and denial Subeg Singh told that a Saint's curse could never be revoked. (21) Feeling highly scared in his own mind of Bhai Taru Singh's rebuff, Subeg Singh thought better not to meddle into mighty Singh's affairs. Lest Bhai Taru Singh should heap a curse on him as well, Which would then damn his family for generations to come. (22) Thereafter, did Subeg Singh maintain a stony silence, Upon this, prostrating himself in front of Subeg Singh, The Nawab touched his feet begging for mercy. (23) Thereupon a second thought did Subeg Singh feel, That he should convey Nawab's plea to Bhai Taru Singh. Entreating Subeg Singh to pay his respects to the great Singh, The Nawab begged him to be relieved of his affliction. (24) Beseaching Subeg Singh to touch Bhai Taru Singh's feet on his behalf, He authorized Subeg Singh to make any commitment from his side. Never again would the Nawab ever torture the Singhs in future, If his life could be spared now by Bhai Taru Singh. (25) In case Bhai Taru Singh did not pardon the Nawab, The latter would meet his end with an excruciating pain. Volunteering to die but begging to be relieved of urinary blockage, The Nawab begged Bhai Taru Singh to let him die without torture. (26) Whatever pleas had the Nawab made to Subeg Singh, The latter conveyed all those appeals to Bhai Taru Singh. Reacting sharply to the narration made by Subeg Singh, He accused the latter of vouching for a wicked tyrant. pages.searchText: Bhai Taru Singh refuses to plead for the Nawab Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom Bhai Taru Singh responds by laying down a clear principle: he would sacrifice everything for a Sikh, but he will not advocate for a wicked oppressor who has earned a righteous curse. The page stresses that Khalsa Panth alone being empowered to annul that curse does not mean the Panth is obliged to excuse injustice lightly. Meanwhile the Nawab's treatment fails, and each attempted remedy only worsens his condition. His desperation keeps sending petitions back through intermediaries, but Taru Singh's moral clarity remains intact. The result is a page about disciplined mercy rather than simple vengeance. pages.searchText: The Nawab appeals to the Khalsa's mercy Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom The Nawab tries a new line of argument by invoking Sikh teaching about collective prayer and saintly compassion. He repeats that Wherever the five Singhs prayed together with folded hands, divine authority was present among them. He also cites scriptural language to argue that even one who has wronged a saint may still be forgiven if the saint so wills it. On that basis he begs the Khalsa to prove the truth of Gurbani through a public act of mercy. The page therefore turns his petition into a theological appeal rather than a merely political one. pages.searchText: The Khalsa debates how to answer Lahore Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom Subeg Singh carries the plea into a Sikh gathering presided over by leaders of the Khalsa, where Bhai Taru Singh's martyrdom is first remembered with grief and anger. The sangat curses the Nawab's cruelty before anyone even considers the request for mercy. Soon The Singhs became desperate to launch an attack on Lahore, debating disguise, night assault, and martyrdom as better answers than negotiation. Their first impulse is not softness, but a warrior's instinct to avenge sacrilege and defend the Panth's honor. This page is therefore charged with communal energy and strategic debate. pages.searchText: Holding a religious congregation of the Singhs, Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom Holding a religious congregation of the Singhs, They accorded a respectable welcome to Subeg Singh. S. Kapoor Singh occupied the Singh chief's seat. (46) He cursed the wicked Nawab while kicking the ground. Uttering words of lavish praise for Bhai Taru Singh, He heaped curses on the Nawab of Lahore. (47) Who had upheld the Sikh ideology at the cost of his life. As he had offered his scalp to be removed from his head. (48) Thereafter, narrating in a manner the Nawab had instructed him, S. Subeg Singh conveyed the latter's appeal to the Singhs. Hearing this appeal the Singhs flared up so much, As if a spark of fire had touched a heap of explosives. (49) After listening to Subeg Singh's account of Nawab's misdeeds, The Singhs became desperate to launch an attack on Lahore. Either they must succeed in beheading the Nawab, Or they must make a supreme sacrifice of their own heads. (50) Someone opined that they being very small in number, How could they reach Lahore (to settle scores with the enemy)? Someone else opined that they must enter Lahore in a disguise, Still another suggested that they must sneak and attack at night. (51) Either they must kill the enemy or themselves perish in a fight, So that they become martyrs in the cause of their Sikh faith. They must proceed Bhai Taru Singh in martyrdom, And raise their voice for justice in the Divine court. (52) Some said that they must make their lives worthwhile, And proceed to seek martyrdom after a hasty prayer. With Bhai Taru Singh as their captain on a spiritual voyage, They must board his ship of martyrs to cross the ocean of life. (53) Thereupon listening to the sentiments of devout Singhs, The latter had also resolved to take the wicked Nawab along, After beating him severely with his own shoe-lashings. pages.searchText: The Khalsa weighs mercy, honor, and saintly power Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom Once the first wave of anger settles, the assembly reflects on Bhai Taru Singh's spiritual authority and on the renown of the Panth. His words are treated as sharper than weapons, so any response must honor both justice and the Khalsa's public character. Subeg Singh argues that a generous answer would magnify Sikh glory, because Divine Guru and Khalsa were synonymous with each other in the life of the devout community. The saints' power present in the Khalsa makes mercy meaningful precisely because it is not weakness. The page thus turns from battle-talk to theological self-understanding. pages.searchText: That those saintly attributes had come to be vested in Khalsa Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom Subeg Singh explained that the Nawab had come for protection not merely to save his body, but to test whether the saintly attributes once associated with holy men were now alive within the Khalsa. Bhai Taru Singh, he said, would abide by the Khalsa’s decision, so the Panth treated the appeal as a matter of collective authority rather than private favour. The Khalsa therefore framed terms before any relief would be granted. The Nawab must restore the twelve villages linked with Amritsar, return the old endowments that had been disturbed, and publicly rename the disputed settlement as Singhpura. In this way the Panth turned a dying ruler’s plea into a moment of political and spiritual vindication. The Singhs answered that his cure must itself demonstrate the spiritual authority he had mocked and persecuted. Five devout Singhs were appointed to pray that he be touched by Bhai Taru Singh’s shoe, that his blockage be released, and that his life end before Taru Singh’s own final departure. Subeg Singh carried that hukam to Lahore and then to Bhai Taru Singh, who accepted the Panth’s command without hesitation. The prayer by the five devout Singhs, he said, would carry weight in the Divine Court, so the Nawab’s fate now rested on the authority of the Panth rather than on imperial power. Subeg Singh took this assurance back to Lahore, where the terrified ruler dismissed his attendants and urgently asked for Bhai Taru Singh’s shoes to be brought. Once that symbolic submission was made, the urinary blockage got cleared, and the Nawab’s agony immediately subsided. The narrative then broadens into a precedent from Kashmir, where tyranny and forced conversion had once ended in a ruler’s own humiliating affliction. pages.searchText: Nawab cured, celebrates the Khalsa, and summons Subeg Singh Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom This page closes the Kashmir precedent by recalling that even a ruler who had despised Hindus was told to submit to the symbolic touch of a Hindu’s shoe strapped on to the Nawab’s head. The old story mirrors Lahore closely and prepares the reader to see the Nawab’s relief as proof that the Khalsa Panth had cured him through a power the state could not command. Back in Lahore, the restored Nawab began speaking openly of Sikh truth and of Guru Nanak's Karah Parshad, acknowledging that the Panth had answered him where his own camp had failed. The city illuminated at night in celebration, and the mood in court shifted from mockery to astonishment. With that public change of heart, Subeg Singh summoned to the royal court became the key intermediary between the Nawab and the Sikhs. The page serves as a hinge between miraculous relief and the administrative concessions that soon follow. 316 Sri Gur Panth Prakash cust: HU see Bo Hg gd um | aod fay JH Aa suru | 34 Bas Uu adu guf | gå foes at wre soe it chaupaî: jab navab un bahu dukh pâyô. kahyó kimain ham jan rakhâyô. tab lôkan yau kahyô upâi. jutî hindun kî mâth bandhâi.91. uu Q HY fee tad | su afo sou Hu Ur ot AT | IJ GTA yf ad sore} | HN ó uu US feet 1X21 dukh kç márç im hi kari. tab vahi bachyô jab yaun thi sari. kahyô navâb ab karô badhâî. khals¢ nç dukh dîô mitâî.92. gg 669 das age | tue fee HAI Awe | at Feud Hea AJA | wet HUS dass set |US| gur nanak kó kardâh karâvô. dip mâl vich shahir jalâvô. bajc shadyânc shalak karat. dai kharait kangâlan tâî.93. aaa. dd HniÌ seve ot (...... ffi at ag YA gur) 113. hôr sakhi navab ki (...... sikkhi ki gur paij rakhai) tog: SLA OS EHS we fed HUU aafo ure | nfo Mus At Hrdf A JH wet udsTE 191 dôhrâ =: navab nag bastar laç phir bahyô kachhiri âi. ahi singhan sâchî sâkhî sê ham lai partai. 1. cust: Aaa WW a see yeu | ad Md ÍSH UA SIT | Hrg dg SH A wat | »WHTÍEH JN Bud fart 121 chaupaî: subeg singh kó navâb bulâyâ. kar Adar tis pas bahaya. sach gurâ tum sâchî bani. azmâish ham upar bihânî.2. pages.searchText: Subeg Singh gains authority and the Nawab soon dies painful death of Nawab Khan Bahadur Another Episode About the Nawab Khan Bahadur When the Nawab asked him what reward he desired, Subeg Singh declined mere personal favour and instead asked for a state coin to be struck in his name along with effective political authority. He wanted gains that could actually protect the Panth rather than flatter one man. Armed with that leverage, Subeg Singh Jambar moved quickly against the machinery of persecution. The gallows dismantled, punishments were reversed, and the public signs of state terror against Sikhs began to disappear from Lahore. The Nawab died without further torment soon afterward, exactly as Bhai Taru Singh’s word had implied. pages.searchText: Episode About Bhai Taru Singh Bhai Taru Singh It was in the year seventeen hundred and Ninety-one, That Hakikat Rai's murder had made no impact on the Mughal rule. It was indeed to Bhai Taru Singh's credit to win that glory, That he had decimated the Nawab with shoe-beatings. (15) Thus remained the honour of the Khalsa Panth intact, Thus were the Mughals disgraced and dishonoured. Thus did Bhai Taru Singh and Bhai Subeg Singh, Rendered a great service to the Sikh Panth. (16) Episode 114 (Another) Episode About the Bhai Taru Singh (... was declared the greatest Martyr among Martyrs) Declaring Nawab's sudden death as a good riddance, Did the whole city resound with the news of Nawab's death. Did a Singh break news of Nawab's death to him. (1) Thereupon, Bhai Taru Singh uttering the following instructions, Did ask for his funeral pyre to be prepared. Did pile up wood hastily for his funeral pyre. (2) Thereupon, did Bhai Taru Singh prepare hastily for his departure, As he felt overwhelmed with joy at his wish fulfillment. The Divine Guru had indeed upheld the Khalsa's honour, As this legend would the world remember for ages to come. (3) Asking the water to be brought from the sacred pool at Amritsar, Bhai Taru Singh had his body washed with the sacred water. Making an offering of Karah Parshad! for the fulfillment of his mission, He had the whole of Japji Sahib? recited before him. (4) Offering a prayer after the recitation of Anand Sahib, Prostrating after offering a prayer (to the Divine Satguru), Bhai Taru Singh breathed his last as quietly as a blue Jay's* flight. (5) Subeg Singh Jambar prepared instantly for cremating his dead body. The moment Subeg Singh lit the funeral pyre, The flames leapt up to the skies immediately. (6) Dohra Chaupai: Sri Gur Panth Prakash It was in the year seventeen hundred and Ninety-one, That Hakikat Rai's murder had made no impact on the Mughal rule. (4) Offering a prayer after the recitation of Anand Sahib, He made the devout Singhs stand all around him. Prostrating after offering a prayer (to the Divine Satguru), Bhai Taru Singh breathed his last as quietly as a blue Jay's* flight. (5) The moment Bhai Taru Singh's soul reached its Divine abode, Subeg Singh Jambar prepared instantly for cremating his dead body. The moment Subeg Singh lit the funeral pyre, The flames leapt up to the skies immediately. (6) 321

pages.searchText: Episode About Bhai Taru Singh Bhai Taru Singh After Bhai Taru Singh’s passing, the poem raises him above ordinary remembrance and names him greatest among the martyrs. The contrast is sharpened by the image of the Nawab suffering a hundred shoe beatings a day in the next world, while Taru Singh receives honour among the fearless dead. The narrative then turns from martyrdom to living memory by describing the planting a flag post in memory of Bhai Taru Singh at Lahore. His shrine-like presence becomes a source of blessing, healing, and courage for those who approach it with faith. Whosoever listened to the legend of Bhai Taru Singh, the text says, could hope for worldly aid, bodily recovery, and spiritual firmness. It then turns sharply into a new political landscape following the death of Nawab Khan Bahadur Zakariya Khan. Lahore and Multan became contested centers of succession, and Shah Nawaz seized power while rivals struggled for control. In that unstable court, the old hostility to the Sikhs quickly returned under new hands. pages.searchText: Episode About the Slaughter of Jassu (J du Rai) The killing of Jassu / Jadu Rai after Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom Dohra: It was in the year eighteen hundred and two, In the Bikrami Samvat calendar of time. Was Nawab Khan Bahadur of the Lahore province, Decimated by dragging his soul by Bhai Taru Singh. (16) Episode 115 Episode About the Slaughter of Jassu (J du Rai) (The Singhs seized a lot of treasure after killing Jaspat Rai) Was he succeeded by two of his sons. One becoming the custodian of the province of Lahore, The other became the custodian of the province of Multan. (1) Chaupai: Being known by the names of Ahiya Khan? and Shah Niwaz?, Did both of them take over the reigns of power. Shah Niwaz after taking his brother Ahiya Khan into custody, Did oust him from power after ransacking his province. (2) As some time passed in this internecine strife, Did Shah Nawaz rule as a Nawab of the state. He too started committing oppression on the Singhs, Such being the turn of events at that moment of time. pages.searchText: The Singhs Ravage Lahore and Turn Toward Imnabad The killing of Jassu / Jadu Rai after Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom After striking at Mughal camps and slipping away with horses, the Singhs widened their raids until the Singhs laid waste around Lahore and made the highways unsafe for imperial traffic. They fought while vastly outnumbered, then vanished again into brush, marsh, and broken ground before the larger forces could trap them. The page stresses how poor the Khalsa still was at this stage: they had no stores, weapons, clothing, or money fit for a settled kingdom. Their only wealth was faith in the Guru's word, and that conviction kept them moving even when hunger, wounds, and exhaustion would have broken ordinary soldiers. From that hard experience the narrative draws a political lesson as well as a military one. The Singhs begin reasoning that without forts, war could not be sustained for long, so they look beyond mere raiding and turn their attention toward richer districts such as Imnabad, where supplies and durable strength might be seized. 330 tug dôhrâ gut chaupaî: aug dôhrâ gut chaupaî: Sri Gur Panth Prakash fiu HTSU old ve HO. pages.searchText: The Khalsa Demands Grain at Imnabad The killing of Jassu / Jadu Rai after Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom At Imnabad the story introduces Jaspat Rai as a revenue officer whose exactions had made the countryside miserable. Hungry Jats left their homes and joined the Singhs because the local administration had bound, beaten, and impoverished the people instead of protecting them. The Khalsa nevertheless opens with negotiation rather than plunder. Their message is plain: we have no enmity with you, only with the Turks, and the Singhs have long hungered for food after weeks of fighting and flight. pages.searchText: Jaspat Rai Threatens the Khalsa and Is Slain The killing of Jassu / Jadu Rai after Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom Jaspat Rai's reply is meant to humiliate as much as frighten. The memory of Bhai Mani Singh's dismemberment was revived when he boasted that the Singhs could be cut to pieces, mutilated, and dragged before the Nawab in the same degrading fashion. That threat hardens the Khalsa instead of cowing it. The Singhs first offer ardas and resolve on action, treating the confrontation as a test of honor rather than a mere dispute over provisions. Once battle begins, the encounter ends quickly and decisively. pages.searchText: Lakhpat Rai Swears to Destroy or Convert the Khalsa The killing of Jassu / Jadu Rai after Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom This page acts as a hinge between episodes. After Jaspat's death the Singhs were no longer destitute, because the plunder of Imnabad had given them money, grain, and breathing room, but the narrative immediately turns to a larger and darker retaliation. A new heading shifts the scene to Parol, Kathuha, and Basohli in the Jammu region, opening the Chhota Ghallughara sequence. Lakhpat Rai laid his turban at the Nawab's feet and turned private grief into a public vow of vengeance for his slain brother. He declared that he would not retie that turban until the Khalsa had been either annihilated or driven into apostasy. pages.searchText: Lakhpat Rai Orders the Killing of Every Singh The Chhota Ghallughara at Parol and Kathuha Once the campaign is approved, persecution becomes policy. Lakhpat Rai and the Nawab proclaim that whoever bore the name Singh was to be killed, and they begin the purge by seizing Sikh servants, retainers, and other dependents who could be found within easy reach. The order is not confined to armed fighters alone. Officials are told first seize and kill the Sikh servants, while houses are searched and panic spreads among both Sikhs and their Hindu associates who know that an accusation or even a name may now be enough to bring death. Alarmed by the cruelty of the decree, Hindus gathered together in alarm and petitioned Lakhpat Rai. pages.searchText: Thus entering into collaboration with the Nawab, The Chhota Ghallughara at Parol and Kathuha Thus entering into collaboration with the Nawab, Did Lakhpat Rai vow to eliminate the Singhs everywhere. Let anyone claim himself to be called a Singh, Would Lakhpat Rai destroy whole of his village. (9) In the first attempt did he arrest those Singhs, Who had been in service as officials of the state. Handing them over to the state executioners, He ordered them to behead those Sikh officials. (10) Was there a lot of hue and cry among the populace. Troops are summoned from Multan and Bahawalpur, while additional calls go out to Kasur and Attock so that pressure can be applied from several directions at once. The hill chiefs are warned not to withhold their contingents, and fresh recruits swell the field army gathering under the Nawab's authority. With so many detachments converging, the Khalsa finds that places which once offered cover or negotiation are now being folded into a single hostile net. Lakhpat Rai himself mounted his elephant and advanced with the force, turning the mobilization into a public spectacle of power. pages.searchText: Lakhpat Rai Tightens the Pursuit with Fire and Cannon The Chhota Ghallughara at Parol and Kathuha The Singhs initially strike the enemy's front ranks hard enough to show that courage has not left them. But after the first shock, Lakhpat Rai reorganizes the pursuit so that cannon in front and supporting fire from behind make repeated charges increasingly costly. He then attacks the terrain itself. Pathways are cut through cover, thickets were burned, and the Khalsa is denied the forests and broken ground that had previously let smaller bands escape larger forces. Under this pressure the Singhs are driven from refuge to refuge without rest. pages.searchText: The Famished Khalsa Looks Toward Treacherous Hill Allies The Chhota Ghallughara at Parol and Kathuha By now the Khalsa is near collapse from constant flight. Food and water failed, horses are worn down, and day and night march has left the Singhs with little chance to camp, cook, or tend their wounded before the next movement becomes necessary. Their equipment is failing as badly as their bodies. Broken bows, blunted weapons, and famished mounts show that the campaign is being fought beyond the limits of ordinary endurance, with survival depending more on resolve than on any secure line of supply. In that condition some hope that the hill chiefs or nearby Hindu households might offer relief, but the narrative prepares the reader for betrayal rather than sanctuary. pages.searchText: Thereafter, towards Basohali as the Singhs did proceed, The Chhota Ghallughara at Parol and Kathuha Thereafter, towards Basohali the battered Singhs marched on without provisions, rest, or trustworthy allies. Seeing a large assembly of hill people, some of them hoped for relief and approached in good faith, only to find that the gathering had no intention of sheltering them. Instead, the hilly Hindus slaughtered many Sikhs on the spot and handed others over to the Mughals, who cut them down immediately. The same pattern unfolded around Parol and Kathuha, where fleeing Singhs were trapped, seized, and destroyed rather than allowed to pass through in safety. Driven toward the hills as a last resort, the survivors discovered that forces already summoned by the Nawab of Lahore had occupied the heights above them. pages.searchText: As the Singhs stood on the river bank after beating a retreat, The Chhota Ghallughara at Parol and Kathuha As the Singhs stood on the river bank after beating a retreat, they found the river flowing in full torrent and flood. Whirlpools churned across the current, uprooted trees came hurtling downstream, and even great stones and boulders were being dragged away by the force of the water. The Khalsa called for someone to test the passage so the rest might follow, and two brothers from Dalewal entered the current to sound a crossing. They never returned, and their loss convinced the camp that the river offered no real escape from the tightening Mughal pursuit. After that failed attempt, the Singhs concluded that an open death in battle was better than drowning helplessly in the torrent. Remembering the Guru's praise for one who dies fighting facing the enemy, they abandoned thoughts of a crossing and prepared to meet their attackers on land. 352 Sri Gur Panth Prakash cust: WE us afate ford | mà care H SITS HÙ | Ho go uo Va Ss | WHS Udo sur uds 1921 chaupaî: jai khardc dariyâi kinare. agc daryâi su lahran mârc. shânkai phûnkç chak chak daand. ghumman gheran bhayân parchand.72. ads HJ A dwg wre | 493 ÍH&o at ug! pages.searchText: As the Singhs stood on the river bank after beating a retreat, The Chhota Ghallughara at Parol and Kathuha As the Singhs stood on the river bank after beating a retreat, Was the river flowing in full torrent and flood. Resounding with the rise and fall of its tumultuous current, Were its waters gurgling with the formation of horrible whirlpools. (72) It was uprooting many a tree standing on its banks. How could a human being dare to run through this current, Which was knocking down even the big boulders? (73) Throwing an open challenge, the Khalsa Panth asked everyone, Could anyone of them measure the depth and flow of the current? So that all the Khalsa force could cross the river, Could anyone lead and pave the way through the current? (74) Were there Singhs who had been inhabitants of Dalewal, Of being Kashtriya lineage were they four brothers. Appearing to be of a royal disposition and warrior like looks, Were they in possession of horses of fine exotic breed. (75) Responding to the Khalsa appeal two of them plunged into the river, They were brothers of Gurdial Singh of Dalewal, Whose name came to be associated with the Dalewal principality. (76) Thereafter, did the Khalsa Panth come to the conclusion, That they were really confronted with a moment of extreme exigency. Better than getting drowned in the river one by one, Would it be much better to die killing ten others from the enemy ranks. (77) Thereafter, resolved the Khalsa after deep contemplation, That the moment of truth had indeed arrived. Truly had the revered Guru (Guru Gobind Singh) said, Standing in front of the Khalsa had he declared: (78) The (Sikh) warrior who dies fighting facing the enemy in battle, Would the Guru reckon him among the rarest of the rare warriors. Thereafter, giving up the plan to cross through the river, Did the Khalsa choose the sovereign way of fighting well. (79) Honouring the unanimous resolution of the Khalsa Panth, Did the Singhs obey the Khalsa Panth's dictat. Advancing in the four directions facing the enemy ranks, Did they never turn their faces from the formidable enemy. pages.searchText: Those Singhs as were camping on the hill side, The Chhota Ghallughara at Parol and Kathuha Those Singhs as were camping on the hill side tried again to climb out of the trap, but hill troops guarded the ridges and blocked every pass. From above came stones, bricks and bullets, while Rajput positions added cannon fire that tore through anyone who tried to force a way upward. Even under that barrage, the Singhs briefly seized one enemy post before superior numbers pushed them back. Refusing to give up the ascent, they dug trenches and underground bunkers wherever they could, using knives, daggers, spears, and swords to carve footholds into the slope. That improvised fieldwork let them renew the climb with more order and protection. By sheer persistence they won another hold on the hillside and began cutting some earth with swords for making steps so that men and horses could continue moving above the river. 354 suet chaupaî: dug dôhrâ gut chaupaî: aug dôhrâ gut chaupaî: Sri Gur Panth Prakash: NGGUGAH | Í0Hg ag ugrg Hi 93 | nid HA uss fHurd | A OR adt fiu grd. pages.searchText: Those Singhs as were camping on the hill side, The Chhota Ghallughara at Parol and Kathuha Those Singhs as were camping on the hill side, Did they make attempt to climb up the hills. But the hill troops column which guarded the hills, Did they not allow any passage of escape to the Singhs. (81) Pelting a volley of stones, bricks and bullets from above, Their cannon balls hissed past the climbing Singhs. Ripping apart the Singh's bodies wherever these did hit, Were the enemy defences managed by Rajput soldiers. (82) Nevertheless, exercising their utmost zeal and energy, The Singhs did succeed in capturing an enemy post. But the enemy soldiers being in far greater strength, Did they throw the Singhs back again from the captured post. (83) Thereafter, making a fresh attempt (to consolidate themselves), Did the Singhs make a plan to climb up the mountains. For sheltering themselves in the foot hills of the mountains, Did the Singhs dig up trenches to shelter themselves. (84) For keeping their heads out of the harm's way from above, Did the Singhs dig underground bunkers for their safety. Doing all this digging of earth with knives, daggers and small arms, Did the Singhs use spears, blades and swords for digging. (85) Cutting step-ladders for stepping up the steep mountains, Did the Singhs push their way up with full force. Climbing up to the level of enemy held positions, Did the Singhs engage themselves in a fierce battle with the enemy. (86) Thereupon, as the hill troops advanced amidst shouts, The Singhs, too, confronted them with full force. As the Singhs wielded their weapons upon the enemy, The hilly troops turned back after being hit. (87) Following the retreating hilly troops in hot pursuit, The Singh succeeded in wresting the hill feature from the enemy. While those on foot among the Singhs climbed up, Those on horses could they not go up the mountains. (88) Which was to the lee side of the mountain towards the river. pages.searchText: With some surviving, some others stumbling on steps, The Chhota Ghallughara at Parol and Kathuha With some surviving, some others stumbling on steps, the Singhs tried to push along the narrow mountain route while the river drowned those who tumbled from the slopes below. The passage became so choked with desperate fighters that neither the men behind could reach the front nor those ahead could turn back in any orderly way. Everywhere the retreat turned into a siege, because there was no room to march forward and no path to reverse the movement. Men slipped, collided, and were swept away, while the crush of bodies on the hill made every small mistake fatal. Hunger and thirst then deepened the ordeal until it seemed impossible even to drink a drop of water. As the pressure mounted, the Mughal side hardened the pursuit further by placing a reward of five rupees for each Sikh’s head, turning the retreat into a hunted massacre. 356 dug dôhrâ gut chaupaî: gdr dôhrâ gut chaupaî: Sri Gur Panth Prakash at HU act fra we | fad 30t H care see | HS 5 fuso fag AMIS | fasa À f33 ae H eam Ito! kôî bachai kôî gir jâvai. girai tahan su daryâu dubâvai. milain na pichhlan phir só agl¢. jitak sç tit gaç su vagl¢.90. mà BUS at Aa 5 UG | fue fas fafa use 6 HU | set SE HJ sg ai TJ | fea fesa ss TITI (cq! age lakhan ki jaga na payyç. pichhç kit bidhi palat na Jayyç. bhai bhird bahu bhar gayê rahu. tilkç philkç dubç daryáhu.91.: WIS ad fue® së fues mato sorts | a8 for o afo Hot Bd ara sft ATT IER | agl¢ kahain pichhl¢ bhalç pichhl¢ agânh takâhin. kôû kisai na kahi sakai lagai kahu tahin jahin.92.: fdwo uro at ds vse | ural ule old ge nie | ud fae ae H UdÌ HdÌd | ford ô VBS ug H Ute 1X31 rizak khan ki kaun chalâvai. pant pînôn nahin ban avai. par kichh kala su dharî sarir. girc na chalnô dharu su dhîr.93. a feos at su [Hu | Has Go old Ss fou | Hot HÒ eq H Af | ute oA efe sgas eae its! kai dinan kç bhâkhc sikkh. mangat un nahin labbhai bhikkh. sagvân mârain dçkh su thai. pai rase dei turkan phardâi.94.: HS HI te AS Tet aH GS su | sQ Hsu A wea JJ Eu Q gu ul márat martc dçkh jan gai bhâj un bhôkh. bhayô santókh só khals¢ harç dçkh kç râkh.95. pages.searchText: Lakhpat Rai promised to condone the robbing of Sikhs, The Chhota Ghallughara at Parol and Kathuha Lakhpat Rai promised to condone the robbing of Sikhs only after all of them had been slaughtered, fearing that premature looting would let survivors slip away into the wild. Once that order was given, the Mughals renewed their assault with cannon, cavalry, and close pressure on the trapped Khalsa. The Singhs answered with a fierce counterattack that briefly drove back mounted assailants and revived their spirits in the middle of disaster. In that moment Sukha Singh resolved that the struggle had to be carried directly against the man directing the slaughter. Before striking, however, he learned that Lakhpat Rai stood behind a heavy security cordon around him, protected by infantry, horsemen, camel swivels, and artillery. Sukha Singh still tried to reach him, but a small cannon shot smashed one of his legs and broke the attack before it could be completed. 358 aug dôhrâ suet chaupaî: tug dôhrâ gut chaupaî: Sri Gur Panth Prakash UÈ ge He N ad | ST HS Ad BG aT | ufJ5 Bes Q 3H us | HÍS as SA ffu feg aF etl pâchhai lit mâph main karôn. daçrâ sabh jab katlô karôn. pahilô lûtan kê tam parc. mati kat bhaj singh phir vargn.99. su Wus a fr set Hrg | ges set Su SBE | use H Mu ve fuers | sa ffws st BAS ASTI 1900 | tab singhan kç sir bhai mar. chhâtat bhai tôp talvâr. ghórdan són singh daç pichharg. tab singhan bhi shastar sambhârc.100. ŵ Uo gg a ss fas | J ate fae nat fHurg | JJoo JH Set JU | Saas we feg fue Jc Te 19091 au pun gur kç bachan bicharg. hó thândhc kichh age sidhârg. turkan halla phctâ karyô. turkan dal phir pichhç hat rahyô.101.: Hur fur sa of dl Hud Su ud Ate | THI Aa ore AG A fue ag 5 ute 19021 sukkha singh tab yaun kahi main parôn lakkhê par jai. hamrç sang âvai sôû Jó pichchhai karai na pâi.102.: Hur ffu 34 He ged | TKI fees af CA HIS | dead odl H Jü â wre | HJ ENG ôl MU ae 19031 sukkhâ singh tab sad halkârc. rahi divân jahin dassô sarc. halkarg kahi su hatth na avai. bahu phaujan kç maddh rahâvai.103. pages.searchText: Beating a retreat from where he was hit, The Chhota Ghallughara at Parol and Kathuha Beating a retreat from where he was hit, Sukha Singh repeatedly turned back toward the fight instead of yielding to his wound. He refused to disarm himself despite a grievous wound and kept placing himself wherever the endangered Singhs needed steadiness most. The battle raged partly on the mountains and partly on the foothills, while the Khalsa measured their shrinking strength against a far larger enemy that was still closing from every side. Outnumbered, hungry, and trying to move horses through broken terrain, they recognized that stubbornness alone would not win the day. A fresh resolution followed: they would scatter, preserve as many lives as possible, and return later with better preparation. pages.searchText: Khalsa scatters and Sukha Singh directs the retreat The Chhota Ghallughara at Parol and Kathuha The Khalsa then declared that they must scatter themselves in all the directions and later reassemble in the Majha region to renew the struggle. The decision acknowledged that the present battlefield could no longer be held, but it also turned dispersal into an organized plan for survival and future resistance. Sukha Singh counseled the Singhs on how to carry out the retreat, telling those on foot to keep climbing while mounted men guarded them from below. He tried to preserve some order in the breakup so the weakest parties would not be abandoned immediately under Mughal pressure. Even with that guidance, the separation was painful and chaotic, as comrades and families were torn apart in the confusion. The movement away from the hills thus became both a military dispersal and an emotional sundering for a community already battered by hunger, pursuit, and loss. 362 tug dôhrâ gut chaupaî: gdr dôhrâ gut chaupaî: tug dôhrâ gut chaupaî: Sri Gur Panth Prakash: SW HSM ò ad fis Hoe Sg | fed HS J Fad Ma HTS Hd 19921 tabe khals¢ nç kahi khindô su chârôn ór. phir mâjhc hó çkthç ân machâvain shôr.117.: sy Ña ffu ad Aes | MR JN Aa fU&& ote | H 9 a8 Ae fAw | gg udd ad o Re 19a | tab sukkhâ singh kari salah. âvô ham sang pichhle dai. jô hai kôû sajâdâ singh. chardhô pahârdî karô na dhill.118. pages.searchText: Sukha Singh leads a breakout through Mughal lines The Chhota Ghallughara at Parol and Kathuha Sukha Singh rejected the hope that the Singhs could ever survive through stealth alone while the enemy kept closing in. He called on them to follow after him and strike straight at the strongest Mughal defences rather than wait to be hunted down piecemeal. That charge shattered several forward posts, and the Singhs seized weapons from those who resisted before pushing ahead again. Their brief success opened a way toward cover, letting a large part of the battered force move off instead of dying where it stood. Seeing a way out, Sukha Singh led them toward a wild growth that promised concealment, but the danger did not end with that movement. pages.searchText: Night refuge in the jungle and the Mughal use of civilians The Chhota Ghallughara at Parol and Kathuha As darkness did descend, the Singhs finally gained a little shelter in the jungle while the Mughal camp drew back for the night. That pause gave the fugitives a few hours to breathe, but it did not restore the strength of men already fatigued, famished and naked from continuous fighting and flight. At midnight they moved again, only to find the hunt renewed as Mughal detachments closed in on the forest routes. The Singhs realized that desertion and escape alone would not avail, so they fought in bursts while trying to reach a bigger patch of jungle where pursuit might be blunted. The Mughals answered by widening the chase beyond their own regular troops. Once the Khalsa rushed at the armed intruders, the Jat intruders started fleeing, leaving horses, garments, and weapons behind as they scattered. That reprieve gave the survivors a moment to regroup and head for the Majha region rather than remain trapped in the same killing ground. They forced a rapid march through hostile country and then faced yet another river barrier on the road to safety. To cross it, the Singhs had to make-shift boats of reeds and grass and trust the current once more. pages.searchText: Transition from Sukha Singh’s Escape to the Parol–Kathua Survivors The Chhota Ghallughara at Parol and Kathuha This page finishes the escape after the slaughter by describing the Singhs crossing into Majha after forcing their way through the river country. They move through the hot Jaito tract, gather again in the jungle, and tend Sukha Singh’s shattered leg while the survivors pause to recover after months of strain. The repair notes that Sukha Singh remained laid up for many months while the rest of the band slowly reorganized itself. The scene is less about triumph than endurance, showing how a broken remnant kept itself alive after the massacre. The page then turns into a hinge and opens the next episode by returning to the survivors left at Parol and Kathua. pages.searchText: Episode 117: Starvation, Betrayal, and the Turn Against the Hills Counting the Singhs after the massacre The trapped survivors discover that the hills are no refuge. Men who descend are hunted, those who remain above are encircled, and hunger becomes as deadly as the enemy because food cannot be secured anywhere in safety. The strongest emotional note on the page is betrayal by the hill chiefs. The Singhs reflect that they had fought Mughal power in ways that also benefited the hill rulers, yet the same chiefs now help tighten the noose instead of offering shelter. Out of that anger and desperation the survivors harden themselves again. Thus thousands of Singhs crossed through the mountains, As they could no longer afford to stay put among the hills. (10) With Mughal troops being in hot pursuit of the Singhs, They kept on being beheaded as had fallen on the way. Even as the Mughals got fed up with massacring the Singhs, Some of the Singhs still did survive this massacre. (11) Dohra: At places would the Singhs get into a fight with the Mughals, At places would the famished Singhs rob others for food. At places where they could not buy provisions even for a price, Would the Singhs survive on pulling and eating vegetation. (12)

pages.searchText: From Disguised Escape to the Kiratpur Muster Roll Counting the Singhs after the massacre This page records the cruel aftermath of the mountain flight: provisions are scarce, even money cannot reliably buy grain, and many Singhs die from hunger before they can find a secure route away from the cordon. The survivors endure not only military pursuit but a landscape in which ordinary sustenance has been cut off. Those who manage to live do so by concealment and improvisation. Some bind up their hair, alter their appearance, and move quietly through Mandi and Kullu until they finally reached Kiratpur in disguise instead of marching openly as warriors. The page closes the episode with a reckoning in the sixth month, distinguishing the dead from those who straggled through alive. It serves as a muster roll of loss before the narrative turns from escape and survival toward those marked for death in the slaughter. 374 Sri Gur Panth Prakash oust: sot word fana ot set | Mw H Hg ae 99 ast | NS Td ot eo ees | ASS 3 TAHT 1931 chaupaî: tahan lachâr rijak ki bhai. singh su mar gaç bhukkhg kai. mull ju mangain nâ dhukkain duvârc. jau lâtain tau râjc mârcn.13. lee de Wee Sd | wer O utfg u=rdl set | ag ad 2 de Aa wre | Sc ac feo TH ATES 1981 kharidan gaç su d¢vain nahin. khals¢ kó yahi khavârî bhai. kôu kahai ç bandg sang âc. lût kit in ham santâc.14. pages.searchText: Episode 118 Close: Basoli Captives, Uncertain Death Toll, and the Turn to Shah Nawaz the Destined Death of Lakhu and Shah Narat This fragment gathers the fate of those who did not escape. Captives from Parol and the men who collapsed in the hills are carried into Basoli jail and severed heads are displayed as trophies, reducing the massacre to an inventory of humiliation as well as death. The page emphasizes how little of the Khalsa remnant remained. Only a small number survive, very few horses are left, and even the poet admits that the total slaughter could not be counted exactly because the dead lay scattered across many routes of flight and capture. The closing lines date the great disaster and pivot to the next moral sequence. After recounting the uncertain death toll, the narrative turns toward the destined downfall of Lakhpat Rai and Shah Nawaz, whose pride and cruelty invite their own destruction. 376 Sri Gur Panth Prakash Muse SSH | At uoga N gd grƏ | Yds NIH HHS IO aga | Ja JddÌ dI5 ca saa 121 au ju pardôl phardg¢ só mêre. kai pahârdan main rahe hârç. bahutc jghal basôlîan karkc. hatth hathaurdi gal tank bharkc.2. pages.searchText: Condemnation of Shah Nawaz and Lakhpat Rai Ram Rauni and the Sikh defensive position After the massacre, Shah Nawaz is presented as drunk on power and dreaming of a still higher station, while Lakhpat Rai shares in the same swollen arrogance. The page frames both men as rulers whose apparent success has already made them fit objects of divine judgment. It then lingers on their anti-Sikh persecution in deliberate detail, stressing that the word Guru was forbidden, the name of Nanak was twisted into insult, and listeners to the Guru’s bani were pressured toward Islam by men who treated reverence itself as a crime. The page also remembers desecration of scripture as part of the same campaign of contempt. By gathering these offenses together, the narrative prepares the complaint that heaven itself will answer in the pages that follow. 378 Sri Gur Panth Prakash dôhrâ: shah navaz garrô vadhyó singhan kó tab mar. kahi patishâhî main karún jâ dill? takhat sambhar. 1. pages.searchText: Laying his claim to the sovereignty over India, Ram Rauni and the Sikh defensive position Laying his claim to the sovereignty over India, Did he dream of occupying the Mughal throne at Delhi. (1) Doomed to be burdened with doing evil deeds. Such indeed being the will of the Satguru Divine, Destined were these two to be damned indeed. (2) Such indeed is the working of the fate inexorable, That it makes sinners commit more and more sins. Do they sink and perish under the burden of their own sins. (3) What to talk of their bigger atrocities and excesses, They even prohibited the uttering of the word Guru. The word Gurd (jaggery) being co-terminus with word Guru, They ordered its nomenclature to be changed to sweets. (4) That the word Nanak be mispronounced as Nanu. That whosoever was found listening to hymns of Nanak, Let he be immediately converted to Islam under duress. (5) That wherever he happened to lay his hands upon the Sikh sacred text, He ordered it to be thrown instantly into the river. That after he had wiped out the name of Nanak's Khalsa Panth, Would he claim himself to be a true Kshtriya indeed. (6) As such atrocities and excesses occurred in this world, The information about these reached the Divine Court. Summoning the divine messengers visiting the earth, The Divine Lord enquired how did all these excesses happen? (7) Narrating the whole account the Divine messengers did say, That (Guru) Nanak's name was being maligned in the world. As the Divine Lord did not punish the evil-doers, There spread darkness of evil throughout the world. (8) As darkness disappears with the lighting of a lamp at home, As the whole sky gets illuminated with the rise of the sun, So illuminating were the hymns of (Guru) Nanak indeed, That the whole mankind got enlightenment from his hymns. (9) Dohra Chaupai: Dohra Sri Gur Panth Prakash 379 Laying his claim to the sovereignty over India, Did he dream of occupying the Mughal throne at Delhi. (1) Thus were both (Lakhu) Lakhpat Rai and (Nawab) Shah Nawaz, Doomed to be burdened with doing evil deeds. Such indeed being the will of the Satguru Divine, Destined were these two to be damned indeed. (2) Such indeed is the working of the fate inexorable, That it makes sinners commit more and more sins. Having committed sins in such great excess, Do they sink and perish under the burden of their own sins. (3) What to talk of their bigger atrocities and excesses, They even prohibited the uttering of the word Guru. The word Gurd (jaggery) being co-terminus with word Guru, They ordered its nomenclature to be changed to sweets. (4) Thereafter, did Lakhpat Rai make a public proclamation, That the word Nanak be mispronounced as Nanu. That whosoever was found listening to hymns of Nanak, Let he be immediately converted to Islam under duress. (5) That wherever he happened to lay his hands upon the Sikh sacred text, He ordered it to be thrown instantly into the river. That after he had wiped out the name of Nanak's Khalsa Panth, Would he claim himself to be a true Kshtriya indeed. (6) As such atrocities and excesses occurred in this world, The information about these reached the Divine Court. Summoning the divine messengers visiting the earth, The Divine Lord enquired how did all these excesses happen? (7) Narrating the whole account the Divine messengers did say, That (Guru) Nanak's name was being maligned in the world. As the Divine Lord did not punish the evil-doers, There spread darkness of evil throughout the world. (8) As darkness disappears with the lighting of a lamp at home, As the whole sky gets illuminated with the rise of the sun, So illuminating were the hymns of (Guru) Nanak indeed, That the whole mankind got enlightenment from his hymns. pages.searchText: Divine Retribution and Abdali’s Advance Ram Rauni and the Sikh defensive position The response to the complaint is immediate and theological: divine punishment was decreed against the slanderers who had mocked the Guru and oppressed the Sikhs. The page makes clear that worldly upheaval is not random but the chosen instrument of that judgment. From that point the narrative turns to history in motion as the Kabul ruler is driven toward Lahore and Ahmad Shah Abdali advances into Punjab. Lakhpat Rai and Shah Nawaz attempt to work within the Afghan invasion, but the movement of armies now serves a justice they do not control. The page leads directly toward the fighting around Sirhind. pages.searchText: Thereupon, the Lord Divine did make His will declare, Ram Rauni and the Sikh defensive position Thereupon, the Lord Divine did make His will declare, That the contemnors be meted out an exemplary punishment. Let those be punished who deserved to be punished, Let they be instantly presented with their evil deeds. (10) As soon as the Divine Lord did express His Will Divine, Fate, the Divine instrument, did decide to fulfil His Will. Prompting the (Afghan) ruler ruling at Kabul, Destiny made him move on the road to Lahore. (11) As a sharp thorn takes out another thorn embedded in the flesh, It was in the year eighteen hundred and four? of (B.S.), That there rose a storm of (vengeance and aggression). It was after the death of Nadir Shah*, the Afghan ruler, That Ahmad Shah Abdali? intruded into India. (13) Taimur Shah* being the son of Ahmad Shah Abdali, Both father and son had had a glimpse of Delhi's grandeur. Thus, with Delhi having been the object of their desires, They captured Lahore after their advent in India. (14) As Dewan Lakhpat Rai became an ally of the Afghan ruler, Nawab Shah Nawaz too became a camp follower of the Afghans. By keeping the loss secret and pressing the fight, he helps reverse the field at the very moment when collapse seemed possible. The page then notes the Afghan setback and the recovery of Mughal authority, with Abdali forced back toward Kabul and away from Lahore. Victory in battle is immediately joined to a second reckoning in politics, because the man who survives the field now decides whom to punish at home. That political reckoning falls on Lakhpat Rai. pages.searchText: The Khalsa Resolve to Defend Amritsar from the Sacred Shrines Kaura Mal and the Sikh alliance This page records the inner debate over where the Khalsa should make its stand. The argument that wins is spiritual as much as military: it is better to die near the Guru's shrines than to seek a safer but less meaningful refuge elsewhere. The discussion turns repeatedly to the sanctity of Amritsar and the memory attached to its sacred places. Instead of abandoning the center of Sikh devotion, the Singhs weigh the five holy sites and imagine defense growing out of the geography blessed by the Gurus themselves. By the end of the page, the decision is moving toward action. The sacred shrines of Amritsar are no longer only places of pilgrimage; they are becoming the ground from which a new fortification will be raised. 386 dôhrâ gut chaupaî: aug dôhrâ gut chaupaî: tug dôhrâ gut chaupaî: gdr dôhrâ Sri Gur Panth Prakash: jaisî bhûm kulchhctri taisî dhig gurdavar. marai su dhig gurdavâr ke sikkh hô su janam hazâr.5.: 3X SHer tus ud | adt HIS fea HUTô wÑ | US AT A dig wee | Wess 3 MATA gee IÉ | tabai bhâmkâ dçkhan chahai. kari bat ik sayânc ahai. pâfich sar jô gurâ banag. kulchhctar tc adhik rachâc.6. fen 3 g id a3 ast | fea sfa YG BES nfo VT | TI ot Has TEH | vis ôd fan AS TRU 121 is tç bhâ aur kat bhali. ih taji aur laîc jahi chal. gurdavârg hî marnôn chahiyai. aur thaur kim jan gavyyai.7.: Sut H oU sete fae JJoô H ad AT | HY 3t Hed frog 9 ae BS UÍSH'dÌ nig IC | îhân su kandh banâi kichhu turkan són karô jang. marain tân savrag sidhâr hain bach lacn patishâhî ang.8.: Sa Hu ô MA Cores | JN tua fea niga ard | fea sot Sat 35 Jdt | AS Rames Sot set I! çk sikkh nç ais uchara. ham dçkhyó ik achraj bhara. ik chheli Ghan bhul rahi. sôâ biâit âhân bhaî.9. pages.searchText: The Singhs Build Ram Rauni with Their Own Hands Kaura Mal and the Sikh alliance Once the site is chosen, the page becomes practical and communal. A foundation is laid near the sacred complex, and the fort begins not as a royal project but as a labor shared directly by the Khalsa itself. The text stresses that Singhs themselves served as masons, diggers, and builders. Walls rise quickly, gates are prepared, and the work of defense is performed by the same hands that will soon be required to fight. pages.searchText: The Mughal Assault on Ram Rauni Begins Kaura Mal and the Sikh alliance The building of Ram Rauni is answered almost immediately by siege. When news reaches the Mughal side, Mir Mannu dispatches Dina Beg with Kaura Mal, Sadiq Beg, Aziz Khan, artillery, and allied hill forces to crush the Sikh concentration before it can settle into strength. Inside the fort, the Khalsa understands that the enemy is numerically heavier and better supplied. The defenders still choose open resistance, sending out small bands ready for martyrdom rather than accepting confinement as a slow surrender. The page also begins the technical struggle of siege warfare. pages.searchText: The Besieged Singhs Choose Assault over Dishonor Kaura Mal and the Sikh alliance With provisions thinning and pressure mounting, the Khalsa refuses the idea of saving itself through flight or humiliation. The page states the choice in martial terms: better to die fighting than flee in disgrace when the Panth’s honor is already on trial before the world. That resolve becomes action in coordinated assaults against Mughal posts. The defenders strike from one side, seize positions where they can, and try to turn a siege into a series of sudden local reversals that keep the enemy off balance. Even when losses mount, the example draws in more fighters rather than breaking morale. pages.searchText: The Besieged Khalsa Hears Jassa Singh Seek Reunion Kaura Mal and the Sikh alliance The siege tightens as the attackers reduce the remaining openings around Ram Rauni and try to shut every avenue of relief. The defenders understand that the Mughals blocked every entrance, yet their answer is not surrender but a renewed resolve to die fighting if no other path remains. At that moment the page introduces an important reconciliation. News arrives that Jassa Singh and the men once estranged from the Khalsa now want reunion with the Panth and wish to share the same danger instead of remaining apart from the besieged Singhs. The request matters because Ram Rauni is becoming a place where old divisions are burned away by common peril. pages.searchText: As the Singhs kept on duplicating in place of each dead, Kaura Mal and the Sikh alliance As the Singhs kept on duplicating in place of each dead, Did the Mughals realize the real strength of the Singhs. Leaving no passage whatsoever for the Singhs entrance or exist. (41) It was through these open spaces that the Singhs entered the fort, As well as managed to bring some sort of ammunition. Now when every kind of entrance was barred and blocked, Did the Singhs realize that was their death imminent then. (42) Let the Singhs slaughter those whosoever dared to attack them, Was this indeed a unanimous resolution of the Singhs. Let the Singhs slaughter, kill and make a supreme sacrifice, No sooner did the Khalsa Panth arrive at the above resolution, Than there did arrive a Singh from outside to join their ranks. In the following words did he address the Khalsa Singhs: That the approaching contingent of soldiers consisted of enlisted Singhs. (44) There used to be one Jassa Singh from the family of carpenters, Whom the Khalsa Panth had turned out for committing female foeticide. (Being an outcast) had he joined the army of Dina Beg, Along with hundreds of his camp followers as well. (45) Thereupon, the messenger Singh conveyed the sentiments of approaching Singhs, That they (Jassa Singh's followers) too would sacrifice along with the Singhs. pages.searchText: Episode 123: Ahmad Shah Abdali Invited into India Ahmad Shah, Sukha Singh, and the Afghan pressure The narrative opens a larger imperial crisis by describing confusion in Delhi after Muhammad Shah and the rivalry of grandees who cannot hold the center together. Court disorder, factional ambition, and regional distrust create the conditions in which outside invasion becomes possible rather than surprising. Into that weakness steps the Afghan power, and the page emphasizes that Najib Khan Ruhela invites Abdali into the struggle as an ally who can tip the balance. Ahmad Shah Abdali is therefore not only an invader from afar but a force summoned through Indian political fracture itself. By the end of the page, the disorder of the empire has become the prelude to a much wider war.
