pages.searchText: Dewan Kaura Mal Appeals to the Singhs Ahmad Shah, Sukha Singh, and the Afghan pressure As Abdali’s advance unsettles Lahore and Sirhind, local calculations change quickly. The page shows how men who once maneuvered within Mughal politics begin seeking stronger partners, because the Afghan threat makes older arrangements look fragile and incomplete. The key development is that Dewan Kaura Mal invites the Singhs into alliance instead of treating them as expendable auxiliaries. He offers assurance, support, and recognition in exchange for help against Abdali, giving the Khalsa a role defined by negotiation rather than mere persecution. This marks a major shift in the story’s political logic. The Singhs are acknowledged as a power whose friendship matters, and Kaura Mal emerges as the courtly figure most willing to bind his fortunes to theirs. 406 Sri Gur Panth Prakash fost: Ae Ae Hdde UdU WS TE | fan 3 MÊJHE pfs afo uot H Su Sete 1 | dôhrâ: gâjdîn saddç marhatg ghçryô ruhglô âi. tis tc âhimad shâhi kahi pathân su layó bulai.9. suet: 3a Go ufoHe mI ge | Ma BAS AG goer | add fade GAS Hat | gate wet HIS 3 fest 190! chaupaî: tab un ahimad shah bulâyâ. ân usç ng sda chhudaâyâ. lahaur sarihand usai nç malli. chhudaâi lai marhtg tç dillî.10. pages.searchText: Internal Strife, Lahore Unrest, and Sukha Singh’s Crossing Ahmad Shah, Sukha Singh, and the Afghan pressure The page begins with disorder inside the Sikh world itself, where factional violence follows the killing of Kushal Singh and prompts retaliation against the Bhangis. Instead of a single united front, the narrative pauses to show how internal wounds can interrupt broader strategy. It then returns to Lahore, where tensions flare into clashes with butchers and townspeople near the city gates. Urban hostility and factional confusion together create a turbulent setting in which bold action feels both risky and necessary. Against that background Sukha Singh crosses the Ravi with a small chosen band and moves toward Abdali’s camp. The page makes the numerical imbalance unmistakable, because Sukha Singh and his companions are moving against a force far larger than their own. What matters most is Sukha Singh’s moral choice under those odds. He openly chooses martyrdom over retreat, telling his companions that honor is worth more than survival purchased by withdrawal in the face of Abdali. pages.searchText: Sukha Singh’s Charge and Martyrdom Ahmad Shah, Sukha Singh, and the Afghan pressure The companions who follow Sukha Singh enter the battle determined to be counted among the martyrs rather than to preserve themselves at any cost. Their charge briefly shakes the Afghan line and gives the page its fierce momentum, because the assault is driven by chosen sacrifice rather than by hope of easy victory. In the confusion of combat, Sukha Singh presses toward Ahmad Shah Abdali himself and tries to strike at the center of enemy power. The effort ends in martyrdom, but the attack leaves a lasting memory precisely because it carries the Khalsa spirit into the heart of the danger. After the clash, the survivors must disengage and begin a retreat towards Lahore under pressure. The withdrawal is sober and practical, shaped by the loss of Sukha Singh and the recognition that survival now requires regrouping elsewhere. The page then turns from immediate aftermath to a larger historical accounting. It dates Sukha Singh’s martyrdom and asks how Abdali advanced so far, drawing the answer through the deaths of allies such as Dewan Kaura Mal and the submission of Mir Mannu under Afghan pressure. pages.searchText: Adina Beg Seeks Alliance with Wadbhag Singh Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Adina Beg is shown as politically strained and unable to recover his position through ordinary means alone. His advisers therefore push him toward alliance with Wadbhag Singh, recognizing that strength now lies in coalitions forged from shared grievance as much as from state office. The page also explains why such a partnership is plausible from the other side. Wadbhag Singh carries his own memory of violence and desecration at Kartarpur, so revenge and justice can converge with Adina Beg’s practical need for support. Negotiation follows from that overlap of motives, and the account keeps alliance with Wadbhag Singh at the center of the page. The episode thus opens by showing politics rebuilt through injury, ambition, and careful approach rather than through inherited stability. 418 tug dôhrâ gut chaupaî: gdr dôhrâ gut chaupaî: Sri Gur Panth Prakash HÈ HTI THH dur ag | feat we ae BA afs Hd | H «íd frost fes X aad | Gur CA ae EA at IKI mârdç shahi jim khcpân bharc. binân dav kuchh us nahin sarc. só vahi gintî dil main karâhî. upâu usai kuchh dissai nahin.9.: Yds HôHW va Ja Hó 5 fag GUE | SÀ fit fea fear g3 faa faa vet sate 1901 bahut mansûbç chak rahyô banai na kichhâ upâi. usai sikkh ik dhig hutô tin bidh daî batâi.10.: aso [Hu A Aye ore | WW we R ses Here | WN owe H MAT Hôl | CA a Bs set ddIôl 1991 badabhag singh sôn jau ban âvai. singh lakh só turat mangâvai. jabai nabab su aisi suni. us kó lord bhai chauguni.11. fed ffws ud as g Ml | Hô fw SH THE Sal | used Ñu uses H JIG | adsTdud AE ASS BF 1921 phir singhan par bat hûn ái. sunôn singh tum gurmukh bhai. badabhâg singh parbat main rahyô. kartârpurc jab katlô bhayô.12. pages.searchText: Dina Beg Meets Wadbhag Singh at the Midway Camp Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Dina Beg and Wadbhag Singh agree to a midway meeting, where the Nawab arrives after the Sikh leader and receives him with deliberate warmth. They sit together, exchange assurances of respect, and speak openly about Dina Beg's failure to recover his province without Khalsa support. Dina Beg then asks for help recovering Jalandhar and says he will become Wadbhag Singh's disciple if the latter acts as his guide in the crisis. Wadbhag Singh answers that he first wants a written assurance allowing him to avenge the Pathans of Jalandhar and Kartarpur, including the destruction associated with Nasir Ali and the seizure of Muslim households. Only after that demand is accepted does the Nawab swear an oath on the Koran and promise to keep his word. With that written assurance secured, Wadbhag Singh prepares to summon the Khalsa so the campaign can proceed as both a political alliance and a religiously charged act of vengeance. 420 Sri Gur Panth Prakash aS fad ws ofJdreÌ | mU frase Aer erl | yaaa Mu ur ufos wart | 393 ose Sot JS MUT IAT | dônôn milnai bat thahirâî. addh bichalg jaga thai. badabhâg singh â pahilân khardâyâ. turat nabâb tahan chal âyâ.18. vo Gsd fea Wore | TES W da dig ewe | ga adu SH UNIT GH | dg adt ÍEHTô Hen fees 1A | dónón utar ik jâ âc. hâthan main hatth gurâ dabac. navâb kahyô tum pir hamárç. gurû kahi imân salamat didârc.19. pages.searchText: Khalsa Mobilization Toward Jalandhar Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Once the pact is sealed, Dina Beg prepared his contingent and moved his own camp toward the coming theater of war. Messages go out to the Sikh chiefs, gifts and pay are arranged, and the allied force begins to gather in strength for the push toward Jalandhar. As the Khalsa assembles, the opposing Pathans drew up opposite and their presence unsettles the Nawab's men. Dina Beg's camp senses the seriousness of the clash, and the Nawab leans on Wadbhag Singh to steady nerves and bring the Sikh force fully into the field. Wadbhag Singh reassures him that the Guru's Panth does not withdraw once it has given its word. He assured the Singhs as well through a written message, That they would find his forces stationed around Jalandhar. (27) He would deploy his troops ahead of the Singhs position, As he would take positions in the foothills of hilly slopes. As the Pathan troops put up a camp near village Panchat!?, Nawab Dina Beg felt threatened by this Pathan concentration. His Mughal troops having lost their wits under this threat, They found it even difficult to stay where they had positioned themselves. (29) Dohra: Hearing these developments of troop movements on both sides, Looting, plundering and ransacking through the region, Chaupai: Those, being mighty warriors among the Singhs proposed, But the veterans among them being in favour of Nawab's participation, They wished the Nawab's troops to start the fight first with the Pathans. (31) Let the Nawab's soldiers test their mettle first of all, Later on would the Singhs lead the attack on the Pathans. As the Nawab received the (good) news of Khalsa force's arrival, He felt as if a devout Muslim's wish had been fulfilled. (32) Dohra: Only then did the Nawab's forces get down from the hilly slopes, When they had spotted the Singhs with their own eyes. But very soon did he feel threatened at heart, Lest the Singhs themselves should seize power from him. (33) That the Nawab need not feel scared of the Singhs. After the Nawab felt convinced with Wadbagh Singh's assurances, Dohra: Thereafter, (Wadbagh Singh having made arrangements for a meeting), He arranged a summit between Shiam Singh!, Jassa Singh and Dina Beg. There (the Singh chiefs) not only received a ransom from the Nawab, They also imposed some amount of penalty on this Mughal chief. (35) Sri Gur Panth Prakash 423 Thereafter, Nawab Dina Beg getting his own contingent ready, He sent an intimation to the hill chiefs to wage a war. He assured the Singhs as well through a written message, That they would find his forces stationed around Jalandhar. (27) He would deploy his troops ahead of the Singhs position, As he would take positions in the foothills of hilly slopes. The (Gilja) Pathans having received information about troop movements, They themselves positioned their troops facing Dina Beg's troops. (28) As the Pathan troops put up a camp near village Panchat!?, Nawab Dina Beg felt threatened by this Pathan concentration. His Mughal troops having lost their wits under this threat, They found it even difficult to stay where they had positioned themselves. (29) Dohra: Hearing these developments of troop movements on both sides, Did the Khalsa Panth troops started a march towards Jalandhar. Looting, plundering and ransacking through the region, Did they reach near the forces of Nawab Dina Beg. (30) Chaupai: Those, being mighty warriors among the Singhs proposed, That they themselves should ransack Jalandhar without Nawab's forces. But the veterans among them being in favour of Nawab's participation, They wished the Nawab's troops to start the fight first with the Pathans. (31) Let the Nawab's soldiers test their mettle first of all, Later on would the Singhs lead the attack on the Pathans. pages.searchText: The Joint Attack and the Green Leaves Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Before the battle opens, Dina Beg proposes a joint morning attack so his troops and the Khalsa can strike the Pathans together. The Singhs bluntly warn him that once the fighting begins they will cut down whoever stands before them and will not pause to distinguish friend from foe. To prevent confusion, Dina Beg orders his own soldiers to wear green leaves on their headgear as a visible sign for the Sikh warriors. With that precaution settled, the hostile line is surveyed and the enemy is described in formal deployment, with artillery in the front and musketeers on both flanks. Even so, the Nawab remains anxious when the Khalsa does not appear at the exact moment he expects. pages.searchText: Karam Singh Leads the Khalsa Charge Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh The Khalsa now enters the field in its own manner, tying their turbans, fastening their arms, and reciting Gurbani before advancing. Their martial devotion is presented as the real preparation for combat, and they move forward only when spiritually and physically ready. When the Singhs reach the fiercest section of the line, the clash tightens and the Gilja front resists hard. At that moment Karam Singh of Paijgarh pushes toward the highest concentration of Gilja Pathans, making himself the spearhead of the Sikh assault. His charge turns the page from anxious waiting into heroic action. pages.searchText: Karam Singh’s Breakthrough and the Durrani Retreat Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Karam Singh's reckless bravery becomes the emblem of the Khalsa attack, and even after losing his turban he keeps pressing forward bare-headed into the fight. The Pathans shelter behind the cannons and try to stabilize their line, but the Sikh advance refuses to break. As the pressure mounts, the Durrani formation begins to collapse and signs of surrender and confusion appear, including white flags raised amid the disorder. Dina Beg sends word praising the Singhs for the victory and asking them to hold their ground rather than scatter into uncontrolled pursuit. The key instruction is do not pursue the fleeing enemy, because the Nawab wants the field secured before the rout becomes a looting chase. Even so, the page ends with the Khalsa conscious that it has broken the enemy's confidence and forced a major retreat. 428 suet chaupaî: tug dôhrâ suet chaupaî tug dôhrâ gut chaupaî Sri Gur Panth Prakash TIH ffu ua fae usu mo fae TA aera | fšsg fs fred usd dua GA dì af jus karam singh pagg bin paryô jan bin bâj kulâhi. tittar jim giljô paryô rakkhyô us hî thâi.54.: Safa wen der ot | Hrg gwed mà Ud HG I wet Ge Ba Sus Hod | HIK £a [HJ di$ vas luu! tabhi khâlsg halla kîyô. mâr talvar age dhar lîyô. lat ôt un tôpan muhrg. mârhin chhalak jih gôlç duhr¢.55. mt cfonio ot Sst vere | fu Hg sg ford fos urefg | 34 fuo ag ýsa SG | Tedo A wT TH AA ue au takian ki thailî chalâvain. singh sûr bahu gir gir pâvhin. tab singhan kachhu thambhan lîyô. bandûkan kô bahu râbâ kîyô.56. gas Hag dol fag | Ses Se Gare [HO | Had 5S 5 HST H 39 | čo UTS 395 AHS UDI bandôkan són bahu durani girg. natthan ôt lukavain sirg. shutar nal lai shutar su turg. natth durant dagran kó murdg.57.: SH aaa H CÍNG SS UA Ue | SŠ uJrôl uu [So 5a AE use |UC | tab navâb só dckhi6 phatg khâlsô pai. nathg durânî dçkh tin jhanda dió khardâi.58.: sea [Hu Ú col ese | Mur at e wet Hue | MA eH 5 AG We | Stat aA Sa gS uc navab singhan pai vakil durdâc. singh ji phatç lai tum pai. age kadam na ki6 jag. than kîjô dacrâ thâc.59. pages.searchText: Night Pursuit to Jalandhar Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Despite the earlier warning, sections of the Khalsa continue after the broken enemy and turn the retreat into a running night pursuit. They fall upon the fleeing Durrani troops at midnight, seize horses, weapons, and baggage, and keep the pressure on until the whole countryside feels the panic of defeat. By dawn the chase has reached the approaches to Jalandhar, where plundered columns and scattered survivors spread alarm through the city. The Khalsa strips the roads and outer quarters so aggressively that Jalandhar appealed to Dina Beg for protection through payment before the city should be fully sacked. The page therefore turns battlefield victory into political leverage. pages.searchText: By that time, the darkness of the night had descended on the scene, Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh By that time, the darkness of the night had descended on the scene, Such being the situation that prevailed over there. As all the Durrani troops fled to enter their base camp, Everyone ran for his life despite their commader's orders. (63) Dohra: Those being more smart and impatient among the Singhs, Did they go in hot pursuit of the fleeing Pathan troops. As they observed the Pathan troops running for their lives, They plundered and robbed them of their horses. (64) The (pursuing) Singhs sent a messenger to the camping Singhs. Announcing a call for plunder with the beat of a drum, The Singhs started plundering whatever they could lay their hands on. (65) As everyone kept with himself whatever he plundered, Everyone got rid of his poverty and want of things. The Singhs also warned the Nawab through a messenger, That no one from his own camp should go on a looting spree. (66) The Singhs would plunder the Nawab's men as well if they went out, Besides crushing their heads if they dared to join this looting spree. Thus, the Singhs took possession of all equipment of the fleeing Pathans, Including the artillery guns which they deignited after capturing these. (67) Dohra: As the Pathan Chief Sir Balandkhan!? deserted his base camp, It was the time of midnight (as he made his departure). As all his equipage along with carriages was left behind, He could hardly reach Jalandhar by the break of dawn. (68) Chaupai: Hardly could he stay at Jalandhar for a few minutes, When the Singh forces arrived in hot pursuit of him. Many of his loaded carriages got stuck in the rivulets, As his troops ran on foot abandoning their horses as well. (69) All hell broke among the fleeing people of Jalandhar, As a band of plunderers and arsonists entered the city. Thereupon, the Singhs being at complete liberty to plunder, They robbed and plundered the fleeing people thoroughly. pages.searchText: Dina Beg’s Secret Petition to Jassa Singh Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Alarmed by the scale of the Sikh advance, Dina Beg looks for a way to save Jalandhar without openly breaking faith with Wadbhag Singh. He sends a secret petition to Jassa Singh, hoping the leading Sikh chief can restrain the sack in return for money and preserve the city under a negotiated settlement. The appeal reaches the Khalsa assembly, but Wadbhag Singh answers from a position of strength and insists that the old Pathan offenses must first be avenged. His challenge stiffens the whole gathering, and Dina Beg learns that payment alone will not override the moral claims already made in the name of the Panth. Only by humbling himself further can he keep the situation from spinning beyond his control. pages.searchText: Jalandhar Settlement and Karah Parshad Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Wadbhag Singh now dictates the terms in practice, warning Dina Beg to keep his own troops inside camp while the Khalsa enters Jalandhar. The city is subjected to selective vengeance and humiliation against its enemies, and the Nawab is left to prove submission rather than command events. Once the pressure has done its work, Dina Beg returns with one lakh rupees and karah parshad as a visible acknowledgment of Sikh ascendancy. The money is handed over before the Khalsa, and the sacred offering is distributed in a setting that blends triumph, thanksgiving, and political settlement. The Nawab even praises the karah parshad as he tastes it, underscoring how far he has moved from bargaining partner to dependent ally. The page closes with cash, ritual, and public deference combining to ratify the Sikh victory at Jalandhar. 434 suet chaupaî: gdr dôhrâ gut chaupaî: tug dôhrâ gut chaupaî: Sri Gur Panth Prakash: dasa SG afo AG | SH MUS Sg 3 festes 5 lu | for We ast 9 Aas | fed Ge THs ws ITAI dina beg nûn yau kahi dîyô. tum apng daçrç tç niklan na dîyô. kia jânôn kôî havai jc bat. vichôn hôvai tumrô ghat.81. dor da sau ald ata | M ma sud fa 9 sgt | asx MUN gHƏ 3G | ÍHH wd BH jl gq 5U It dina beg tab yau kahi dîyô. main ab tumrô sikkh havai rahy6. bhôdaâ sikkh main tumrô bhayô. jim châhô tim hi rakh lay6.82. pages.searchText: Doaba Settlement and the Maratha Transition Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh The Dina Beg-Wadbhag Singh episode closes with further payment, praise for the sacred offering, and a final reckoning of the region's revenues. An additional sum is settled, the Doaba assessment is fixed at one and a quarter lakh, and the Khalsa agrees to stop the ransacking of Doaba once these terms are secured. The page then deliberately pivots into Episode 125, signaling that a new political landscape is opening beyond the immediate Jalandhar settlement. Mughal weakness around Delhi, Ahmad Shah Abdali's Kandahari power, and the rising role of the Marathas and the Khalsa are introduced as connected forces reshaping North India. Dina Beg again recognizes that major conflict cannot be managed without Sikh participation, so the transition leads directly into new negotiations and campaigns. This hinge page therefore both concludes one and a quarter lakh as the settlement figure and opens the wider story of Marathas and the Khalsa. 436 tug dôhrâ gut chaupaî: Sri Gur Panth Prakash JN A See aì Ud wet | 9 Wd TAH Sea Ft TST | udt dad nig aT BS | worse cor Her wy gE ito! ham sç budadahan kó yah khânâ. hai yah bahishtôn nanak ji ana. pachi hazâr aur kar 10. duâbç taka savâ lakh thîô.90. Marathas And the Khalsa Panth The alliance with Dina Beg now turns toward Sirhind, but the Singhs make clear that they will not be bought off as hired auxiliaries. They refuse ordinary payment, demand formal license to plunder the hostile city, and insist that the Nawab confirm the arrangement with an oath on the holy Koran before the campaign proceeds. Once that sanction is secured, the Khalsa throws itself into the attack on Sirhind with the same hard resolve it had shown in the Doaba fighting. The city and its fort are struck with such force that the expedition becomes both a military assault and a contest over who will control the spoils of victory. That success quickly creates friction with the Marathas, who resent the scale of Sikh plunder and prestige. Marathas And the Khalsa Panth As the quarrel sharpens, Dina Beg warned the Singhs that the Marathas were preparing to strike their camp under cover of alliance. Keeping faith with his earlier pledge, he gives them just enough notice to withdraw in good order rather than be caught in a surprise attack. The Singhs leave camp in the afternoon and allow the Maratha force to believe they are retreating for good. Once the pursuers have come far enough, the Khalsa turns the movement into a trap, turned back and fired on the Marathas, and punishes the chase with disciplined violence. After that sharp reversal, the Singhs pull away toward their own ground while the wider wreckage of Sirhind and Samand Khan's defeat remains in the background. pages.searchText: Sikh Ascendancy and the Opening of Sadiq Beg’s Betrayal Marathas And the Khalsa Panth The aftermath of the Sirhind struggle is described as a moment of expanding Sikh dominance, with Lahore and Multan laid open, forts raised, and revenue gathered under Khalsa pressure. The balance of power has shifted so visibly that even allied elites begin calculating how to contain the Singhs before their authority grows further. One result of that unease is that the Marathas captured Dina Beg, revealing how unstable the recent partnership had become. Political advantage, not loyalty, now drives the field, and the page uses that seizure to close the Maratha-Khalsa episode on a note of distrust and fractured ambition. It then turns into the next narrative, as the Khalsa prepares for Hola Mohalla and movement toward Anandpur from the Raipur Gujarwal side. Tara Singh led the contingent, and the gathering is presented as both martial and devotional before politics again interrupts the journey. Sadiq Beg has failed to honor earlier obligations, so resentment follows him even before open fighting resumes. When his revenue interests appear exposed, Sikh action against them helps turn suspicion into war and convinces him to answer with force rather than payment. He therefore launches a sudden attack near Srainwal, trying to hit the Khalsa while it is not yet fully concentrated. (2) As Sadiq Beg was ruling as ruler of the Sirhind state, He had chosen not to pay the agreed ransom to the Singhs. As Khalsa's representatives had returned empty handed from Sirhind, This breach of trust rankled in the minds of Khalsa Singhs. (3) As the Singh contingents were proceeding to Anandpur Sahib, They were passing through the area in the vicinity of Sirhind. As Sadiq Beg's officials and troops were collecting revenues, The Singhs spotted their movement amidst the dust and din. (4) As the Singhs turned their face towards Sadiq Beg's contingent, The Mughal contingent also spotted out the Khalsa contingents. As this contingent endeavoured to turn back towards Sirhind, They could think of no other alternative at that moment of time. (5) As the Singhs observed the Mughal official party turning back, They attacked the revenue collecting party all of a sudden. Suddenly did they attack where the Singhs were camping, At a wayside inn in the vicinity of the village Srainwal. (7) As there was a sudden burst of fire from guns and muskets, The Singhs were at their wits ends to combat this sudden attack. As majority of best warriors had gone to celebrate Hola Mohalla, Others had gone into the countryside to purchase provisions. (8) As many among them had gone to fetch fodder and fuel wood, The whole Khalsa Panth force had scattered over the area. pages.searchText: Episode About Sadiq Beg's Betrayal in Friendship Sadiq Beg's Betrayal in Friendship The surprise attack throws parts of the Khalsa camp into confusion, but the Sikh chiefs rapidly begin to regroup around their banners and armed circles. Sangat Singh / Shyam Singh / Karora Singh and other leaders emerge in the narrative as rallying figures who help transform shock into organized resistance. The Singhs form a fortified circular camp, absorb heavy cannon fire and close-range punishment, and refuse to let the Mughals finish the battle in a single rush. Even when some of the line gives way, the chiefs steady the force and restore its willingness to fight at close quarters. Once the panic passes, the Khalsa rallies and charges back against men, horses, and gun positions alike. (12) As these veterans and chiefs took up positions to face the enemy, They did succeed in combating the enemy for a short while. Thereafter, as Sadig Beg's troops planting their cannons there, They fired a volley of copper pellets from their loaded guns. pages.searchText: Wounded Chiefs, Negotiation, and the Gazdi Transition Sadiq Beg's Betrayal in Friendship By the close of the fighting, many chiefs were wounded, and the cost of the battle is measured through the battered bodies of leading sardars. Jassa Singh received two grievous wounds, making his suffering emblematic of the price paid by the Khalsa in a fight triggered by treachery. Sadiq Beg now falls back on negotiation and tries to repair the breach through envoys, compensation, and renewed promises of settlement. The Singhs hear the offer, but their answer is stern: delay in ransom would bring renewed plunder, because bad faith has already been proved in the field. This settlement talk also becomes a transition into the next political sequence. pages.searchText: Episode About Gazdi (The Minister) Gazdi (The Minister) As Delhi's sovereign became slack in supervision, Gazdi grows swollen with pride and begins treating his ministerial authority as a stage for self-glorification. To fix that vanity in words, Gazdi asked Gang Bhat for praise and expected the bard to turn political power into poetic immortality. Gang Bhat refuses to flatter what he does not believe, insisting that he would not eulogize what was not true. His refusal costs him his life, and the killing becomes a moral indictment of Gazdi's arrogance rather than a display of legitimate strength. The page then broadens the accusation by suggesting that the same pride would damage Gazdi's larger alliances as well. What begins as a courtly demand for praise becomes an omen that Gazdi ruined the Marathas as well through the same blindness and overreach. 450 Sri Gur Panth Prakash cet: mo fest AAS ASU | Stes one gg su | HS M girl: ate mHE | sorte dat se ATG ges 131 chaupaî: shâhu dill? kó susat su bhayô. vajîr gâjdîn gâjat bhayô. man main gâjdîn kîô abhimân. bulâi gang bhat kahyô bakhân.3. pages.searchText: As Delhi's sovereign became somewhat slack in supervision, Gazdi (The Minister) As Delhi's sovereign became somewhat slack in supervision, His minister Ghazdi started boasting about his own eminence. As Gazdi felt very arrogant about his military exploits, He asked the poet laureate? to compose verses in his praise. (3) Asking the court poet to sing verses eulogizing his achievements, Gazdi wished his name to be declared supreme among the ministers. Claiming to have earned the title of being a bridegroom, He boasted of having been honoured by the king himself. (4) That he would not eulogize what had not been true. Only what was truth and real would he state, Even if he had to sacrifice his life for truth. (5) Even his predecessors had never sung false praises, Though they had to sacrifice their lives for being truthful. He too would sacrifice his life to uphold the truth. (6) Gang Verses From a Bridegroom he lowered himself to a lowly Bride, By having entered into an alliance with Malhar Rao Maratha chief. Not the slightest harm could he cause to the Jat ruler, Although he had plundered the entire region of Delhi. (7) Having been stung by the plain speaking by Gangbhat, The dying statement that this poet had made, Became a well-known maxim the world over: (8) Never can an impotent (coward) wage a war, Nor can the beat of his war-drum frighten anyone. pages.searchText: Whole of India and the Gilja Pathans Gazdi (The Minister) The narrative now widens from individual intrigue to a subcontinental struggle, explicitly signaling Episode 128 and the shift to Whole of India and the Gilja Pathans. The concern is no longer only Gazdi's character, but the effort to recover authority across Hindustan after repeated upheaval. In that larger frame, Mughal and Pathan forces united in response to Maratha advance and political fragmentation. Lahore is re-entered with strength, and the story presents the coalition as an attempt to restore order by consolidating Muslim power under renewed leadership. The proposed arrangement imagines three ministers and a Kandhari sovereign overseeing the realm, a formula meant to stabilize what war had broken apart. pages.searchText: Episode About Hattoo Singh Majhail Hattoo Singh Majhail The page first closes the preceding campaign against the Khalsa by showing how Jahan Khan kept chasing the Khalsa Singhs while scattered bands answered with sudden counterattacks. Even under pursuit, the Singhs looted from the vanguard and rearguard, avoided being pinned down, and many Singhs withdrew into Malwa, forests, and other hiding places until they could regroup. It then opens Episode About Hattoo Singh Majhail by introducing Hattoo Singh as a brave Majhail Sikh from the Kanna Kachha side whose night raid went wrong when his horse slipped beneath him. Captured alive and brought before Ahmad Shah Abdali, he is presented as a steadfast Singh who will not yield even when royal punishment is prepared. Abdali therefore ordered to be crushed by a ferocious elephant, expecting the spectacle to terrify the Khalsa. Instead the elephant would not kill him, and even when Hattoo Singh was fastened for trampling the execution failed, turning the page into the opening of a martyrdom narrative rather than a routine execution. 454 Sri Gur Panth Prakash 34 =fg ffws Hga Ud | ATS YS H dÌ& Jd | Hurd HE ge ore | afo ug ffws Ja S ware 121 tab vahi singhan mâray chahai. jahân khan su gailai rahai. só marai jôî hath avai. vahi bahu singhan hatth na lagâvai.2. cog: fu ot fan Hg GS ord ure =s | Gf ug ag Sue ad [Hu ud feu HW as 131 dôhrâ: singh bhi tiskô bahu lutain âgai pâchhai daurd. ui mârç bahu tumman kar singh mârain bidh sayón thôrd.3. suet: ag ffu ga Srfg JO | ag Wu 35 HU BA | MI fu a Hee =3 | aò u5 TE WAS 81 chaupaî: kachhû singh luk deshin rahe. kachhû singh jhal madh luk rahc. aur singh ja málvç vardg. ikthç dal hui rahe su khardg.4. aso. pages.searchText: Episode About Bikaner Bikaner Hattoo Singh's ordeal ends here when the second elephant did not crush Hattoo Singh either, further enraging Ahmad Shah. The ruler finally had him tied between two elephants and torn apart, presenting his death as a public martyrdom rather than a defeat in battle. The page then turns to Episode About Bikaner, with Abdali still entrenched at Lahore while the Khalsa in Malwa struggled through want and accepted an invitation to aid Bikaner in its conflict with Jaisalmer. The Singhs fought effectively, but the Bikaner side broke faith and the Singhs were not paid the promised wages after the campaign was done. Because the Khalsa could not make both ends meet under those conditions, the narrative explains why they began planning fresh raids for subsistence instead of remaining dependent on unreliable allies. pages.searchText: Episode About the Bangar Region the Bangar Region This page continues the Bangar expedition by showing the Khalsa consulting chiefs such as Alo Singh, Budho Singh, and Gurbakhsh Singh before moving through the region. Their negotiations determined which settlements would be protected, and eight villages saved from plunder after local intermediaries secured terms with the Singhs. Once those understandings were made, the Khalsa rode more aggressively across the surrounding tract, and Hansi, Narnaul, and Hissar were raided along with other vulnerable places. The page presents these movements as organized campaigning rather than random disorder, with the Singhs distinguishing between hostile targets and those placed under safeguard. Jaipur sent envoys to the Singhs to ask that their state be spared, invoking shared reverence for the Gurus and the practical value of peace. pages.snippet: The page closes the Bangar expedition: Malwa chiefs such as Bhai Alo Singh, Bhai Budho Singh, and Bhai Gurbakhsh Singh helped lead the Khalsa force, arranged settlements, and protected those under their care. Alo Singh saved eight Kaithal villages, while chief
pages.searchText: Bangar Expedition and Mit Singh’s Proposal Mit Singh — The Martyr The page closes the Bangar expedition: Malwa chiefs such as Bhai Alo Singh, Bhai Budho Singh, and Bhai Gurbakhsh Singh helped lead the Khalsa force, arranged settlements, and protected those under their care. Alo Singh saved eight Kaithal villages, while chiefs at Jind and Safidon sent ransom through the Malwa Singhs. The Khalsa then raided Hansi, Narnaul, Hissar, and the hill fort of Kama, after which Jaipur sent envoys asking to be spared as fellow followers of the Guru. The Singhs accepted the plea, turned back, and camped near the Yamuna. Episode 133 begins by introducing Tara Singh Gaiba of the Dalewalia Misl and Mit Singh, who would become a martyr fighting Jahan Khan’s forces. Mit Singh proposed that ten thousand independent-minded Singhs should cross the Yamuna at dawn, but Tara Singh warned that Mit Singh was acting on his own. Dohra Chaupai: Dohra Chaupai: Dohra Chaupai: Sri Gur Panth Prakash 459 Among those Malwa chiefs were Bhai Alo Singh and Bhai Budho Singh, Bhai Gurbax Singh* being another among the invited. (2) Putting their representatives at the head of Khalsa Panth force, They made them lead the Khalsa Panth expedition. Bringing about settlements between Singhs and those others, They protected those whom they considered their own. (3) Bringing about settlement between Singhs and chiefs of Kaithal, Alo Singh saved eight villages from plunder by Khalsa Panth. Striking a deal with the chiefs of Jind* and Safidon after a raid, Some amount of ransom was sent to the Singhs through Malwa Singhs. (4) With a rush, did the Khalsa Panth ransack the distant Hansi°, They also plundered the more remote towns of Narnaul and Hissar, Thereafter, plundering the hill fort Kama at the hill top, Khalsa Panth forces sent a message about their arrival to the Jaipur ruler. (5) Thereafter, the Jaipur chief sent his representatives to the Singhs, Professing himself to be as devout a Sikh of the Gurus as the Singhs, When Guru Tegh Bahadur had conquered the southern region, The Rajput ruler had sought Guru Tegh Bahadur's protection. (6) Both Rajputs and Singhs, being followers of the same Guru, The Rajputs begged the Singhs to spare their territory from plunder. Thereupon, the Singhs retracing their steps from there, They put up their camp in the vicinity of river Yamuna. (7) Episode 133 Episode About Mit Singh, the Martyr (Mit Singh had made the Supreme Sacrifice in this way As he had put up a brave fight against Jahan khan's forces) There was one Singh known as Tara Singh (Gaiba), Who belonged the Khalsa Panth Mis! of Dalewalia. There was also one Mit Singh (the rioteer in this Misl), Who arrived at an (independent) resolution of his own: (1) That ten thousand Singhs, having an independent mind, They should raid across the Yamuna river the early morning. Overhearing this conversation did Tara Singh tell Mit Singh, That the latter alone was an egocentric among the Khalsa Panth. (2)

pages.searchText: Episode About Mit Singh — The Martyr Mit Singh — The Martyr Tara Singh had warned Mit Singh against crossing Yamuna with a smaller force, arguing that a lightly supported raid would invite disaster once word reached larger enemy centers. Mit Singh pressed on anyway, leading a mobile Sikh band across the river into Rohilla territory and spending several days gathering plunder around Meerut. The warning proved true when Rohilla resistance hardened and troops from Lahore and Sirhind arrived to reinforce the pursuit. Their combined force attacked at sunrise with such force that the booty-laden Singhs were thrown into confusion, and many were cut down before they could form a proper defense. Even in that reversal, Mit Singh kept fighting as a martyr rather than retreating in panic. pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Mit Singh — The Martyr
pages.snippet: The battle's cost is counted bluntly here, with the poem stating that five to six thousand Singhs perished in the defeat around Mit Singh's final stand. Enemy victors severed heads for display and loaded as many as eighteen cartloads of severed heads to carry
pages.searchText: Shahid Ganj and the Opening of Mir Mannu Mit Singh — The Martyr The battle's cost is counted bluntly here, with the poem stating that five to six thousand Singhs perished in the defeat around Mit Singh's final stand. Enemy victors severed heads for display and loaded as many as eighteen cartloads of severed heads to carry off as trophies for their patrons. That grim procession did not reach its destination unchanged, because alarm spread near a Ghaggar-side sarai that Sikh forces were approaching. The carts were abandoned there, and Bhag Singh and Bhanga Singh gathered the heads, gave them cremation rites, and preserved the memory of the dead at the place came to be known as Shahid Ganj. After closing Mit Singh's martyrdom, the page deliberately shifts tone and opens Episode About Mir Mannu. pages.searchText: Episode About Mir Mannu Mir Mannu Mir Mannu responds to repeated Sikh raids near Lahore's outskirts by deciding that ordinary policing is no longer enough and that the Khalsa must be rooted out completely. Orders go out across the province to seize or kill Singhs wherever they can be found, turning his administration into an instrument of systematic persecution. The pressure becomes so severe that whole Sikh families lose safe refuge in Majha and depend on scattered sympathizers for survival. One important hiding place is Pandori in the Majha area, where the household associated with saint Dadu Ram shelters vulnerable women connected to the Sikh community. When informers expose the arrangement, Mir Mannu's men descend on the site, arrest the grandson of saint Dadu Ram, and search the monastery for fugitives. The women escape immediate discovery only by taking on the red robes of that sect, a detail that underscores both the danger and the ingenuity of those being hunted. 464 aug dôhrâ suet chaupaî: gdr dôhrâ suet chaupaî: Sri Gur Panth Prakash lahaur dhig ghôrdg jai durdâc. gail pardain ralain jhardan jas. thôrdan kô singh murd bhî mârain. bahutan kô kit agârdai pachhârdain.3. 3 ante & faw KH mah | SSS uTSHT HS HIR | od Sg vet Gx ese | Mm [HU fsa Hrg ase |8| tau bajîr kç dil im ai. dçiç khâlsâ sabh marvaî. châr ôr daî phauj durdâc. dîc singh tin mâr kadahâc.4. pages.searchText: As well as their larger contingents from the vanguard and the rearguard. (3) Mir Mannu As well as their larger contingents from the vanguard and the rearguard. (3) Thereupon, the minister (Mir Mannu) felt in his heart of hearts, That he must get all the Singhs eliminated from his region. Despatching his forces in all the four directions forthwith, He did beat the Singhs to turn them out of his province. (4) The foot soldiers among the Singhs sheltered themselves here and there, Surviving purely on what they could lay their hands on. The minister, hearing of these incidents of wayside robberies, Himself led a crusade against these highwaymen. (5) Dohra: Mir Mannu would despatch his messengers to a place, From where he got the slightest information about Singhs. Wherever he heard about the settlements of Singh families, There would he order to take them out after laying a siege. (6) Chaupai: Daily would Mir Mannu go on a hunting spree to kill the Singhs, Even those Singhs who were (peacefully) engaged in agriculture, They, too, were eliminated after searching them out. (7) Such an uprour and panick gripped the Majha region, That Sikh families could not find shelter anywhere. There was a village named Pandori in the Majha area, Where lived a famous saint by name of Dadu Ram. (8) As my (the author's) mother and grandmother had taken refuge there, Some state informers leaked out their whereabouts to the minister. There itself did the minister himself arrive post haste, Laying a siege to the village after a meticulous planning. (9) Dohra: The young boy, who was the grandson of saint Dadu Ram, Was he summoned before the minister after arresting him. Accusing him of sheltering those guilty of treachery, The minister ordered him to handover those to the authorities. (10) Chaupai: As the young mendicant denied having any fugitives, Mir Mannu's minister ordered his monastry to be searched. pages.searchText: Mir Mannu's Death and the Opening of Mathura And Koel Mir Mannu The Mir Mannu episode reaches its climax as the trapped Sikh households lament that mothers and sisters had no one to share their grief while the minister's terror campaign seemed unstoppable. In the middle of that chaos, Mir Mannu's horse suddenly reared, threw him down, and his feet got entangled in the stirrup so that he was dragged to a painful death. His fall is treated as divine reversal: the persecutor who meant to crush the Khalsa dies helplessly, and the machinery of the hunt breaks apart almost at once. Captives are released, the immediate panic lifts, and the narrative closes his episode by tying political justice to the downfall of a tyrant. The same page then opens Episode About Mathura And Koel, widening the frame back to imperial politics after Panipat. pages.searchText: Episode About Mathura And Koel Mathura And Koel The siege narrative sharpens here when Abdali refuses to ignore the taunts coming from the Jat stronghold at Koel and insists that he will not proceed farther until the fort is mastered. To him the drumming and bravado from inside are proof that the Jats were poking fun at him, so the campaign becomes a test of prestige as much as a military necessity. As his officers review the problem, the fort stocked with plenty of provisions is described as difficult to reduce by ordinary means. Its defenders are well supplied, the position is strong, and the discussion makes clear that a prolonged effort may be required before the road to Agra can be secured. pages.searchText: Episode About Mathura And Koel Mathura And Koel Even after the plan is prepared, the Muslim chiefs keep entreating Abdali to defer the assault and move on toward Agra, arguing that delay at Koel is wasteful. Abdali rejects that advice, convinced that Agra itself cannot be controlled unless the surrounding Jat resistance is first broken. He then spreads his army around the fort from multiple directions while the defenders remain steady under Rai Mal's leadership. Fire from outside proves less decisive than hoped, water and fortifications frustrate mining, and the garrison's confidence makes the siege feel heavier with each passing day. By this stage Seven days having been wasted, impatience and embarrassment are growing among the attackers. pages.searchText: Episode About Mathura And Koel Mathura And Koel Abdali next changes tactics by riding out with little ceremony so he can study the ground without revealing too much of his intention. He reconnoitres the approaches, measures heights and distances, and keeps the defenders guessing by shifting men forward and back instead of committing to an obvious assault. Once darkness falls, he summons his commanders and reveals the engineering answer he has chosen. A forty feet high wall is ordered at the commanding point near the fort, and the work is pressed so quickly that the defenders cannot interfere before dawn. By morning the Jats are astonished to find a new elevation towering over their position as if a mountain had risen overnight. pages.searchText: Episode About Mathura And Koel Mathura And Koel From the newly raised position, Abdali begins a crushing bombardment with several thousand musketeers on the top backed by artillery, arrows, and incendiaries. Smoke, fire, and noise overwhelm the fort so completely that day itself seems darkened, and the defenders are battered from above in a way they had not anticipated. As the pressure intensifies, Abdali allows one direction of escape to remain open, calculating that panic will do what direct slaughter cannot. Men begin fleeing toward the Yamuna, the fort's will collapses, and the siege ends less by negotiated surrender than by terror and exhaustion. Rai Mal's final humiliation seals the page: unable to bear the dishonor of defeat, he throws himself into the river after the stronghold is lost. The fall of Koel therefore becomes both a tactical victory for Abdali and a moral catastrophe for the Jat defenders. 478 Sri Gur Panth Prakash nag UA À ee vate | adt garg dea vet oe wel sea UT Woo ad | Te ret fea 3 TS aT 1891 Jambârg pafij sai daç chardhâi. kai hazâr bandôk dai lâi. dai chhalak bahu banan keri. hui gai din tc rat hanhcrî.41. cos: GS gS A Se H HU no vel Hg Sa | gimit gahi init HY Ja F JA 182 | dôhrâ: gôlc ban au tîr sôn madh agan dai bahu phik. chhurîân burîân tikkhîân mârain hath són châk.42. cust: mae famh HO ud | vied So HS HON S9 | Add Woo at FAS Barret | Mila 3 ale nit derah 193 | chaupaî: asmânôn bijli Janu parai. andar 16k sabh sahmg bharai. pages.searchText: He deployed several thousand musketeers on the top. Mathura And Koel He deployed several thousand musketeers on the top. Such a heavy volley of fire and arrows did they open, That their smoke created pitch darkness even during the day. (41) Dohra: With fireballs, bows and arrows (such a heavy attack did he launch), That (this impregnable Jat fort) was set on fire from inside, That they never failed to hit the Jat soldiers enconsed inside the fort. (42) Chaupai: With such speed of lightening from the skies did Abdali's firearms strike, With the strategy of shooting arrows laced with poisons, Many of those hit with these arrows were rendered blind. (43) As these deadly arrows and fireballs set the fort on fire, Those guarding the fort from inside panicked with fear. Even the cannons which had been positioned on the fort, Those also could not stand the massive firing from outside. (44) Lifting a siege from all the sides around this fort, Abdali ordered his troops to let those flee who wished to escape. As many of the fort inmates fled for fear of being killed, The rest of the Jat troops also looked forward to run away. (45) As majority of them were wounded and charred with fire. With Agra and surrounding positions subdued, the narrative briefly surveys his larger settlement of north Indian affairs through appointments and renewed control in places such as Delhi, Sirhind, Lahore, and Amritsar. pages.searchText: The Khalsa Remained Inexhaustible (Ghallughara) Near Malerkotla, Kup And Policed ie Episode 136 opens by insisting that even after terrible losses the Khalsa remained inexhaustible, because Sikh bands kept re-forming wherever pressure fell hardest. Families were hidden in Malwa while armed Singhs continued to strike opportunistically, refusing to let persecution extinguish the Panth. The page emphasizes that mobility itself became a weapon: the Singhs kept plundering the vanguard and the rearguard day and night, forcing larger armies to feel hunted even when they believed themselves in command. This combination of concealment for families and relentless harassment by fighters explains why the Khalsa seemed impossible to finish off. Abdali then lashes out symbolically as well as militarily by moving against Amritsar and violating the holy Harmandar Sahib and its sacred pool. pages.searchText: The Singhs Would Steal Their Horses and Get Lost (Ghallughara) Near Malerkotla, Kup And Policed ie The Afghan effort to pin down the Khalsa remains ineffective because the Singhs would steal their horses and get lost before any disciplined pursuit could catch them. Advisers warn that chasing Majhail Sikh bands through jungle and scrub will only exhaust imperial troops, who do not know the terrain and cannot survive long without secure water and supply. This argument becomes a grudging acknowledgment of Khalsa resilience: the brave Majhail Singhs know how to disperse, reassemble, and strike again while stronger-looking armies blunder after them. The page therefore treats the question of how could the mighty Khalsa Panth be annihilated? as a real strategic dilemma rather than a boast. At the same time, the Sikhs themselves decide they cannot preserve families and community merely by hiding. pages.searchText: Debating Malerkotla Before Abdali's Trap Closes (Ghallughara) Near Malerkotla, Kup And Policed ie The Khalsa camp near Malerkotla becomes a place of sharp debate, because While some favoured destroying Malerkotla there and then, others recalled that the town had once received the Guru's grace and should not be treated like an ordinary enemy target. The disagreement slows decisive action just as hostile forces are drawing together in the background. pages.searchText: The Battle Turns Toward Malwa (Ghallughara) Near Malerkotla, Kup And Policed ie Battle erupts before the Sikhs can complete their preparations, so suddenly did the fight start with swords and arrows that organized maneuver gives way to immediate resistance. Even under surprise, the Singhs stood their ground fighting hard, treating the clash as a defense of faith, families, and honor rather than as a simple skirmish. Losses mount quickly in the foremost ranks, and the fighting swirls across the field with muskets, blades, and mounted charges breaking any stable line. The page does not soften the chaos; it presents the combat as a brutal test of endurance in which survival depends on constant regrouping. Recognizing that the whole community cannot remain fixed in one killing ground, the Sikh leaders decide that Towards the Malwa region should they move their contingents under experienced guidance. pages.searchText: Sham Singh Rallies the Caravan (Ghallughara) Near Malerkotla, Kup And Policed ie Hardly had the Sikh caravan gone for three miles before fresh pressure fell on it from Jain Khan and Malerkotla forces, proving that even partial withdrawal offered no safety. The caravan is still exposed, the enemy remains aggressive, and the Khalsa must decide how to preserve both its fighting core and its noncombatants. From that crisis comes the judgment that the Sikh caravans must be accompanied by a warrior chief who can hold the attackers off while the column keeps moving. Responsibility falls on Sham Singh, who accepts the burden of shielding the convoy even though it means entering the thickest danger rather than escaping it. He rallies misl forces with drums, standards, and a direct call to action, then carves a path toward the endangered column and restores enough order for it to move farther on. The page therefore remembers not only disaster, but also the kind of disciplined sacrifice by which Sikh leadership kept the community alive in the middle of catastrophe. 490 Sri Gur Panth Prakash tug: HdÌd OH efe [45 aG 3 mà ug fou nig | Ho ms HANE HI GF sg te |SÊI dôhrâ —: bahîr kôs dui tinn gayô tau âgc parç ripu aur. jainâ ate malçriç mârc unhain bahu daur.36. gut: BT TU 8 Ho 39 | g3 ge s Ba Hd ae | wid sts Go ste Ud | faH MUS Ñ e= a Ag 1321 chaupaî: bahir gayô thô sunnôn tôâ. hutô sardâr na un sang kôû. agyôn bahîr un lînô gher. jim ayyard men vard gayô sher.37. The Singhs resolve to protect the moving caravan for the sake of their religion and ideology, even if that means exposing themselves as a rear guard. They fight like lions against Biland Khan, Jahan Khan, and the pressing Pathan line, repeatedly throwing themselves into the path of the assault so women, children, and noncombatants can keep moving. Dust, noise, and repeated charges make the field chaotic, yet the Singhs continue to cover the retreat with their own bodies. The crisis deepens when Ahmad Shah Abdali himself attacked the Singhs and pushes in from the rear with greater force. For protecting the dignity and honour of Guru's Khalsa Panth, For the sake of their religion and ideology did they wage a war. As Ahmad Shah Abdali himself attacked the Singhs, The raging dust made things invisible on the battlefield. The rebuke carries a clear political sting: if such strength cannot hold the Khalsa at the front, then Jain Khan's earlier confidence means little. Jain Khan launches another attempt, but Sham Singh's men throw it back and prove again that a frontal check will not come easily. He returns from the field admitting that it is better to attack the Singhs instead of invading the caravan, because the armed jathas are the shield that keeps the rest of the column alive. Abdali accepts that logic and shifts the pressure toward the fighting Sikhs themselves. (71) If he (Jain Khan) could check the Singhs movement from the front, Abdali's own troops would eliminate the Singhs in a few hours. Without getting encircled and blocked would the Singhs be not eliminated, Such a conclusion he had arrived at after a thorough deliberation. (72) As a sleeping lion gets disturbed from his deep slumber. As he made a dash to block and check the Singhs advance, He was repulsed by a counter attack by Sham Singh's contingent. (73) Impossible it was to check the Singhs from the front. Fewer though they appeared to be in numerical strength, So many more they proved in strength during fight. (74) In no way could he block the Singhs passage, such dare devils they were. Suggesting Abdali to attack the Singhs instead of invading the caravan, Accepting Jain Khan's proposal after listening to his plan, Abdali did launch an attack on the Khalsa Panth force. Opening a volley of bullets after taking up positions, A few Singhs did kill those who dared to attack them. pages.searchText: Jassa Singh Refuses to Yield and Gurmukh Singh Gives Him a Horse (Ghallughara) Near Malerkotla, Kup And Policed ie Jassa Singh Ahluwalia refuses to leave the field even after receiving many wounds and riding a horse that can barely move any farther. His stubbornness comes from honor rather than recklessness: he would rather die fighting than let the fleeing caravan think its leaders abandoned them. Companions plead with him to withdraw before he is completely trapped, but he continues to resist the idea of retreat. The exchange sharpens into a moving act of service when Gurmukh Singh made Jassa Singh mount his own horse so the wounded chief could continue directing the struggle instead of being lost on foot. That gesture preserves both leadership and morale in the middle of a collapsing battlefield. The report shocks the assembled Sikh chiefs, but the shock quickly hardens into resolve as leaders from several contingents prepare to answer the crisis together. The chiefs declare that none of them should think of survival without first meeting the enemy head-on. Their shared determination gives the page a collective tone: Jassa Singh's suffering becomes a rallying point that binds the misls more tightly in the middle of the Ghallughara. Out of that resolve, Charat Singh rides forward searching for Abdali's line and crashing into the Gilja fighters with sword, spear, and gun. pages.searchText: Charat Singh Mounts Foot Soldiers and Fights Across the Flanks (Ghallughara) Near Malerkotla, Kup And Policed ie Charat Singh repeatedly throws himself toward whatever side of the caravan is taking the hardest pressure. Whenever the attackers gather in strength, he races there first, cuts down Pathans, and restores just enough space for the caravan to keep moving. His intervention is practical as well as brave, because captured horses immediately become new mobility for the defenders. After seizing enemy mounts, many a Singh foot soldiers did he mount on these so exhausted or dismounted fighters could rejoin the running battle instead of being left behind. Even while wounded, Charat Singh keeps shifting from flank to flank and maintaining reserve horses for the next charge. pages.searchText: Charat Singh’s Marksmanship and the Split of the Caravan (Ghallughara) Near Malerkotla, Kup And Policed ie The page opens with praise of Charat Singh's speed and accuracy in battle, showing him firing one loaded musket after another and snatching fresh weapons from nearby comrades without breaking momentum. His marksmanship is remembered as exceptional even among seasoned Sikh fighters. Amid that struggle, The caravan carried two copies of holy Guru Granth Sahib, a detail that raises the emotional and religious stakes of the retreat. The defenders are not only saving lives but also trying to protect sacred manuscripts while Abdali's troops close in around them. As the pressure mounts, the Singhs are driven into a harsher fight in which firearms run low and even sticks and stones are used. pages.searchText: The Caravan Finds No Refuge in the Village (Ghallughara) Near Malerkotla, Kup And Policed ie Seeking a moment of shelter, the battered caravan turns toward a nearby village, but the inhabitants shut their doors and refuse entry. Those who hide in stacks or enclosures are discovered, plundered, and in some cases burned alive, making the page one of the bleakest scenes in the whole Ghallughara sequence. Charat Singh returns to the defense in anger and keeps up such steady fire that loaders must keep handing him fresh muskets. His intervention wins a brief breathing space, especially when Abdali's line momentarily pauses for water and the caravan can be drawn together again. In that interval The Singhs guarded the caravan from both the flanks, enclosing the survivors as protectively as they could. The page emphasizes that the Khalsa could not rely on local refuge and had to become its own moving wall of defense. 508 Sri Gur Panth Prakash suet: saad ô fs sem | fs Bas ô ud m= | fis H e325 5 dS aS | Md ast ada H 38 199E | chaupaî: tab bahir ng pind takâyô. pind lôkan nç bâhô ardáyó. pind main vardan na dînô kôâ. aukhi bani bahîr su tôâ.116. fad za us TS Hifg | A fasa ô &8 oid | uîHnirdo PISS Q AS FS | aru BAS 3 MIT AT 1999 | kichhu luk pardç guharan manhi. sê giljan nç chhódaç nanhi. chamiâran chûhrdan kai jurd vards. kêdah lôkan tç bahar karg.117. pages.searchText: Kutabo-Brahmini and the Midday Stalemate (Ghallughara) Near Malerkotla, Kup And Policed ie The moving caravan reaches a pair of villages, Which were known by the names of Kutabo-Brahmini. Many of the desperate travelers rush toward them hoping for shelter, but the Pathans and hostile villagers treat the arrival as an opportunity for loot and slaughter instead. Their violence draws Charat Singh back into action once more as he hears the cries of the trapped Sikhs and strikes at the plundering assailants. The page shows how every possible refuge becomes another battlefield, forcing the defenders to rescue their own people again and again. By the end, both sides are visibly exhausted under the punishing summer sun, and the struggle settles into a grim midday stalemate rather than a clean escape or victory. Even so, the Sikhs continue to fight after taking water and keep dragging the caravan farther from Lahore. 510 Sri Gur Panth Prakash cos: gSH JHA 8 aos So fis a oH | uJs JIE sfg == CU H TAS TH 19u 1 dôhrâ: kutbó bahmani thé kahat tha pind kó nam. bahut bahiri¢ tahin vardg dçkh su vastç gâm.125. oust: Gus gé uergs ad | SÌE weds SIS wes | fS TH Sas afo «ui | Hid Be So Wus Se 192€ | chaupaî: rayyat hutî pathânan keri. lîç malerîan tahin vai gheri. tinhai garâm lôkan kahi dîyô. mâr lât un singhan lîyô.126. df g fad wg ue | de ada 3 st ue | 3 adhd su voa | H ug Wu â wat vars 19201 bajai dahôl phir bahar dhac. gail bahîrai tç bhi paç. tau bahîr bhayô hâhâkâr. sô chardah singh nc sunî pukâr.127. ad es ud fisar | Hd Jus fed ae IOT | Hos [Hu fSo we sete | HÌ dua ya gE 192c I kari daurd par pindnavar. mar ranghard vich kadhg talvâr. marat singh tin lag bachâi. mârç ranghard khûb banâi.128. nì fis 3 aod va WG | HS ae ÍSH HÌH aes | BS HT HS S5 N IH | Ade Bd ug fs TH | HSS ò A SIG gee | feat wan HS afg Seh 192 | jô pind tç bahar hath âyô. mar kit tis sis katâyô. unhain mar murd dal men rala. karan lagô par giljan hala. sayânan nç só lîô hatâi. ihân lardan murd nânhi bhalâi.129. cod: few ot ë= Ho ud ua gg Sto TE | fu ot mai oft <ë uta ë AH 3 APE 1930 | dôhrâ: giljç bhi lard thak parç khardg rahe tahin hôi. singh bhi agyôn nahin talain pîy jal sam tc sôi.130. suet: Hg Hu Got go USE | ore was aT ald | ug ad 8o A aid At | ÍEH ad s> H fawn gH 1934 chaupaî: sabh singh than rahe khalôi. âc lardtg bârân kôhi. daurd kari un sau kôh sari. is kar bhag su giljc hari. 131. cos: fs gufo gfe am ug uu aÌ FS | 55 66 US US HS BSS SIA J3 [US AS 1982 | dôhrâ: shikhar duphirô hui gayô parai dhap ki tard. nath nath khard khard murd lardat taras hôt chit sârd.132. suet: Ws Hee AMMA së | ABO Q HH HOH TÈ | AS HAS JH ô MU | +T yr 3 Ue ag ur 19331

pages.searchText: At the Reservoir, the Khalsa Hold the Line So the Caravan Can Drink (Ghallughara) Near Malerkotla, Kup And Policed ie After miles of flight under the summer sun, both Sikhs and Pathans are near collapse from thirst and realize that no water was available ahead for a long distance. When a reservoir finally appears, the whole field surges toward it as if life itself has suddenly returned. The Khalsa leadership refuses to let the caravan dissolve into panic at the water's edge. Instead, the Khalsa Singhs stand guard and protect the Sikh caravan even at the cost of their lives, making sure the defenseless and exhausted can drink before the attackers turn the pause into slaughter. For a brief moment both the combatants drank water from the same source, but the truce is only accidental and temporary. As all of them spotted a water reservoir nearby, All of them felt as if they had got a new lease of life. (134) Seeing a huge water reservoir, both rushed towards it, Even the unarmed members of the caravan yearned to take water, Hardly mindful were they of the sword blows of the Pathans. (135) Even the Gilja Pathans forgot to fight for a while, As they also rushed to take water towards the reservoir. Hardly caring whether they lived or died during the attempt. (136) Then did the Malwa Singhs tell the other Singh contingents, That no water was available ahead for a long distance. Whosoever moved from there without taking water, Surely would he die of thirst on the way ahead. (137) Thereupon, the Khalsa Panth Singhs standing for a while, confabulated, That the Singhs must make sacrifices for their brethren in the caravan, That they must protect the Sikh caravan even at the cost of their lives. (138) After this resolution, did the Khalsa Singhs stand guard, So that no Gilja Pathan soldier set foot on their territory. With the protection provided by Singh on both the sides, All the other Singhs joined their contingents after drinking water. (139) For protecting the helpless, defenceless Sikhs in the caravan. The Singhs started wielding their weapons once again, Who had returned so soon after quenching their thirst. (140) As the Gilja Pathans, too, resolved to make use of water, Both the combatants drank water from the same source. As if they had forgotten to fight for the time-being. Voices around him say that the entire Khalsa Panth might accept his leadership, imagining a future in which his authority and renown spread far beyond the present battlefield. Those blessings also carry a practical judgment: wherever Charat Singh moves, the Khalsa will trust him to guide, defend, and regroup them after catastrophe. The page therefore ends Episode 136 not with triumph, but with gratitude and political hope born from communal survival. It then turns sharply into a new conflict by opening the rift between the Singhs and the Brars. pages.searchText: Rift Between the Khalsa Panth and the Brars the Rift between Khalsa Panth And the Brars As the Khalsa rested in Brar territory after a heavy defeat, the Brars stole Sikh property, preyed on outsider Singhs, and committed insults while the Singhs avoided open conflict. The Singhs held back because they were far-sighted and still faced the larger Mughal threat. The Singhs had taken shelter among the Brars, so the page says the Brars should have lived peacefully with them while the Khalsa fought the Muslims. Instead, the Brars harassed Singh households, mocked individual Singhs, twisted their names, told them to leave the villages, and made fun of advice to receive Khalsa initiation. The Majhail Singhs stayed mainly around Jaitu, with others at Ablu, Mehma, Bhagtu, Binjhu, Kauni, Doad, Matti, Charik, Gholia, Faridkot, and Deena Kangar. (5) They would cast an evil eye on some Singhs spouses, On another Singh would they poke fun for nothing. Addressing Singhs by their half, distorted names, They would tell them to vacate their villages. (6) Though being quite formidable and capable of teaching them a lesson, The Majhail Singhs preferred to put off a confrontation. Though the Brars kept indulging in acts of beating and plundering, The Majhail Singhs kept on bearing with their excesses. (7) Even if the Majhail Singhs proffered the Brars a sane advice, The latter made fun of even their well-meaning counsel. As the Majhail Singhs asked the Brars to get themselves initiated, The latter chided Maijhails to get initiated through their assholes. As the Brar ancestors had gone through the initiation once, That one-time initiation held good for their bloodline forever. (8) The Majhail Singhs would keep silent after hearing such rebuffs, Pitying them for being unfortunate in remaining deprived of Guru's grace. Feeling that the Brars having been cursed by the Divine Guru, How could they ever hope to be sovereigns of their region? (9) Majority of the Majhail Singhs stayed put at Jaitu?, While some stayed at villages Ablu?, Mehma* and Bhagtu. Whereas some found shelter at Binjhu*, Kauni, Doad* and Matti, A few others started putting up in the surrounding territory. (10) Thus Singhs makeshift settlements extended from village Charik to Gholia!9, As well as from Faridkot upto Deena Kangar. Thus did the Singhs seek shelter for their respective contingents, Wherever they could with their new and old acguaintances. (11) 519

pages.searchText: Brar Arrogance Deepens the Rift with the Scattered Singhs the Rift between Khalsa Panth And the Brars Seeing the Khalsa scattered and weakened after repeated invasions, the Brars turned very arrogant and began taunting the Majhail Singhs instead of helping them. They mocked the refugees' hardship, forgot how often the Singhs had taken shelter in the Malwa region, and treated Sikh vulnerability as a chance for domination. Their threats soon became openly political as some Brars boasted that they had threatened the Singhs to eliminate them by inviting the Mughals. That swagger transforms local insult into something far more dangerous, because it hints that old Sikh-Muslim enmity could be used as a weapon inside Malwa itself. The page also folds in the provocation around Ganda Singh's household, showing how everyday humiliation and rumor begin to harden into a larger communal breach. pages.searchText: The Singh Families Are Removed and Binjhu Declares War the Rift between Khalsa Panth And the Brars Once the harassment becomes intolerable, the Singhs start pulling their families out of Brar households and placing them in safer settlements such as village Guru-ke-Kothay. The move makes clear that the conflict is no longer a matter of insults alone; both communities are preparing for sustained hostility. From there the dispute escalates into open organization for war, and the Brars of Binjhu declared war rather than stepping back from the provocation. Armed bands gather, attacks become regular, and the countryside begins to take on the feel of a local campaign rather than a village quarrel. The page closes by setting up an armed encounter between the Singhs and the Brars, with the Brars leaning on spear warfare while the Singhs answer with tighter discipline and firearms. pages.searchText: The Brars Are Routed and Binjhu Is Emptied the Rift between Khalsa Panth And the Brars After enduring repeated nuisance and attack, the Singhs resolve to end the trouble decisively and meet the Brars in open fighting. Dust, smoke, and confusion fill the field, but the balance steadily tilts toward the Sikh side as mounted Brars are shot down or driven away. The scale of the reversal is marked by the capture of fifteen hundred horses, a detail that shows how thoroughly the Brar strength collapses once the battle turns. What began as harassment now ends in rout, with the Singhs seizing animals, prisoners, and the initiative. A follow-up strike leaves the village Binjhu of the Brars largely emptied as survivors flee toward places like Kotkapoora and Faridkot. pages.searchText: The Brars Return by Night and Plot a Pathan Disguise the Rift between Khalsa Panth And the Brars With the Singhs dominant in the area by day, displaced Brars can only come back at night to look at their abandoned homes and judge what has been lost. The memory is preserved as an ordered account rather than rumor, giving the episode the feel of a remembered local history. The page then shifts into a new plan of revenge: Resolving to disguise themselves in the guise of Gilja Pathans, the Brars decide that deception will accomplish what open fighting could not. Red robes, borrowed appearance, and calculated fear become tools for another round of conflict. This transition also serves as the hinge into the next Brar episode, where disguise and surprise replace the previous battle line. pages.searchText: The Pathan Disguise Is Exposed Among the Brars the Brars The Brars try to recover the initiative by returning in Pathan disguise, but the ruse falters once the Singhs see they cannot safely keep retreating into waterless ground. The Khalsa halts where it stands, yields the outcome to the Guru's will, and turns back under raised drums, standards, and shouted orders. From the rear guard, Charat Singh recognizes the Brars beneath their Pathan disguise and calls the alarm. His warning sends the Singhs charging back so quickly that some Brars are seized on the spot while others break and run. The page closes by widening the quarrel into a longer campaign of pressure on Brar villages. pages.searchText: Kapoora Refuses the Guru and Meets the Foretold Hanging Kapoora Brar Kapoora explains his refusal in blunt political terms: we are servants of the Turks, and if he shelters the Guru in his fort the imperial authorities will destroy him. His speech shows a chief trying to preserve his worldly position by abandoning the higher obligation of hospitality and loyalty. The Guru answers that such caution will not save him, because faithlessness itself has already chosen his ruin. The page frames the warning as a prophecy whose force is both temporal and spiritual, insisting that the Guru's word does not go in vain. The narrative then moves toward fulfillment as Isa Khan Manjh enters the story and Kapoora's intrigues rebound against him. (8) The Guru did depart after uttering these prophetic words, Many a day did pass after this prediction was made. (9) These was a custodian known by the name of Isa Khan Manjh, This Rajput Muslim convert had built a fort at Kot Isekhan. As the destined death of Kapoora Brar arrived near, It made him sell some horses to Isa Khan Manjh. (10) Making a promissory note for paying after collecting revenues from Doab, Isa Khan proceeded to Doab from across the river. As fate was destined to make an end of Kapoora, It made him think of committing a sin against Isakhan. (11) Despatching a band of thieves after Isa Khan for a consideration, Kapoora got them take possession of the entire revenue proceeds. As his conspiracy against Isa Khan came to be exposed, His destined death confronted him in the face. (12) How could Guru's prophetic words remain unfulfilled, Though Dharav? and the Dhaval* might shift their positions. Thus, getting Kapoora Brar arrested by his armed men, Was he hanged to death by the orders of Isa Khan. (13) Such indeed were the prophetic words of the Guru, That Kapoora Brar would die after being hanged. Let no body else be held responsible for his death, As it were the Guru's prophecy that found its expression. (14) In the center of a makeshift platform made of mud, Did the (renegade) Kapoora Brar meet his fatal end. Exactly in the same manner had Rattan Singh narrated, As he heard of Kapoora's end from his revered elders. (15) 533

pages.searchText: Thirsty Singhs Are Provoked at Morinda the Slaughter At Maida; i The page begins with hesitation at the top: Jassa Singh Ahluwalia wished to put it off because Abdali's forces might still be close, yet the poem insists that what is fated has to happen. The march therefore continues under a sense that providence is driving the encounter forward whether the chiefs want it or not. That inevitability turns concrete when thirsty Singhs went to Morinda for water instead of pressing on in silence. From the town, armed Ranghars stand on the rooftops, watch the Sikhs below, and begin a campaign of provocation rather than letting the travelers pass. What might have remained a delayed quarrel is thus made immediate by insult, posture, and the refusal of Morinda's men to keep peace. pages.searchText: Ranghar Taunts Turn the Morinda March into Battle the Slaughter At Maida; i The rooftop abuse now sharpens into sacrilege and challenge. The Ranghars mock the Sikhs with references to the Sahibzadas, boast about earlier cruelty, and openly dare the Khalsa to stop and fight instead of marching on. When the Sikh side answers back, the Ranghars opened a volley of fire and the quarrel crosses the line into bloodshed. A shot hit one of Tara Singh's Singhs, making it impossible to treat the exchange as mere abuse. News of the firing races through the marching force and turns outrage into mobilization. By the end of the page the war drum is beaten and Morinda is no longer a place to bypass, but a target that must be punished. 538 Sri Gur Panth Prakash cust: Wus ad fud wee AIS | SU uss HJS ad | MA TH HT â€ CAS | THA Mg Q AT HTS IACI chaupai: singhan kahain yih balan sîrd. bhayô purânô bahut gahir. ab ham bal navçn dc jâvô. ham sôn khard kai jang machâvô.18. pages.searchText: The Drum Call Summons the Misls Back to Morinda the Slaughter At Maida; i Once the insult and shooting are reported, senior leaders are briefed and the attack on Morinda is launched in earnest. The narrative stresses that this is not a private retaliation by a few offended men, but a deliberate response taken up by the Khalsa leadership. Many misls turned back at the drum beat, and contingent after contingent rejoins the action. The page takes care to present the return of these bodies as a collective rally, giving the coming assault the force of the wider Panth rather than a single jatha. With that strength gathered, the Khalsa attacks Morinda from all sides. pages.searchText: Charat Singh Covers Sirhind While the Fort Is Stormed the Slaughter At Maida; i At the critical pause before the breach, Charat Singh made a bold declaration that he would hold the Sirhind side himself. By taking responsibility for that flank, he frees the rest of the Khalsa to concentrate on opening the fort and carrying the assault inward. His movement unsettles the Pathan side and helps spread panic beyond the walls, while the main Sikh force prepares to storm the enclosure at close quarters. The page presents coordinated action rather than chaotic fury: one side contains reinforcement, the other presses the breach. Once the attack gathers full force, the Singhs climb without ladders and force their way into the stronghold with improvised means and relentless momentum. pages.searchText: Jaani Khan and Maani Khan's Progeny Is Uprooted at Morinda the Slaughter At Maida; i Inside Morinda, the fighting becomes intensely personal and punitive. The Singhs strike down the Ranghar leadership at close range, crushing many heads with hammers as they identify those held responsible for earlier crimes. Among the names singled out above all others are Jaani Khan and Maani Khan, remembered here as the men who had handed over the Sahibzadas. The attack on their houses and heirs is narrated not as incidental battlefield killing, but as targeted vengeance against a known line of guilt. The page frames that destruction as fulfillment rather than accident. pages.searchText: Morinda Closes and the Lakhmi Narayan Episode Opens the Slaughter At Maida; i This transition page first records the last shadows of Morinda's punishment. Those who had taken refuge in Hindu households are turned out under cover of night, while Jaani Khan and Maani Khan remain fixed in memory as the brothers tied to the arrest of the younger Sahibzadas. The narrator then closes the Morinda account with the Guru's judgment and an explicit statement that Rattan Singh has narrated what he heard. That closure gives the massacre an ending in testimony as well as in action. Before the page is done, however, a new episode opens around Lakhmi Narayan Kshtriya, a revenue officer whose movements and wealth draw Khalsa attention in the Doaba. The custodian of Sirhind who ruled over Sirhind province, He utilized the services of Kshtriya Luxmi Narayan. pages.searchText: The Brahmin of Kasur Appeals to the Khalsa First Invasion on Kasur The new Kasur episode begins with ordinary Khalsa discipline at Amritsar before a crisis interrupts it. There arrived a Brahmin from the city of Kasur, and he appears not as a court envoy but as a distressed petitioner demanding public justice from the Panth. His complaint is direct and urgent: his spouse had been abducted by Kasur Pathans, and he frames the outrage as a test of Khalsa responsibility toward vulnerable Hindus. The appeal presses on the old claim that the Khalsa having been created for the protection of the Hindus cannot ignore such tyranny without dishonor. The page closes with the matter moving from raw lament into formal hearing.
