pages.searchText: Hari Singh Weighs the Odds but Refuses to Abandon Kasur First Invasion on Kasur The Brahmin's insistence now forces the congregation into strategic debate. Veteran Singhs admit that the Singhs were in minority as compared to the Pathans, and the strength of Kasur's garrison cannot be dismissed as a minor local problem. Even so, the moral weight of the petition keeps the question alive. Hari Singh treats the Brahmin's threatened self-destruction before the sangat as a disgrace the Panth cannot allow, and discussion shifts from whether the problem exists to how the Khalsa should answer it. By the end of the page, resolve has hardened. So much delighted the Khalsa felt after listening to Guru's word, As if they had already taken over the city of Kasur. Khalsa slogans of victory did they shout out of joy, As if they were already beating war drums of victory. (29) Hari Singh Bhangi, somehow, spending the night at Amritsar, Khalsa march did he order early in the morning. He, having listened to the Guru's word from the Guru, No astrologer did he consult for any auspicious moment. (30) With Khalsa putting up the first camp at a place Pipli, Excellently prepared five thousand Sikh warriors were they indeed. With the forces from the four other Misls joining them here, Nearly ten thousand excellent horses did they possess. (31) Hari Singh dispatched dispatches to the Singhs all around, That the Khalsa was lauching a crusade for the protection of Brahmins. Whosoever was keen to uphold the Khalsa Panth's dignity, Must he join this Khalsa crusade to do or die for the cause. (32) Ordering the forces march after dispatching such epistles, They put up a second camp at Guru-ki-Wadali. Nearly five thousand more Singhs joined the Khalsa force here, Really great warriors and devout at heart were they indeed. (33) Beginning their march further from Guru-ki-Wadali, They put up the next camp at the town of Raja Taal. Nearly four thousand more joined the Khalsa force, Voluntarily did they become a part and parcel of the Khalsa. (34) Merely four thousand and twenty was the Khalsa in number, Full twelve lakhs were the Kasuri Pathans in strength. So huge being the difference between the two combatants, Terribly concerned did the elderly veterans feel at this disparity. (35) Despite such a large statistical difference would Hari Singh not budge, So much did S. Charat Singh do to boost Hari Singh's morale. But the difference in numerical strength of the two armies disheartened the cowards, Who reckoned never could the Khalsa ever conquer Kasur. (36) Those brave hearts who looked at the bravery quotient of the two armies, They reckoned surely would the Khalsa overpower the Kasur Pathans.

pages.searchText: Debate, Reconnaissance, and Resolve Before Kasur First Invasion on Kasur As the Khalsa nears Kasur, the imbalance in numbers sharpens argument inside the camp. The timid imagine disaster while the resolute insist that the Panth must either prevail or die honorably rather than retreat from a righteous cause. Into this debate comes timely intelligence: A Sikh traveler from Kasur happened to pass by them, and the chiefs immediately draw him into council. He becomes the means by which rumor is replaced with actionable knowledge about Kasur's gates, habits, and weak points. The page therefore holds together two kinds of preparation at once. At midday noon should the Khalsa Singhs enter the city of Kasur becomes the tactical principle that organizes the whole assault. The plan depends on discipline rather than spectacle. Without unfurling their continental emblems and beating of battle drums, the Singhs are to pass inward quietly, as if they were traders rather than an attacking force. As the Singhs occupied many of the Kasur forts, The Muslim Pathans of Kasur came to recognize Singhs identity. The Brahmin appears again before the chiefs, Reminding the Khalsa about his wife's captivity under the Pathans and forcing them to prove that the campaign will answer the original wrong rather than vanish into general loot. Hari Singh directs the matter into a formal and then practical resolution. Guided by the Brahmin to the responsible house, the Khalsa kills the abductors and restores the woman, completing the justice claim that had justified the march on Kasur in the first place. pages.searchText: The Ramgharia Grievance Closes as Dileram's Wealth Appears Dileramian This page first completes the brief grievance against the Ramgharia-related offenders by recalling how their revenues spread across several regions and how shocking their conduct had become. They had the audacity to capture Jassa Singh Ahluwalia, and the narrative treats that act as one that doomed their line to male extinction. Having closed that moral reckoning, the poem opens a wider Lahore-centered story around Dileram. He is introduced as a man of rank, enormous stored wealth, and political importance in a period unsettled by Abdali, Maratha movement, and pressure on the Lahore nawab. The page therefore works as another hinge. His sons in Lahore transferred all their assets to Kasur, sending ornaments, cash, and dependents away for protection, but the move itself exposes how fear and hurried transport are already unraveling the family estate. The poem then turns back to Dileram's haveli, where the first wave of plunder strips away what lies openly at hand and rough opportunists are pushed aside by stronger claimants. What seemed like an ordinary sack quickly becomes a more methodical search for hidden or buried treasure inside the mansion. By the end of the page the conflict is no longer only about punishing a political enemy. pages.searchText: The Ramgharias and Ghanaiyas Hunt Dileram's Hidden Wealth Dileramian contd Once the allied misls settle around the estate, the Ramgharias and Ghanaiyas divide the plunder in equal parts and begin acting together against Dileram's surviving family. Their partnership gives the search both military discipline and a sense that every new discovery will immediately become a contested prize. Dileram's eldest son is seized, pressured, and forced to reveal where wealth has been hidden and who still controls portions of it. Under torture and fear of death, he yields locations, names, and caches that the attackers would not have found so quickly on their own. The page therefore turns the story from open looting to coerced extraction. pages.searchText: Maali Singh Demands the Richest Chest Dileramian contd Maali Singh asks not for scattered goods but for the single object that holds the finest value, pressing Dileram to name the choicest possession in the house. The answer points to a guarded steel chest taken from beneath the stairs and hidden in a protected room rather than among ordinary loot. Dileram identifies it as the repository of Begum Noor Jahan's jewels, a cache whose prestige matters as much as its price. The page lingers over the distinction between common plunder and courtly treasure, making clear why this particular discovery inflames ambition beyond the earlier division of spoils. From this point onward, the struggle is no longer only about who conquered Dileram. pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Dileramian contd.

pages.searchText: Greed Overtakes Maali Singh Dileramian contd The jewel inventory continues through rings, ornaments, gold vessels, and other luxury pieces that suggest the chest contains an entire courtly treasury. Dileram can barely finish naming the contents before desire outruns description and the value of the hoard begins to distort every judgment around it. Hearing what lies inside, the more greedy did Maali Singh become, until greed itself reads like the true subject of the page. What had begun as shared conquest now tempts him toward secrecy, private advantage, and a deliberate breach with the Ghanaiyas. Unable to contain himself, he hurries to Jassa Singh with a proposal that the best treasure should be concealed rather than divided. The page closes on that conspiratorial turn, preparing the moral collapse that follows. 574 Sri Gur Panth Prakash adt gas aet Us go Uu | el rg act uf& fea | at »idIôl Hes Adi | arasa YW faor MôdÌ 133 | kai hathan kai pair tan payyç. kai jardti kai parôi dikhyyg. kai angûthî mardan keri. bâjâband au jiga ghancrî.33. pages.searchText: Jassa Singh Wavers Over the Hidden Treasure Dileramian contd Jassa Singh initially answers Maali Singh in the language of honour, reminding him that the Ramgharias and Ghanaiyas had pledged to share what they captured together. He warns that wealth gained by breaking one's vow cannot remain clean profit, because the stain of dishonour will cling to it longer than the gold itself. Maali Singh refuses to yield, arguing from possession, kinship, and martial pride instead of from principle. He makes the dispute intensely personal, pressing his brother to choose blood loyalty over the public obligation created by alliance. That pressure changes the moral register of the story. pages.searchText: A Secret Plan Forms Around Dileram's Chest Dileramian contd After resisting for a time, Jassa Singh chalked out a strategy that would let the Ramgharias keep the finest treasure out of Ghanaiya hands. The first step is secrecy: those who know the chest's value must be controlled before the wider Khalsa can demand an open accounting. Maali Singh accordingly removes the prized box from Dileram's old house and transfers it into his own camp, but concealment proves harder than seizure. Rumour spreads, tempers flare, and the allied camp fills with accusation as both sides suspect that the richest find has been withheld. When Charat Singh insists that Dileram himself be questioned, the conspirators recognize the danger of truthful testimony. pages.searchText: Hirday Ram Is Murdered to Bury the Evidence Dileramian contd The Ramgharia party now treats murder as the price of preserving stolen wealth. A hired killer is rewarded, and Hirday Ram is lured into a routine scene of grooming and ease rather than into anything that looks openly violent. While attendants are smearing his head with curd and preparing him as if for a bath, he is made vulnerable and then suddenly beheaded. pages.searchText: Bishambhar Dass Challenges the Khalsa in Doaba Dileramian contd This hinge page leaves the Dileram affair behind and opens a fresh Doaba confrontation around Bishambhar Dass, the powerful agent of Dina Beg's widow. He appears with troops, artillery, and allied hill support, so the new episode begins not with covert theft but with a public challenge over territory and authority. Bishambhar's message is blunt: the Buddha Dal must vacate the Doaba region if it wants peace. Instead of yielding, the Singhs receive the demand in congregation, take offense at the tone of the order, and answer by insisting that he should pay rather than command them. The page therefore functions as a clean narrative reset. One cycle of betrayal closes, and another opens in which control of land, military prestige, and ransom will determine the next clash. 582 Sri Gur Panth Prakash agu, me ema Q das at (... As the Buddha Dal could not fight without their younger compatriots, He could easily chase Buddha Dal out of Doab. (4) Thus did Bishambar Dass go after them from Dina Nagar, Doaba region did he enter after crossing the Beas. Putting up a camp a few miles behind their camp, He sent a written challenge to the Buddha Dal Singhs. (5) Thus did he write a message to the Singhs: If they were desirous of their survival and well-being. Must they vacate the Doaba region forth with, Surely would he eliminate them if they tarried. (6) Highly incensed did the Singhs feel hearing this, A resolution did they pass holding a congregation. Must they occupy his territory after killing the Kshtriya upstart, As it was an excellent opportunity for the Khalsa's cause. (7) A ransom money from him should they demand first, Which he would not pay and would speak foul. Thus did the Khalsa send a message to him, Must he pay the ransom if he wished to live. (8) 583

pages.searchText: The Buddha Dal Refuses to Quit Doaba the Occupation of Doaba Bishambhar Dass answers the Sikh demand with defiance, saying ransom will be paid only if the entire Khalsa speaks with one voice and only after the Buddha Dal withdraws. The Singhs reject that posture by recalling that Dina Beg had an agreement with the Singhs, so Bishambhar has no right to pose as if he alone can rewrite the terms of the region. With negotiation hardening into challenge, both sides are pushed toward a test of nerve. The page stresses that neither camp is willing to budge, and that questions of alliance, honour, and coercion have become inseparable from the coming battle. Emboldened by numbers and support from hill chiefs, Bishambhar moves against a Sikh force that is scattered and comparatively thin on the ground. pages.searchText: Bishambhar Falls as Sikh Reinforcements Arrive the Occupation of Doaba The battle first appears to go against the Singhs, whose smaller force is pressed by cavalry and driven back under the weight of the assault. That early advantage collapses when thousands of Singhs arrived after hearing the exchange of fire, turning what looked like a local setback into a massed Sikh counterattack. Bishambhar realizes too late that the field is slipping from him. He dismounts and stands his ground, but the Singhs close around him, kill him in the fighting, and break the coherence of his army at the moment its confidence should have mattered most. What follows is not a restrained victory but a sweeping seizure of camp wealth, animals, arms, and supplies. pages.snippet: With Bishambhar defeated, the poem shifts from battlefield action to the political work of settlement. After collective resolve and prayer, the Singhs spread out to occupied villages in the Doaba region, turning a single victory into a broader pattern of local
pages.searchText: The Khalsa Consolidates Its Hold on Doaba the Occupation of Doaba With Bishambhar defeated, the poem shifts from battlefield action to the political work of settlement. After collective resolve and prayer, the Singhs spread out to occupied villages in the Doaba region, turning a single victory into a broader pattern of local control. Possession is shown taking several forms at once: some settlements invite Sikh protection, some are retained through old relationships, and others are held because no one can dislodge the first claimant. Where rival claims arise, misl authority begins to matter more than raw momentum, because disputes must now be judged rather than merely fought. The page therefore explains how plunder matures into governance. Revenue, recognized possession, and expanding contingents show the Buddha Dal becoming not just a raiding force but a power able to stabilize and enlarge its own territorial order. 588 Sri Gur Panth Prakash a8€. mà HEU Hes at m sdÌ (MAT sig 3tì HBA H M...) 146. âgai mulakh mallan ki sakhi turi (aisi bhant bhayô mulak su mall...) tug dôhrâ gut chaupaî: gdr dôhrâ gut chaupaî:: PH JS BUSA fre SoG od Md MAS MITA | H afd dus mk fH& afo fis GR fHu um iai im hut thé khâlsô mith turyô kar bungc akâl ardâs. jau jahin rayyat âi milai rahi pind usai singh pas.1. 3T oes MU HÈ us H Haaf Ss | H fan Wer es HJU aeu 5 fas fer ôd 121 dacrâ luttau singh murdg¢ pard¢ su mulkhahi daurd. jô jis Jâgâ vard bahyô kadahyô na kin is thaur.2.: AA Ug HJ d us gad | far foods 5 aS Bui | scl aor &u EC =š | €S HANG foes =š uš 131 Jisai pair jahan kó pard rahyô. kisai nikârat na kôâ bhayô. chhôtî jaga lakh chhôtc vardg. vada shahiran sirdâr vada khardg.3. fads ma fas fime oe wet | fads dus A Ha Ae | fad masa Het SA | PH ad StS H&o HET 18 | kinai sak kin sian kadah lai. kinai rayyat sôn marzî kai. kinai achânak suni takâî. im kar lînô mulak malâî.4. zat ooJrÍes at A dlr | AG ATENG =š TGS BI | fas fas Hart ATG das geet | 95 Go A dI5 ug Temah UI vadaî thakrâit ki Jó jaga. sôâ sardâran vada gal laga. jin jin marjî sath rayyat ralâî. un un sôn gal bahu baniâî.5. fas fas das A fsa geet | 8o ô o St aeret | MAT Sis SU HBA AHS | HE Jso Wu f3H adt des IE jin jin rayyat só shitâb guvâî. un nç dinó vahî kadahai. aisi bhant bhayê mulak su mall. sun ratan singh tim kahi gall.6.: Aa fen a fed ae 3 UAS Bugs SE | A ufos o e= HJu BA fees AE 191: JÓ kó kis kó phir kadahai tó misal uprâlô hôi. jô pahilôn kó vard bahyô usai divâvai sôi.7.: UKS & fHu gË wierd | Hoa Se JS of uÍN TS | met Cadt Gad uA | fads Had fas Ju UTA It pahilôn the singh hutç akârc. mulak lutt hôç dui dui charg. ai ugrâhî unkai pas. kinai sainkar kin rakkh¢ pachâs.8.

pages.searchText: Another Episode About the Taruna Dal Further Occupation of More Territory Episode 147 opens by turning to the Taruna Dal, which had grown wealthy after the sack of Kasur and then heard that Bishambhar Das had been killed and the Doaba occupied by the Buddha Dal. Since the Buddha Dal had taken Doaba alone, the Taruna Dal wondered whether to fight them as a united group or seek another opportunity elsewhere. Both factions envied the other’s gains, yet the narrative says each received what destiny gave. The Taruna Dal saw the region around Lahore lying open, sent three misls ahead and two toward Majha and the hills, and the Singhs of Majha began establishing control in their own villages. The Nakai contingent moved toward Nakka and the Bhangis toward Multan, while S. Charat Singh focused on Lahore’s outskirts. He occupied scattered pockets, placed a post at Gujranwala, and remained in long conflict with the Bhangi chiefs who held territory on both sides of the river. 590 Sri Gur Panth Prakash q82. (As the Khalsa gained in prosperity and strength Truly had the Mughals fallen on bad days) Now listen to the account of the other faction (Taruna Dal), Who had enriched themselves after ransacking of Kasur. And their occupation of the Doaba region after that. (1) As they (Buddha Dal) had occupied Doaba on their own, Why would they agree to share their possession with Taruna Dal? Or should they try their luck elsewhere in (Punjab). (2) The Buddha Dal regretted that they were deprived of the booty, Though Taruna Dal had enriched themselves after Kasur's ransacking. Now what would it avail to repent over the past, In no way would Kasur's looted booty fall into their hands. (3) Both the factions repented for each other's exploits, Though each faction received what was in store for them. Thereafter, the Taruna Dal had an impulse to take an initiative, As they found the surrounding areas of Lahore unguarded. (4) The Singhs who belonged to the villages in Majha region, In those villages did they establish their hegemony. (5) As the Nakai* contingent advanced towards the Nakka region, The Bhangi contingent marched towards Multan* in the west. S. T This page closes the Taruna Dal episode by explaining how Sikh expansion after the Lahore-side raids kept widening the zone of Mughal weakness. So much land and revenue passed beyond effective control that the Lahore administration could no longer collect revenue with confidence outside the city itself. The political consequence is immediate. What had looked like scattered Sikh mobility now appears as a structural threat to Lahore's ability to govern, punish, and tax the countryside that sustained it. The page therefore serves as a bridge into the next confrontation. pages.searchText: The Nawab Besieges Gujranwala Both Budha Dal and Tapuna Dal Episode 148 opens by showing how Sikh territorial gains in Doaba and around Gujranwala unsettle Lahore's governor. In anger and alarm, he besieged Gujranwala with artillery, hoping to break Charat Singh's growing position before it could attract wider Khalsa support. Yet the siege is not as secure as it appears from the outside. Sikh sympathizers and paid troops within the Nawab's own camp begin to think in terms of defection, coordination, and the advantages of aiding the besieged rather than the besieger. The result is a tense reversal of perspective. pages.searchText: The Nawab Flees and Charat Singh Grows in Strength Both Budha Dal and Tapuna Dal The siege unravels when reports spread that a larger Sikh host is approaching the field. Faced with warnings of an approaching Khalsa force, the Nawab loses nerve, and the cohesion of his camp begins to dissolve before the feared reinforcement even fully arrives. Night flight, confusion, and opportunistic looting follow. The same encirclement meant to crush Charat Singh instead enriches him, raises his standing, and helps extend Sikh influence across a wider northern belt. By the end of the page, the episode has shifted from siege survival to strategic expansion. Charat Singh crossed the Jhelum, assessed the fort and its defenders, and then used feigned withdrawal and altered movement to make the Pathans misread his intent. That deception matters more than brute force. By returning through another approach and closing in before the garrison can reset itself, he turns the confidence of the fort into vulnerability and panic. The page therefore introduces the capture sequence through cunning rather than frontal assault. pages.searchText: Sar Buland Khan Submits Under Pressure The Capture of Sir Buland Khan Once the position is lost, Sar Buland Khan abandons the hope of recovering it by force and turns to negotiation. Charat Singh's advance and seizure of the surrounding advantage make clear that resistance now risks humiliation without any realistic path to victory. Envoys pass between the camps while the Sikhs tighten their hold, confiscate wealth, and treat the captive commander as a figure whose status itself can be monetized. In that atmosphere, a huge ransom was demanded, turning the khan's surrender into a public measure of Sikh leverage. The page thus joins military success to political theatre. pages.searchText: Sar Buland Khan Is Released and Sirhind Comes Into View The Capture of Sir Buland Khan This hinge page first lets Sar Buland Khan plead for subordinate status and mercy rather than continued imprisonment. Charat Singh answers from a position of sovereign confidence, stressing that even Ahmad Shah's uncle had been taken and that Sikh power now speaks in its own right rather than as a client of older courts. After that display of superiority, clemency follows. Provisions are given for the journey, safe onward movement is allowed, and the released noble becomes a witness to Charat Singh's prestige rather than a martyr to it. The page then pivots decisively toward Sirhind. pages.searchText: The Khalsa Moves Against an Exposed Sirhind Occupation of Sirhind And Slaughter of AN Khan The Sirhind episode opens with timely intelligence rather than immediate combat. News spreads that Sirhind was exposed because its officer was away on revenue collection, and that temporary weakness invites a rapid Khalsa move before the city can be properly secured again. The Singhs respond through consultation and collective resolve, treating the moment as one that must be seized rather than merely observed. Their decision turns scattered information into operational momentum. On the other side, warning reaches Zain Khan and forces him into anxious movement. pages.searchText: Zain Khan Moves Quietly While the Singhs Close In Occupation of Sirhind And Slaughter of AN Khan Trying to avoid entrapment, Zain Khan advances carefully and suppresses the noise that would normally announce a commander on the move. Keeping all his war drums in the rear guard, he hopes to slip toward Sirhind before the Sikhs can concentrate fully against him. That caution does not save him, because intelligence passes quickly among the Singh contingents. Majhail and Buddha Dal forces converge, musket fire opens, and the conversation among the Sikhs hardens into a common resolve that Zain Khan must be stopped outside the city. The page is therefore about pursuit under pressure. pages.searchText: Sirhind Is Marked for Destruction Sirhind The opening of the new Sirhind sequence explains why the city has become a moral target as well as a military one. The Singhs remember that innocent infants had been beheaded here, and that the city's name remains bound to the murder of the Guru's young sons and the oppression associated with their killers. That memory transforms vengeance into collective policy. Sirhind is not merely to be raided but to be humbled, broken, and symbolically undone so that its punishment answers a long-carried grievance. The page therefore frames the coming destruction as deliberate historical reckoning. (2) That even the revered Guru cried in grief. So much oppression had been committed at this place, That innocent infants! had been beheaded here. (7) As they had resolved before entering the city of Sirhind, Each one came out making an opening in the wall. Thereafter, many a donkey did they summon there, Many a Singh chief did handle the ploughshare, Vindicating what the revered Guru had commanded. pages.searchText: The Khalsa Marks the Sahibzadas' Martyrdom Site Sirhind This transition page carries the narrative from the destruction of Sirhind into a work of remembrance. After identifying the places tied to the younger Sahibzadas, the Khalsa agrees that a single memorial shrine should be established so the memory of their martyrdom will remain embodied in a public sacred site. Local elders are called to indicate the exact place and to recount what happened there in earlier days. The page therefore replaces the heat of battle with communal recollection, testimony, and the desire to anchor grief in durable form. It also opens the next episode by showing that post-victory authority includes the power to consecrate memory. The Khalsa does not only punish Sirhind; it begins shaping how that punishment and martyrdom will be remembered. 612 Sri Gur Panth Prakash qu2. må ŵg$ a Ya aì a (... pages.searchText: A Memorial Is Proposed at the Precise Martyrdom Site Construction of A Memorial at Sirhind Episode 152 continues by describing how the aftermath of the Sahibzadas' killing lingers as an affliction in Muslim memory and local conscience. Ordinary consolations fail, and the narrative pushes toward a remedy that acknowledges the sanctity of the place where the crime was committed. The solution offered is explicit: a memorial be built at the precise place where the Guru's sons were put to death. The page imagines the site not as abandoned ground but as a kept, illuminated, and attended place of reverence. In this way the memorial becomes both historical witness and devotional practice. pages.searchText: The Panth Furnishes the Sirhind Memorial Construction of A Memorial at Sirhind Once the plan is accepted, the Khalsa moves from proposal to institution. The Panth gathered there in ceremony, turning the site into a formal space of assembly rather than a merely remembered ruin. The page describes the furnishing of that space with a platform, canopy, lit lamps, recitation, and appointed service. Weapons and devotional music alike help frame the memorial as a living extension of Guru-centered presence within the Panth. What emerges is not a simple monument but a functioning shrine. pages.searchText: The Memorial Account Closes and Sirhind's Hidden Wealth Reappears Construction of A Memorial at Sirhind This page closes the memorial episode by stressing the purpose of written preservation. The account is said to have been set down so the Khalsa could hear, read and pray at the shrine, giving the memorial both literary and devotional continuity. From there the poem pivots into a new Sirhind-centered episode focused on remaining forts, buried treasure, and unfinished seizure. The city has already been judged and damaged, yet the search for what lies hidden beneath its structures shows that conquest is not materially complete. The result is another hinge in the broader sequence. A site of memory remains behind, while the narrative moves back toward possession, excavation, and the struggle over what Sirhind still contains. 618 Sri Gur Panth Prakash ratan singh jim suni thi pita ápnç pas. likhî su khatar khâlsai pardah sun karai ardâs.26. aus. The way that treasure was unearthed by the Khalsa, Listen to the account of that treasure's unearthing. (1) Chaupai: The peripheral articles were taken away by the ordinary people, Who had joined the Khalsa force in the disguise of Sikhs. As the liquid cash and coins were robbed by the populace, They had buried it underneath the building foundations. (2) They had buried it deep for reasons of safety, But the Guru's curse had actually made them to do so. As they had hidden their wealth deep in the earth, The whole city was dug right upto its foundations. (3) As the Guru had ordained it to be turned upside down, As the Guru had spoken these words in deep anguish, The Guru's anguished cry reverberated upto the bottom of the earth. (4) The Guru's words being sharper than a sharp sword, They would unearth things from the nether world's surface. As the city of Sirhind came to be ransacked for the third time, The Khalsa chiefs came in possession of a lot of wealth. (6) Chaupai: As all the moneyed people had taken shelter there, The Khalsa chiefs got wind of this construction. pages.searchText: Bhai Buddha Singh Secures the Fort at Great Cost Occupation And Handing Over of Sirhind The Khalsa chiefs first decide that the stronghold must be secured before its wealth is fully apportioned. In that setting Bhai Buddha Singh emerges as the key actor, negotiating for possession while others weigh whether purchase, seizure, and political necessity can be separated at all. The page underscores the scale of his payment and ambition: Rupees eighty thousands had he paid in public view, with further maneuvering needed to clinch control. Yet the acquisition is darkened by cruelty toward the women of the fort, so possession arrives with both status and curse. This makes the page morally unstable in an important way. Divested of both religion and wealth was he, Downslide went his fortunes since that cursed day. (12) The same fort did the Singhs select for their stay, As it was located outside the cursed city of Sirhind. Its name, too, was distinct from the Sirhind city, Guru Gobind Singh himself had uttered the name Jatpura. (13) After paying a reasonable sum as ransom, The Singhs established a police post in the fort. Then with folded hands did Buddha Singh plead, And took over the fort again for a year's lease. (14) Thereupon, Buddha Singh took over the fort, Along with the orchards upto the village periphery. The surrounding area was occupied by the Singhs, Which caused a lot of heart burning among the wicked. (15) 621

The debate reveals diverging strategic instincts, the clearest of them being that Buddha Dal Singhs opined that the Khalsa must march towards Delhi in order to exploit momentum against major centers of power. Other factions imagine different horizons, including renewed pressure toward Lahore and other regional objectives. Muslims remain within territories now shaped by Sikh power, but the Pathans of Malerkotla are explicitly spared in keeping with the Guru's remembered word and the distinctive moral status attached to that house. From there the poem moves into negotiated governance: tribute, shared tracts, and coordinated misl control replace indiscriminate devastation. pages.searchText: Khalsa Occupation on Both Sides of Lahore Occupation And Handing Over of Towns to the Descendents of Bhai Bhagtu And Baba Phool The page closes the previous account by saying that Bhai Bhagtu’s descendants, the people of Mehraj, Ranghars, and Pathans kept some land common so Khalsa forces could rest on the road to Delhi. If one Misl tried to seize that shared land, two others would oppose it, and local Muslim chiefs learned how gifts or ransom could divide the Khalsa Misls. The narrator adds that he is reporting what he heard from his father, who had been close to the Khalsa Panth. pages.searchText: Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh as Warrior and Disciple Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh This page sketches Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh as a saint-soldier whose devotion and courage were already famous in the Panth. Wherever there is a war being waged, he is described as the Singh who moves first beneath the Khalsa standard and answers the beat of the war drum without hesitation. The narrative then grounds him in lineage and place. From his revered hands had he received Khandey-ki-Pahul from Bhai Mani Singh, he came from one village named Leel near Khemkaran, and within the Akal Takht premises did he keep his seat while facing the Guru's court in disciplined service. By ending with these details, the page prepares the reader for the coming ordeal. pages.searchText: Panic in the Panth and the Gathering at Akal Bunga Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh The crisis worsens after Abdali is summoned with promises of money and support for the enemies of the Sikhs. As the rumors spread, families of the Sikhs started deserting in panic, and suffering follows every path: some flee toward the hills, some hide in forests, and others remain exposed to plunder and loss. Against that fear, the Khalsa gathers itself in prayer and counsel. Rehras verses were recited in Khalsa congregation held at Akal Bunga near the Akal Takht, and the Singhs first see their families to safety before turning to the question of how the Panth should answer this danger. Out of that assembly Gurbakhsh Singh raises the demand for true sacrifice. He asks whether there is any one such Singh among the Khalsa Panth who can offer his life in a way that will bring divine favor upon the community and steady the hearts of those who remain. 634 aug dôhrâ suet chaupaî: gdr dôhrâ Sri Gur Panth Prakash ste ac GA cor fu AS | none ato ÍSH Hes wU | MU met we GA ot set | Mur cudo Sas uct Ic! tîn kót us taka likh dió. ahmad shâhi tis maddat ahyô. âyô ai jab us ki bhai. singh tabbran bhâjard paî.18. As rumours of Ahmed Shah Abdali's arrival spread, Families of the Sikhs started deserting in panick. (18) Those who rushed towards the hills for shelter, By the hill people were they looted and plundered. Those who tried to hide among the wilds and rivers bed, By the wild animals and decoits were they devoured. (19) Those who dared to stay in their own houses, By their adversaries were they got arrested. Wherever the Singhs arrived after deserting their homes, To many hardships and tribulations were they subjected. (20) Those who escaped into the forests and wilds, (Truly) did they become homeless at the mercy of others. As Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh heard these heart-rending tales, (Seriously) did he contemplate on the entire situation. (21) Rehras verses (Evening prayer) were recited in Khalsa congregation, It was held at Akal Bunga near the Akal Takht. The caravan of Sikh families was made to depart after a resolution, Khalsa force, without the families, remained stationed there. (22) Thereupon Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh made a declaration; Was there any one such Singh among the Khalsa Panth, Who, with his supreme sacrifice, could invoke Divine intervention, Whose invocation could get answered by the Divine Lord. For community's welfare must he be ready to sacrifice, Like (Martyr) Taru Singh must he annihilate the Mughals. Who else but he had the power to move heavens, His prayer alone could reach the Divine Court. (25) Hearing this, Gurbax Singh accepted the congregation's will, Before the Khalsa Panth's verdict, did he bow down, Presenting himself with folded hands before the Khalsa Panth, Readily did he agree to wed the beauteous death. (22) Thereupon Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh made a declaration; Was there any one such Singh among the Khalsa Panth, Who, with his supreme sacrifice, could invoke Divine intervention, Whose invocation could get answered by the Divine Lord. (23) Must he be firm of conviction, character and meditation, A true follower of the Sikh code of conduct he must be. For community's welfare must he be ready to sacrifice, Like (Martyr) Taru Singh must he annihilate the Mughals. (24) Hearing this declaration, the congregated Singhs replied, None else could exceed him in character and piety. Who else but he had the power to move heavens, His prayer alone could reach the Divine Court. (25) Hearing this, Gurbax Singh accepted the congregation's will, Before the Khalsa Panth's verdict, did he bow down, Presenting himself with folded hands before the Khalsa Panth, Readily did he agree to wed the beauteous death. pages.searchText: Volunteers for the Fatal Wedding of Martyrdom Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh The congregation answers Gurbakhsh Singh's challenge by recognizing both his resolve and the gravity of the moment. He asks who would accompany him on this fatal wedding expedition, and the image of martyrdom as a wedding with death turns the coming battle into a consciously embraced offering rather than a desperate last stand. The Singhs respond immediately. Many a Singh volunteered, bowing at his feet and declaring that they too were ready to give their heads, for by sacrificing their lives would they be wedding death in the Guru's cause and making good on the ideals taught in the Panth. The page also frames their zeal within scriptural and historical memory. pages.searchText: The Martyr Procession Is Prepared Like a Wedding Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Once the volunteers are chosen, the Singhs begin to prepare as if for both battle and ceremony. Ever ready were they to make a sacrifice, so they arm themselves carefully, cleanse their minds through prayer, and transform their readiness for death into a disciplined liturgy of the Panth. The rites are explicitly devotional. Gurbani did they recite from Sri Guru Granth Sahib, they complete five verses of Anand Sahib, and sacred food is distributed in a mood that resembles both a congregation and a wedding feast arranged for a blessed occasion. Gurbakhsh Singh is then dressed and honored as the bridegroom of martyrdom. pages.searchText: Prayer at Harmandir Sahib and the March to Battle Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh The ceremonial movement now becomes a public procession. Carrying the Khalsa standard a Singh moved in front, the war drums sounded, and gifts were distributed like alms from a wedding household as the jatha advanced through the sacred precincts. The heart of the page is the prayer. Standing before the Guru in Harmandir Sahib, Gurbakhsh Singh bows, circles the shrine, and asks that his faith in Guru's ideology be vindicated so that his death may truly serve the Panth rather than merely display personal bravery. At the same time the enemy prepares in its own way. pages.searchText: The Wedding Songs Give Way to Battle at Dawn Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Even on the threshold of combat the Singhs continue to surround Gurbakhsh Singh with devotional music. Gurbani verses were sung to the accompaniment of music, and the wedding imagery remains deliberate: the page insists that martyrdom should be entered with the same solemn joy that accompanies a sacred union. That mood shifts with the first light. With the break of dawn did the Pathans arrive, and Gurbakhsh Singh answers not with fear but with exhortation, reminding the Panth that retreat would stain their honor when the Guru's cause has already summoned them forward. pages.searchText: Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh’s Martyrdom Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Gurbakhsh Singh and the Singhs did not blink, bow their heads, or look behind; they kept moving forward until the Pathans fled, unable to withstand the Singhs’ sword blows. From a distance the Pathans fired guns and arrows, wounding him so badly that the wounds could not be counted. Shots cut through his flesh and bones, yet he did not accept defeat or show pain. Blood poured from his body like oil from a press and water from a pierced pouch, but Gurbakhsh Singh kept moving forward rather than turn back. As his strength failed, he prayed that the Guru preserve his honor and accept his martyrdom. Deeming it to be the best opportunity, Thus did he finally resolve: Must the get himself beheaded, By facing a sharp sword's blow. (82) Thereupon Gurbakhsh Singh picked up his double-edged sword, With a loud challenge did he threaten the Pathans. He bowed down his head before an attacking Pathan, As solemnly as Guru Tegh Bahadur had offered his own. (83) As the Gilja Pathan struck a (severe) blow on his neck, Instantly his head was severed from his body. Thus had the Singh's solemn pledge been fulfilled, Praise be to such a sacrifice and praise be to such a martyr. (84) Delighted did the Sikh martyrs feel at his sacrifice, Eagerly had they been waiting for their compatriot. In anticipation had their spirits arrived to welcome him, Many a flying chariot had they decked to carry his soul. (85) Many a flying horse had they brought with them, A horse of the most exotic breed had they saddled for him. Saffron standards and war drums had those spirits carried, In blue robes had they stood for receiving his spirit. (86) Majestically did they recite and sing Gurbani verses, To the accompaniment of string and percussion instruments. In splendid dresses did they come in a procession, To take (martyr) Gurbax Singh's spirit (to the heavens). (87) 649

The great Singh martyr Mani Singh's spirit came himself, and Martyr Taru Singh come as well, reversing the loneliness of death by showing Gurbakhsh Singh received into a living fellowship of sacrifice. Coming near, martyrs greeted Gurbakhsh Singh with honor, while the persecutors and executioners who had tormented the Sikhs appear humbled and powerless in that higher court. As the exhausted Gilja Pathans had fallen asleep, the surviving Singhs harry them, seize horses where they can, and force the enemy remnants to withdraw back toward the royal camp in a state of disorder. The narrative then turns tender and communal. Now listen to the account of martyred Singh's corpses: the Singhs gather the bodies from the field, sort friend from foe as best they can, and refuse to leave their dead scattered across the ground. pages.searchText: The Guru Decrees Gurbakhsh Singh's Return to the Panth Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh The heavenly dialogue resumes with Gurbakhsh Singh still intent on remaining among the martyrs. Did he pray to God for an abode among the martyrs, yet the reply redirects that longing toward future service rather than permanent rest in the celestial assembly. The Guru's answer is decisive: That he must take birth again to be with Khalsa Panth. His martyrdom has earned him authority, so the closer he had stepped toward death in battle, the greater the host and leadership that will one day stand under his charge. The page closes by linking sacrifice to command. The martyrs acknowledge his new station, and the promise is made that his death before the Giljas has not ended his role, but prepared him to return as a leader whose courage will again serve the Panth in history. 654 tug dôhrâ gut chaupaî: egg dôhrâ gut chaupaî: Sri Gur Panth Prakash: dIGgHHN Mul ve of fret ne adh Hdleo UTA | aie su ad Ad fea HÍSdId adt MITA 190€ | gurbakhash singh man yaun mithi ab rahiai shahidan pas. thândh bhayô kar jêr dhig satigur kahi ardâs.106.: mal HÍSdId & wat we | of KUS did Ju sure | unt mast u= Mus WIRI | TH urd HU UE for ATE 19021 agai satigur the Jani jan. hôi karipal gur kahyô vakhân. .. sae Ua Ud mà niet fr ureét | ÍS3 das GWerd weet | 3 Hago H dd Aves | SU HdÌ€ H KISAS HT 1900! pag dhar agai shahidi jin pai. tits hazâr phaujdâr banvâî. tân sabhan main hôhu sardar. bhayô shahîd ju giljan mar. 108. 3 Ava Adtes GUHTÍEH adi | dag adi feo fag ug Ud | aA ad ufo gd dad | UN Ue ATE HOH ATT 190€] tau sarab shahîdan phurmâish kari. hazûr kahi in sir par dhari. baras bârân yahi rahai hajâr. dhârai panth jai Janam zarôr.109. pages.searchText: The Martyrs Petition for Gurbakhsh Singh's Future Birth Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh The conclusion of the episode binds divine power, martyrdom, and future history together. For twelve years let the martyr's soul live in Divine presence becomes the request of the assembled martyrs, who ask that Gurbakhsh Singh remain in bliss for a time before returning again to earthly struggle. The Guru's assurance also defines the nature of that return. Never is the Guru distinct from his Sikhs, and The whole Khalsa Panth would abide by his command because the authority granted to Gurbakhsh Singh is presented as an extension of the Guru's own strength within the Panth. pages.searchText: Abdali Is Alarmed by the Khalsa-Jat Alliance Ahmed Shah Abdali, Jawahar Mal of Bhara And Najib Khan Rohilla News of the new alliance spreads quickly through Abdali's camp. Listening about this new development, Ahmad Shah Abdali feel a sharp blow to his confidence, because he knows that any campaign against Jawahar Mal becomes far more dangerous once Sikh horsemen join the field. The political meaning is obvious to him. The young Khalsa Singhs had joined the Jat chief, and that combination threatens to snatch it from him: the prestige he had gathered after defeating other Indian powers could now be undone by a fresh coalition in the north. The page therefore emphasizes fear rather than triumph. Calling an assembly of Rajputs, Marathas and Brars, together with Gosains, hill chiefs, and other allies, he turns the conflict into a wider regional challenge to Afghan power. A new strategy must he devise, and the page shows him searching among surrender, bribery, pressure, and negotiation for any path that might spare him from complete defeat. That search leads him toward mediation. Ragho Malhar is brought into the narrative as the influential Maratha intermediary through whom Rohilla hopes to send his representatives and open a back channel that can defuse Jawahar Mal's anger without forcing a public collapse. Money and persuasion become his chosen tools. pages.searchText: Jawahar Mal Rejects a Cash Settlement and Demands Honor Ahmed Shah Ata Rohilla Episode 158 opens by showing that negotiation alone cannot satisfy Jawahar Mal. Jawahar Mal did not agree to a simple monetary settlement because he is determined to never barter his family's reputation after the murder that had dishonored his house. His position is framed in terms of lineage, vengeance, and public memory. Since he has already spent heavily on the campaign and risked his standing before allies, he will not accept a compromise that looks like a purchased silence rather than justice. The page therefore sets up the symbolic terms of settlement that follow on the next readable page. pages.searchText: Abdali Reorders Sirhind and Misjudges the Khalsa Ahmed Shah Ata Rohilla The page continues Abdali's redistribution of power after the Delhi settlement. Must he turn out the Singhs from Punjab is the governing demand placed upon his dependents, for then alone would he be able to collect revenues and restore Afghan authority in the region. To support that program, did Abdali invite Amar Singh and draw him into the circle of reward and obligation. He conferred the title of a Raja in hopes that local authority, prestige, and Sirhind's administration could be used to steady the frontier against Sikh pressure. Yet the narrative undercuts Abdali's confidence. pages.searchText: Abdali's Running Retreat Grows Desperate Ahmed Shah Ata Rohilla The retreat hardens into a running battle in which Afghan tactics fail to restore control. Many a strategy did the Pathan soldiers adopt, but armored men and horses alike are broken by the Singh's mighty swords as the Khalsa keeps closing the distance. The page stresses how precarious Abdali's situation becomes. Impossible indeed it became for them to reach Kabul in peace, because every march segment invites another Sikh strike and every delay deepens the appearance of imperial weakness. In response Abdali looks for reinforcement and coordination. Thereafter, he rushed sufficient troops in the rearguard, As he was already expecting an attack from the Singhs, The (younger) Singhs launched a massive attack on his troops, As both the combatants opened a volley of fire on each other, Much Bloodshed and loss of life took place on both the sides. As the Khalsa Panth chiefs noticed the younger Singhs being beaten, The Misl chiefs rushed to block the advance of the Pathans. (36) As Abdali's troops were crossing the river Ravi, The (wise) Misl chiefs did not attack his troops. But as the hot headed younger Singhs could not restrain themselves, They had to retreat unceremoniously after being thrashed. (37) Ahmad Shah Abdali had already made preparations, As he had anticipated the Khalsa attack on his troops. So the short-ranged guns and the camel loaded guns that he had, He ordered these guns to be taken across first of all. (38) Thereafter, he made members of his entourage cross the river, Providing them with a strong defence after a good planning. Thereafter, he rushed sufficient troops in the rearguard, Strongly did they rush much like a river in flood. (39) As he was already expecting an attack from the Singhs, The (younger) Singhs launched a massive attack on his troops, As both the combatants opened a volley of fire on each other, Much Bloodshed and loss of life took place on both the sides. (40) As the main Misl chiefs had not invaded Abdali's troops, The Pathans repulsed the younger Singhs and pushed them back. As the Khalsa Panth chiefs noticed the younger Singhs being beaten, The Misl chiefs rushed to block the advance of the Pathans. (41) Thereafter, the Gilja Pathans managed to cross the river, They were too keen to find an escape from the Singhs. Thereafter, vacating the whole territory around Lahore, Hastily did they march in the direction of Multan. (42) 677

pages.searchText: Abdali Dies in Regret and the Khalsa Reclaims Punjab Ahmed Shah Ata Rohilla This damaged closing page completes the Abdali retreat with a note of humiliation rather than triumph. The invader's remorse deepens into an admission that God had supported the Singhs, and that the very campaign meant to discipline Punjab instead exposed the limits of imperial force. The narrative pushes that reversal to its personal end. Abdali is shown traveling back in grief, warning that any descendant who returned in the same spirit would meet the same regret, and then falling short of his destination to die short of Kabul. With that, the author hands the moral victory to the Panth. The Khalsa Panth occupy the territory that had been their native country from the beginning, so the episode closes not with Afghan consolidation but with Sikh endurance and recovery. 680 suet chaupaî: aug dôhrâ suet chaupaî: Sri Gur Panth Prakash o qué. mg ymd (Hst sis f35 nae SorÍE, gd noel ofo sou afte) 159. aur parsang (sabhî bhânt tin mugal jhuthâi, duhin jahanin nahin rahyô thai) : ad gsô ffu Hdl cuss | ad Gsusì ffws cars | ores mHE aur ufos ate | THU së aur fue wrfe 191 kahî ratan singh mari kaptân. kar utpattî singhan dhayân. nâdar ahmad kaya pahilô thai. singh bhag kaya pichchhai âi.1. adt Hae A festa | edt set o nid set WS | Aur Id wane vate ô Fa | sur Sa sored AA S 390 12 | kahi mugal jô dillîvâl. vahi bhai kai aur bhai chal. kaya gur arjan daryâi na bôryô. kaya teg bahâdar sis na tôryô.2. am Wf o age wd | eR Tea a HÌd ud 5 HrƏ | ur gJa ud ô HagHd WE | sfg Cod aa dau HF 131 kaya sahibzadg¢ na kuhâc charg. bidôshô balak kaya shir khórç na mars. kaya turak parc na mukatsar jai. nahin unkô kuchh rôkyô thai.3. It then traces the line through Mali, a Sandhu Jat at village Narla, and explains how the young Shyam Singh came under the influence of Mastan Singh and the Khalsa discipline around him. Those Singhs who travelled from the Majha region were received as honored guests, and Never would a Singh eat alone while companions or travelers remained to be served. From that ethic of hospitality the narrative moves into wider political change. After the divisions of the Panth and the rise of Kapoor Singh, the circle around Shyam Singh expands into a stronger armed following with noted chiefs, retainers, and a growing mounted force. The page therefore marks a transition from household virtue to institutional power. pages.searchText: Baghel Singh Marches On and Warnings Are Ignored S. Sham Singhs Misi Baghel Singh dismisses fearful calculations with a soldier's realism. Nobody vacated an occupied territory without a fight, he argues, so recovery can come only by marching forward and accepting battle rather than by wishful negotiation. The confrontation accordingly becomes unavoidable. Baghel Singh orders his force to march towards Patiala, while Amar Singh reacts in anger and presses his advisers toward immediate action. One voice still counsels caution, warning that the Singhs should not be treated lightly, yet hawkish chiefs brush such advice aside. The page ends with pride overpowering prudence and the clash drawing visibly nearer. 696 aug dôhrâ suet chaupaî: gdr dôhrâ gut chaupaî: Sri Gur Panth Prakash: HBA 9 fore feo 3 fea SK gs | fao 53 Hees faH SA H&o eae 189 | mulak mçrô hai nikat in tau ih lchi chhudaâi. bina lardg malvaîîan kim lîjai mulak chhudaâi.47.: gue ffu GA YA ad JU | Hŵo Sd [Ho fas ES UU | SH 39 VHS HS AG TS | OH me faa cue aud ist! baghçl singh us hass kar kahyô. mulak lard¢ bin kin chhada dayô. tum daar rakhat mat jay6 har. main ân bhirdâân dakkhan kandhâr.48. 25 UWS uu 39 ggg FISTS | Ho TH fes oU au ree | He Fords JAH ad ea | Hrg Mus afa us Š mG 191 vall patyâlc dayô dacrô turat turvâi. sun rajai dil karôdh bhayó âi. sadd sarkârîan hukam kar dayô. mar singhan kadahi ghérdg lai ayô.49. pages.searchText: Dulcha Singh Urges Delay While Others Boast of Easy Victory S. Sham Singhs Misi This page contrasts empty bravado with sober military judgment. Those who had never seen the Singhs fighting a battle talk loosely of loot, horses, and easy fame, as though the Majhail veterans before them were an ordinary enemy. On the Khalsa side, however, the scale of the Malwa preparations causes unease, and practical men begin sending valuables away before the fighting closes in. Dulcha Singh argues that Now he must keep patience for five ten days, holding position and thinking carefully rather than letting pride force a rash move. The page therefore prepares the larger confrontation by showing two mentalities at once. With what face would they retreat at that stage, he asks, if the Malwa forces pursued them and turned their misl into an object of ridicule within the Panth. The decision is then formalized in martial order. Chiefs assemble, the whole Khalsa Panth Misl agreed to obey the battle plan, commanders are assigned to their fronts, and standards and drums signal that hesitation has ended. By the close of the page the Khalsa has moved from debate to motion. pages.searchText: Dust, Noise, and the Opening Clash at Patiala S. Sham Singhs Misi The battle begins in sensory confusion and violent momentum. The sun seemed to have been eclipsed by the rising dust, while drums, musketry, and shouted commands spread panic around Patiala before either side could claim a clear advantage. Amar Singh tries to convert his numerical confidence into a decisive charge, urging his troops to kill the Singhs and seize their horses. Yet once the lines close, the Khalsa steadies itself under fire and answers with disciplined shooting that checks repeated advances. The page presents the first great testing of appearance against reality. What looked like an overwhelming host is forced to meet veteran resistance at close quarters, and the promise of a quick victory begins to fray. 702 tug dôhrâ gut chaupaî: gdr dôhrâ gut chaupaî: gdr dôhrâ Sri Gur Panth Prakash aH dard uct und | forse ucurë ug us TG Hd | UT Sas Bet MG mA | su Te HY HuH E'EÌ 1981 baj¢ nagârc pai ghamghôr. girad patyâlç bahu pard gayô shór. châr taraph bhai 46 a7. bhayô garad main sûraj chhâî.74.: gw tat ade cë Sug Ho HOS | Š age fiat Ags adi BS ma Vw | DU râjc d¢khi garad dal uppar baith mahall. dai bárúd sikkô sabhan kahi lardô ab chall.75.: OH gards wa goH | HrƏ Mus fed us ue | fed TH age UE | U afo 3m fss fes surfe 12] râjc sarkârîan dayô phurmâî. mârô singhan dihô ghôrdg layâî. lihô dushâlc kangan pai. yau kahi bhçjç tin dil vadhâi.76.: US 3 do Ud ad MAS HJdÌ sri=rf= | Sat Ud s= dÎH gm fT MUS HS ugrfe 1221 dal tai chaugun ghôr kar asbî shutrî bajvâi. udaî dhâr rav gumm gayô nahin Apan sujhai parâi.77.: SH OH TH HH SU | gS SO JS JH H adu | THA Gw mfa MAS act | ma Ga ew us aut 12C dçkh phauj râjô khush bhayô. bakîl jhúth hut ham sôn kahyô. hamrî phauj ahi ati bhârî. ab liôgu dal singhan kai mârî.78. pages.snippet: Amar Singh next widens the contest by sending allied contingents against the Khalsa flanks and rear. Sudhrai's men are told to strike from behind, but S. Dulcha Singh's contingent rushed to block their passage while Baghel Singh shifts support where the line i
pages.searchText: Patiala’s Counterstrokes Fail on Both Fronts S. Sham Singhs Misi Amar Singh next widens the contest by sending allied contingents against the Khalsa flanks and rear. Sudhrai's men are told to strike from behind, but S. Dulcha Singh's contingent rushed to block their passage while Baghel Singh shifts support where the line is under greatest pressure. The fighting becomes a prolonged trial of nerve. Whosoever blinked and thought of retracing his steps first would yield the field, yet the Khalsa holds while the opposition begins to break under sustained attack. By the end of the page, Malwa forces got uprooted on both the battle fronts despite the deployment of additional Rohilla and hill infantry. The attempted counterstroke only confirms that Baghel Singh's side now owns the momentum of the battle. 704 suet chaupaî: dug dôhrâ suet chaupaî: tug dôhrâ gut chaupaî: Sri Gur Panth Prakash: Heats uot an urfg | «Ju 8 Ho SAY ure AE | AG Gw ud add ust | SH meet Sr ved [HU wet tS | su durâi pathânî phaujai pâhi. pages.searchText: Chain Singh Argues That the Panth Cannot Be Divided S. Sham Singhs Misi The defeated side tries to explain away the reverse and imagine new combinations of power, but Chain Singh answers with political clarity rather than anger. Both Majhail and Malwai Singhs constituted a Singh fraternity, he insists, so no ruler will prosper by setting one section of the Panth against another. He recommends negotiation through the full repertoire of statecraft rather than renewed adventurism. The familiar logic of Saam, Daam, Dand and Bhaid is invoked not to sanction treachery, but to restore balance after pride has already failed. From this counsel comes a practical settlement. Baghel Singh and physically stops him from riding away in anger. He is brought back into Amar Singh's presence so that defeat can be transformed into a renewed bond rather than an enduring feud. The reconciliation is marked through gifts, esteem, and kin-like language. pages.searchText: A Brahmin Appeals to the Khalsa Against a Tyrant Sayyad S. Sham Singhs Misi A new narrative opens by praising the Khalsa as a power that can act where courts and governors refuse justice. The aggrieved father explains that There is a town known as Luhari Jalalabad near Delhi, where a tyrannical Sayyad has abducted his daughter and terrorized the surrounding people. The page frames his appeal as a test of Khalsa responsibility toward the weak. No official will confront the offender, so the Brahmin comes to the Sikh camp convinced that the Panth alone still acts in the cause of protection and benefaction. Warnings immediately arise about distance, danger, and the Sayyad's influence near Delhi, yet the moral pressure of the plea is stronger than caution. pages.searchText: The Khalsa Crosses the Rivers to Fight for the Brahmin Khalsa Panth The Khalsa accepts the appeal and pushes eastward despite the risks of operating near Delhi's orbit. After crossing the Satluj they camp near the bank of the river Yamuna, and news of their approach sends the local Muslim authorities into hurried defensive preparation. The advance then becomes personal and symbolic at once. With the (aggrieved) Brahmin leading them from the front, the Singhs cross onward, raise their standards, and pray that they may win martyrdom while carrying out an act of welfare for others. Their charge immediately shakes the defenders. pages.searchText: The Hidden Sayyad and His Accomplice Are Punished Khalsa Panth Once the Khalsa breaks into the place, fighting continues through houses, lanes, and secret refuges. The Singhs search room by room and descend even to the underground cellar where the abductor has attempted to hide from the reckoning he thought would never reach him. The Brahmin's daughter identifies the culprit, and the Singhs drag him from concealment to face exemplary punishment. The same investigation exposes the local wine-seller who had served as facilitator and procurer in the search for girls. Justice on the page is therefore both personal and public. The rescued Brahmin girl is questioned with care, acknowledged as a victim of coercion rather than disgrace, and publicly embraced as the daughter of the Khalsa Panth. That declaration immediately creates social obligation. The Singhs resolve to unite her with her in-laws, send messengers to her in-laws, and begin organizing communal support so that her return will be marked by dignity rather than stigma. The page is therefore as important for social repair as for martial justice. pages.searchText: Now listen to the plight of that unfortunate girl, Khalsa Panth Now listen to the plight of that unfortunate girl, Who was the daughter of that supplicant Brahmin. Khalsa Panth called her to their presence, Must she really narrate her tale of woe. (26) What kind of life did she intend to lead in future? She narrated she was helpless as she fell into a stranger's hands, Nor could she end her life to save her honour. (27) She had to share the Sayyad's bed under duress, For which he had been punished by the Khalsa Panth. Thereafter, declaring her a daughter of the Khalsa Panth, The Khalsa Panth resolved to unite her with her in-laws. (28) Thereafter, the Khalsa Panth summoned the Brahmin girl's father, Must he tell them the address of his daughter's in-laws. Thereafter, the Khalsa Panth sent messengers to her in-laws, That soon would the Khalsa Panth approach their family. (29). Either her inlaws could fight it out with the Khalsa Panth, Or they could accept the Khalsa Panth's daughter into their family. As that Brahmin girl was daughter of the Khalsa Panth, Must they now accept her as their own daughter-in-law. (30) After despatching this message to her in-laws, The Khalsa Panth once again beat the war-drum. Thereafter, marching with a dash from there, They arrived at the village of her in-laws. (31) Thereafter, calling an assembly of the village elders, The Singhs narrated the whole sequence of events. The village elders agreed to what the Khalsa proposed, As all-caste delegation had accompanied the Brahmin. (32) As this all-inclusive assembly had resolved, Her in-laws family agreed to accept this girl. Thus, after uniting the two parental and in-laws families, They were given a farewell after serving them meals. (33) As the bridegroom and bride were united in wedlock, The Khalsa Panth thought of another bridal obligation. Asking for a bed-sheet to be spread on ground, They asked everyone to contribute towards the girl's dowry. Khalsa Panth called her to their presence, Must she really narrate her tale of woe. (26) Thereafter, Khalsa Panth asked that Brahmin's daughter, What kind of life did she intend to lead in future? This enraged the Muslims, who asked how they could live or pray without those mosques. Muslim leaders and clerics went together to the emperor, accusing him of impiety for allowing the demolition. The emperor replied that they should have objected earlier, because recanting would break trust with S. Baghel Singh and make the emperor false to his written promise. pages.searchText: An Old Water-Carrier Woman Identifies Sis Ganj Khalsa Panth Attention then turns to the most delicate of the Delhi sites. The seventh Sikh shrine Sis Ganj has become difficult to identify precisely because later construction obscured the original place of martyrdom. Resolution comes through living memory rather than royal paperwork alone. An old water-carrier woman identifies the place, Ram Dyal mediates the tension that follows, and even the surviving structure is negotiated down to one-fourth of Mosgue wall so the sacred location can be marked without igniting needless chaos. pages.searchText: There remained the seventh Sikh shrine Sis Ganj to be reclaimed, Khalsa Panth There remained the seventh Sikh shrine Sis Ganj to be reclaimed, This site being located in a very congested locality. With a well on one side and a mosque on the other, The site of sacred shrine became difficult to be traced. (80) However, there lived an old water-carrier woman, Her did the Singhs call, she being very wise. She remarked that she could locate the site, Where the Hindu Pir ( Guru Tegh Bahadur) had sat on a stool. As the Guru sat at that spot with a face towards the East, His head had rolled down face wards as the sword struck. (82) As many people came to witness the tragic scene, Her own father was filling his leather bucket with water. As the young Singhs rushed to demolish the mosgue wall soon after, There ensued a communal riot with the arrival of a mediator (Ram Dyal). Officials move to fix a meeting on S. Baghel Singh's terms, while promises of Great titles and honours are prepared to make the reception appear magnanimous rather than reluctant. The city is then carefully stage-managed for the day of entry. pages.searchText: Baghel Singh Enters the Emperor’s Court S. Baghel Singh I As Baghel Singh reached the great fort, the emperor sent a minister ahead to welcome him. Baghel Singh dismounted from his elephant, mounted his own favored horse, entered the fort confidently, and was guided to a suitable place to dismount. Dulcha Singh and Sadda Singh were among the chiefs Baghel Singh brought with him. Most of the force remained mounted, while only five to seven chiefs dismounted, fully armed, and moved fearlessly toward the emperor’s court. The emperor sat in court with Hindu and Muslim courtiers and told his Hindu ministers to greet the Singhs with the Khalsa greeting. Dulcha Singh briefed Ram Dyal on protocol, the Singh chiefs advanced with bows in hand, Baghel Singh answered with the Khalsa greeting, and the pleased emperor ordered a chair for him. 736 dôhrâ gut pages.searchText: The Sugarcane Raid Becomes a Courtly Spectacle S. Baghel Singh I The Singhs greet the order with delight and theatrical energy. At a beat on the war drum they arm themselves, rush out under observation from Delhi, and prepare to show a spectacle of looting and plundering that is half demonstration and half rough comedy. The performance is exuberant and physical. Riders and footmen plunged deep into the river Yamuna, burst into the sugarcane, and return laughing, pulling at beards and turbans of each other while carts, horses, and elephants become loaded with the pillaged sugarcane sticks. pages.searchText: The Delhi Spectacle Gives Way to the Deegh Campaign S. Baghel Singh I The closing motion of the Delhi episode lingers on imperial amazement at Sikh methods. The chronicler recalls gauhar ali patishah bhayo parsann dikh panth lut, using the emperor's pleasure at the staged plunder to underline how boldly the Khalsa could turn even mock disorder into political theater. From there the narrative pivots southward. Jab khalso dakkhan chalyo mislain daso bani, the confederate misls move against Suraj Mal, and the remembered line jai suraj mal gheriyo dik ghumarhi mahi announces the struggle around Deegh and Ghumer as the next collective undertaking. This damaged hinge page therefore does two jobs at once. Age khalse panth bahi sarabat lai divan, and when Suraj Mal comes forward sayam singh utth khaloyo, signaling both formal respect and the authority of the assembly. The tribute is then fixed and the conversation shifts from diplomacy to allocation. pages.searchText: The Ransom Is Apportioned Among the Misls Deegh, Ghumer And Bharatpur This page turns from the treaty itself to the internal arithmetic of the Khalsa commonwealth. Specific misls are named and weighed against one another, including the line tim sayam singh bhai phauj savai, as the chronicler records how claims of manpower and status shaped the division. The catalogue broadens into a fuller vision of the Sikh order. The ten misls are treated as a sacred-political formation, and the author culminates in the analogy timai panth gur giljai galvayo, linking the confederacy's ordering principle to its providential struggle against Afghan aggression. Editorially, the page elevates bookkeeping into political theology. Distribution among the misls becomes evidence that the Panth is both an army and a divinely ordered federation. 746 Sri Gur Panth Prakash f30 Hu sts HAS AH set | Hael? Thus, the whole amount was distributed among ten Misls, These ten Khalsa Misls resembled the Yadava* s organization. (19) Dohra: As there were ten Misls of the Yadav clan, So there were ten Misls in the Khalsa Panth. As Lord Krishna commanded the ten Yadav Misls, The tenth Sikh Guru directed the Khalsa Misls. As all the Muslim rulers were annihilated by the Khalsa, The Khalsa Panth shouted slogans of Guru's victory. (22)

pages.searchText: The Early Malwa Forest Settlements Are Introduced Deegh, Ghumer And Bharatpur A fresh section opens under Episode About the Malwa and shifts from confederate campaigning to regional ancestry. The author places the story in Malwa's forests, tracing the setting through the descendents of Mehraj and Phool and the older territorial frame around fifty two villages of Hisar Bawani. This is a scene of frontier formation rather than settled sovereignty. The land is wooded, politically layered, and only partially domesticated, which is why lineage, patronage, and Guru-given legitimacy matter so much in the pages that follow. The page functions as a regional prologue. pages.searchText: Bhai Behlo and Bhai Bhagtu Prepare the Ground the Malwa The genealogy begins by locating sanctified precedent before the rise of the Mehraj line. Bhai Behlo is remembered in direct relation to Guru Arjan Dev ji and the service economy around Taran Taaran, establishing a pattern in which devotion and labor lead to recognition. Alongside him stands Bhai Bhagtoo, whose authority in the forest tract becomes essential for later settlers. Only after this groundwork is laid does the narrative return to Mehraj's descendants, showing why they initially arrive too late and too weak to secure land on their own. pages.searchText: Mohan Appeals at Vaisakhi for Land and Shelter the Malwa The displaced Mehraj family finally seeks help through sacred assembly rather than wandering alone. At the Vaisakhi festival Mohan and Kala are brought before the Guru, turning a problem of survival into a petition framed within darbar and service. Mohan (from Mehraj's family) is presented not as a claimant by force but as a servant asking for a future. Kala offered his services to the Guru's community kitchen, and then the family openly asks for a piece of land for his clan's settlement. The response is prophetic rather than merely administrative. Bhai Bhagtu offered them shelter, and the episode balances the Guru's promise of future establishment with the ordinary necessity of present refuge. The page then widens into a darker political horizon. The chronicler introduces one emperor Chattarsal in the South, a ruler described as perpetually drunk and unstable, preparing the conflict that will soon descend upon the fragile settlers. pages.searchText: The Settlers Pray, Fight, and Overthrow Chattarsal the Malwa As danger closes in, the Mehraj people go first to Bhai Bhagtu rather than to worldly officials. The answer is stark and devotional: bhagatâ kahi ab ôt nahin aurai, meaning that no refuge remains except ardas and trust in the Guru. That prayer becomes the ground of collective resistance. New allies join the threatened settlers, the invader's army is met in battle, and the attacking force is broken badly enough that Chattarsal himself is isolated and killed. This is the true climax of the early Malwa arc. pages.searchText: Baba Mohan Goes to Delhi With Tribute and Anxiety Next Episode About the Malwa A new Malwa episode opens with political aftershocks from Chattarsal's death. Elders fear imperial retaliation, and the discussion turns toward appeasement, diplomacy, and the difficult question of how a vulnerable settlement can survive inside Mughal space. Baba Mohan therefore steps forward with a proposal stated plainly in the raw tradition: kahi môhan ham dillî javain. He prepares offerings, travels to court, and finds that even a clever presentation can expose him to new pressures once the queen notices what he has brought. The page is about courage under uncertainty rather than triumph. Mohan goes not as conqueror but as negotiator, carrying fear, tribute, and reliance on the Guru into the imperial center. 760 dôhrâ gut chaupaî: tug dôhrâ gut chaupaî: Sri Gur Panth Prakash mar lutt raje murdç pari sôch chit ân. pages.searchText: Malwa Settlements and Ala Singh’s Appeal the Phulkians As the sons of Rama and Tiloka grew up, their families expanded and they became eager for more territory. In Bikrami Samvat 1787 a drought and famine struck the forest tract, so Baba Phool’s grandsons consulted about settling a water-rich region. They founded Balyowal, Dhanaula, Bhadaur, Shehna, Adhiayo, and Barnala; in this way six villages were established by the six brothers, and Khalsa forces were invited to take possession of them. Episode 168 begins with the troubles of Malwa: whenever the Khalsa left, Mughal forces and the Malerkotla Pathans raided the region, demanded impossible ransom, and threatened Hindu residents. pages.searchText: Bhai Buddha Singh Brings the Khalsa Near the Battlefield Malwa The Khalsa now advances under Bhai Buddha Singh with deliberate caution. He refuses to rush blindly toward the enemy, warning that they must not put up a camp in close vicinity lest the Pathans scatter or prepare too well for the attack. Meanwhile Ala Singh holds out under strain, counting on the promised arrival and trying to steady his own following until help appears. By dawn the Khalsa has maneuvered close enough to judge the field properly and the impending clash becomes unavoidable. The page is about disciplined preparation rather than battlefield spectacle. pages.searchText: The Khalsa emblems did the Singhs unfurl, Malwa The Khalsa emblems did the Singhs unfurl, Many a time did they beat their wardrums. Pulling at the reins of their war horses, With slogans of war did they launch an attack. (24) As the Khalsa force advanced with the beat of drums, A cloud of dust did the Mughals spot rising. Biru Singh, a striking example of social mobility and military distinction inside the Khalsa. He commands thirteen hundred mounted Singhs, wins Ala Singh's esteem, and receives from him the first gift of a horse in recognition of his battlefield standing. For a time he drifts toward the Mughals, who try to turn his separation into a taunt against the Panth itself. But the Khalsa's rebuke cuts through that experiment immediately, and instantly did he return to the Panth with submission and offering. There existed a hospice in the west, and There used to sit S. Sham Singh in this hospice as a major Budha Dal commander whose authority reached across the city and the wider Panth. The page then gathers the material signs of his standing. Forts, village grants, and the distribution of bungas are all associated with his name, while the later memory of the site remains strong enough that the composition of Gur Panth Prakash is linked back to his fallen establishment. This is both memorial and institutional history. pages.searchText: Gur Panth Prakash Closes With Devotional Assurance The closing fragment turns directly toward the reader and listener. Its promise is devotional rather than political: jô kôî yâkô pardhaigô ar pun sunai ju k6i, and sari satigur ki karipâ tc sikhî parâpat hôi, meaning that this account is meant to strengthen Sikh commitment through grace.
